items.keywords: We Know the W's 2027 WNBA free agency forecast: the players most likely to stay, move or hit a true toss-up, with an interactive movement dashboard. We Know the W home Kelsey Mitchell headshot Indiana Fever logo Napheesa Collier headshot Minnesota Lynx logo Kelsey Plum headshot Phoenix Mercury logo Jackie Young headshot Las Vegas Aces logo Napheesa Collier Minnesota Lynx logo Kelsey Mitchell Indiana Fever logo Kelsey Plum Phoenix Mercury logo Jackie Young Las Vegas Aces logo 2027 WNBA Free Agency Movement Board | We Know the W Skip to the movement board FOOD FOR THOUGHT · FREE AGENCY LAB · UPDATED OCT. 23, 2026 2027 free agency could move the balance of the W. This is not a transaction report. It is a living We Know the W forecast of who looks most likely to stay, who has a real reason to leave, and which teams should already be nervous. Open the movement board Where could they go? See every current-team free agent 2027 market UFA + RFA tracked WKTW editorial odds KELSEY MITCHELL MOVE WATCH NAPHEESA COLLIER LEAN STAY KELSEY PLUM TOSS-UP JACKIE YOUNG LIKELY STAY THE BIG IDEA Money matters. Choice matters more. The most important names in this class are not all chasing the same thing. Some have championship continuity. Some can finally choose their environment. Some are staring at smaller roles than their talent suggests. That is why the same dollar figure can mean very different things to different players. DYNAMIC MOVEMENT DASHBOARD Who is most likely to change teams? Sort the board by movement odds, star power or current team. The percentage is a We Know the W editorial forecast, not a reported probability or betting market. LIVING BOARD · OCT. 6 Show All headliners Move watch Toss-ups Likely stay Rank by Movement odds Star power Current team How the forecast works Movement odds weigh roster role, team trajectory, unrestricted vs. restricted status, recent team changes, contender fit, expected market demand and how much leverage the player appears to have. They are deliberately easy to update as the offseason changes. IF SHE LEAVES: DESTINATION DASHBOARD Okay, but where would she actually go? Pick a headliner to see the five alternative teams that make the most basketball sense right now. The destination share is conditional: it answers where we think she could land only if she leaves her current team . The five modeled alternatives add to 100% and are editorial estimates, not reported negotiations. FIT BOARD · UPDATED OCT. 23 TOP ALTERNATIVE LANDING SPOTS Loading destinations… destination share WKTW fit score LEAGUE HOT ZONES Which teams show up most often as plausible star destinations? This is a WKTW Market Pull Index built from the destination board above. It rewards teams that repeatedly grade as strong fits for multiple important free agents; it is not cap-room ranking or evidence that those teams are recruiting anyone. Why Golden State and Washington keep appearing Golden State finished 32-12 with the league's best opponent scoring mark but ranked 14th in scoring and 13th in assists, making another elite creator an obvious basketball fit. Washington went 28-16 with the No. 2 opponent scoring mark, while ranking 12th in scoring and 11th in assists; adding a veteran shot-creator or organizer next to its young core would attack the clearest offensive weakness. Seattle's 8-36 finish and bottom-tier scoring/playmaking numbers make it a very different pitch: less instant title equity, more opportunity to become the veteran offensive anchor of a rebuild. THE FOUR DOMINOES The stars who can redraw the map. LEAN STAY Napheesa Collier Minnesota still offers an elite basketball situation and a familiar home base. The difference in 2027 is leverage: Collier can listen to everybody before deciding whether home is still the best basketball answer. MOVE WATCH Kelsey Mitchell Indiana still has Caitlin Clark, Aliyah Boston, a strong stage and a chance to reset under new leadership. But the confirmed president departure and The Athletic’s report about Amber Cox add uncertainty before free agency. Mitchell has said she must put her own needs first. The new basketball lead will need to make her role and the title plan convincing. TRUE TOSS-UP Kelsey Plum Phoenix invested to get the first recruiting window, but the roster still has to prove the fit is worth extending. Plum has already shown she will make the decision that works for her, not for the neatest storyline. LIKELY STAY Jackie Young Other contenders should call because they have to. Vegas still has the cleanest pitch: role clarity, title equity and A'ja Wilson. A departure would be one of the biggest surprises of the market. FULL CURRENT-TEAM BOARD Every tracked UFA and RFA, one searchable board. Use this for the full stay/move picture. Restricted players lean toward staying because their incumbent team can retain matching rights after a qualifying offer. Find a player or team Status All calls Move watch Toss-up Lean/likely stay Retirement watch Free agent type UFA + RFA UFA RFA Return-to-W watch: unrestricted players without an incumbent team Kayla Alexander · Lexie Brown · Chennedy Carter · Sha Carter · Mariella Fasoula · Dulcy Fankam Mendjiadeu · Nadia Fingall · Alex Fowler · Aubrey Griffin · Emese Hof · Joyner Holmes · Eliška Joklová · Teaira McCowan · Nikolina Milić · Shey Peddy · Alissa Pili · Tima Pouye · JJ Quinerly · Kamiah Smalls · Sug Sutton · Julie Vanloo · Kiana Williams · Peyton Williams · Alex Wilson · Laura Ziegler. 01 FOOD FOR THOUGHT Kelsey Mitchell is the pressure point. If Mitchell stays, Indiana keeps one of the league’s most dangerous backcourts together. If she leaves, the guard market loses no star, but the Fever lose their leading scorer and a major piece beside Clark. That decision could set the pace for Indiana’s offseason. What changed: The Fever now face an official president departure and a reported GM exit before free agency. A new leader could give Mitchell a fresh reason to stay, but there is no successor or 2027 plan to evaluate yet. We keep our slight lean toward a move, with low confidence. items.title: 2027 WNBA Mock Draft: Toronto or Houston for JuJu Watkins?
items.keywords: The updated We Know the W 2027 mock draft starts with Toronto and Houston tied for the best official lottery odds, with JuJu Watkins still No. 1 and Zhang Ziyu at No. 12. JuJu Watkins Toronto Tempo logo USC logo Toronto Tempo logo Houston Comets logo Zhang Ziyu playing for China 2027 WNBA Mock Draft: Toronto or Houston for JuJu Watkins? | We Know the W Skip to the mock draft board WHO GOT NEXT? · 2027 DRAFT WATCH · UPDATED OCTOBER 30, 2026 Toronto or Houston? DRAFT LOTTERY · NOVEMBER 15 · ESPN Counting down to 7:30 p.m. Eastern on ESPN. The regular season ended in a dead heat. Toronto and Houston share the best official shot at No. 1, Toronto is listed first for now, and JuJu Watkins remains the prospect at the top of the board. By Shak · Shakeema Funchess Edition 02 15 first-round picks Final 2026 order · lottery pending PROVISIONAL PICK 01 JW TORONTO TEMPO SELECT · PROVISIONAL JuJu Watkins USC · 6'2" guard THE DIRECT ANSWER The player is JuJu. The team is unsettled. Watkins is still the class’s cleanest combination of star creation, size, foul pressure and defensive playmaking. Her last full season produced 23.9 points, 6.8 rebounds, 3.4 assists, 2.2 steals and 1.8 blocks per game . After returning to competition on October 25, she remains the top projection if she enters the draft; either Toronto or Houston should turn in the card at No. 1. PROJECTION CONFIDENCE Player: High Team: Dead heat Toronto and Houston each carry an official 32.9% chance at No. 1. Confirmed by the WNBA on October 28. The lottery has not happened. EDITION 02 · THE UPDATE Final night changed the card. The prospect order stays intact. The team assignments moved, and one international center forced her way into Round 1. Health update · South Carolina returns No. 10 Ashlyn Watkins: returned to competition October 23 in the Benedict exhibition, recording eight points and 10 rebounds in 16 minutes. No. 14 Chloe Kitts: returned in the same exhibition and started for South Carolina after missing last season with an ACL injury. Both rankings remain unchanged. Exhibition availability is a useful checkpoint; sustained minutes, movement and regular-season performance remain the next evaluation priorities. Exhibition report and Watkins statistics · Kitts return and starting lineup Returned to competition · October 25, 2026 JuJu Watkins recorded 18 points, three rebounds, three steals and two blocks in 23 minutes in USC’s 78–76 exhibition win over Cal. It was her first competition in 580 days. This exhibition provides new evaluation evidence, not proof of complete recovery or a draft declaration. She remains No. 1 on this board, with her 2027 decision pending. TOP PICK RACE TORONTO 32.9% TIED HOUSTON 32.9% The WNBA confirms 329 of 1,000 combinations each for Houston and Toronto. If neither wins a drawn pick, Houston precedes Toronto: Houston can fall to No. 3, Toronto to No. 4. WORLD CUP RISER · PICK 12 Zhang Ziyu is on the board. The 7-foot-3 Chinese center put up 13 points, six rebounds and two blocks against Team USA on September 4. She turns 20 in 2027, meeting the WNBA’s published age requirement for international draftees. Scout next: mobility, conditioning, screening and defensive coverages. DRAFT WATCH · OCTOBER 16, 2026 Eligible is not the same as declared. The numbered mock and pick ownership remain unchanged. College return options and new scouting opinions add uncertainty, not confirmed withdrawals. 2027 decision pending The NCAA transition lets current athletes with eligibility remaining after 2025–26 use the more beneficial framework. School compliance reviews still determine individual eligibility. The IX flags JuJu Watkins, Madison Booker, Hannah Hidalgo, Mikaylah Williams, Tessa Johnson, MiLaysia Fulwiley, Kymora Johnson, S’Mya Nichols, Clara Strack and KK Arnold as having a college return option beyond 2026–27. WNBA eligibility: a route to entering the draft. Expected declaration: an editorial projection, not a player announcement. A return option does not mean a player has chosen to stay. The scouting watch Tessa Johnson and Kymora Johnson: riser watch after The IX ranked them fifth and eighth. Ashlyn Watkins: lottery watch, with recovery and skill translation still central. Zhang Ziyu: high-variance international evaluation. Her No. 12 projection stays, while her omission from The IX board illustrates disagreement. One board is not a consensus shift. The IX board was published October 10 and updated October 13. These are attributed scouting signals, not revised We Know the W pick numbers. NCAA eligibility framework · The IX scouting board and return-option notes · WNBA draft eligibility Lottery: November 15, 2026 7:30–8 p.m. ET · ESPN. Draft: Monday, April 12, 2027. Official WNBA announcement → THE LOTTERY PICTURE Toronto and Houston share pole position. This is the final 2026 regular-season order with the lottery still pending. This editorial mock keeps Toronto provisionally first, and Houston inherits Connecticut’s lottery rights. Picks 1 and 2 will be drawn, so the top of the board can still flip. Official odds · October 28, 2026 The WNBA confirms Houston 32.9%, Toronto 32.9%, Washington via Chicago 16.1%, Seattle 9.3%, Portland 5.2%, Los Angeles 2.4% and Los Angeles via Phoenix 1.2%. Official WNBA odds, announced October 28. Only picks 1 and 2 are drawn; Houston precedes Toronto if neither wins a drawn pick. Seven lottery picks, six selecting teams Los Angeles owns two chances: its own pick and Phoenix’s. Washington owns Chicago’s pick outright, not a swap. Chicago traded it for Ariel Atkins on February 23, 2025. Phoenix sent its pick and Monique Akoa Makani to Los Angeles for Kelsey Plum on August 2, 2026. How the official odds work Houston (formerly Connecticut), Chicago, Seattle, Los Angeles and Phoenix use combined 2025–26 records. Expansion teams Toronto and Portland use 2026 only. Houston and Toronto both finished at .250; Houston’s 1–2 head-to-head record gives it the fallback tiebreaker. Only Nos. 1 and 2 are drawn. The remaining picks follow the applicable records. Houston cannot fall below No. 3; Toronto cannot fall below No. 4. Verified against the October 28 WNBA announcement on October 29. The mock’s Toronto-first projection is an editorial placeholder, not the official lottery seeding. WE KNOW THE W BIG BOARD · ROUND 1 Fifteen picks. A new destination map. Filter by role or search a player, program or WNBA team. The prospect rankings stay fixed; Edition 02 updates every team assignment affected by the final standings and adds Zhang Ziyu at No. 12. EDITION 02 · SEP. 26 Find a player All Guards Wings Posts SHAK’S TAKE The top player is clear. The landing spot is not. This is the final regular-season order, not the final draft order. The lottery and the 2026-27 season still have plenty to say. Why the first line is still provisional Toronto and Houston reached the end of the regular season in the same place: a .250 cumulative winning percentage and an official 32.9% shot at the first pick. Toronto remains this mock’s editorial placeholder at No. 1. The official fallback order places Houston ahead of Toronto if neither wins a drawn pick. Watkins is the player who changes the scale of either build. She has already shown the hard part: creating quality offense when everybody in the building knows she has to create it. At 6'2", she can see and shoot over smaller guards, punish switches, draw fouls and produce defensive events away from the ball. The health check matters after her ACL injury, but the upside remains No. 1. Houston still gets a franchise guard Hannah Hidalgo owns the loudest two-way résumé after Watkins. Her pressure defense can change possession after possession, and 25.3 points with 5.2 assists shows she is much more than a disruptor. If Houston lands second, she gives the returning Comets an identity on day one. S’Mya Nichols, MiLaysia Fulwiley and Mikaylah Williams make the next tier guard-heavy. Nichols brings size and playmaking, Fulwiley brings burst and defensive chaos, and Williams brings polished shot creation. Clara Strack is the first interior anchor on this board because 6'5" size, double-digit rebounding and 2.5 blocks travel. Why Zhang entered at No. 12 One game does not make a finished prospect, but Zhang’s World Cup debut answered a better question: can her size and touch hold up against WNBA-level strength? Thirteen points, six rebounds and two blocks against Team USA were enough to move her into this first round. The next test is defending away from the rim and staying effective when opponents make her move possession after possession. What could blow up this board The lottery is the obvious answer, but it is not the only one. Watkins has returned to competition; sustained health and performance remain evaluation priorities. Prospects have to enter. New roles and transfers can change usage. International players can rise quickly once front offices get complete medicals and live evaluations. And team fit will look different after another offseason of trades and free agency. So save the screenshot, not the certainty. The value of an early mock is seeing the assumptions before the games start changing them. HOW THIS BOARD WAS BUILT Production, translation and roster need. Current order Final 2026 regular-season records plus published pick ownership, with Toronto provisionally first. Prospect rank Recent production, physical tools, role difficulty and WNBA skill translation. Team fit What the selecting team would be buying, not a claim that its current roster is final. Uncertainty Lottery results, eligibility, health and 2026-27 performance remain open. items.keywords: Meet Shakeema Funchess, creator of We Know the W. Our mission, independent editorial philosophy, and contact information. Shakeema Funchess, creator of We Know the W, smiling in colorful glasses and a patterned shirt About We Know the W | Shakeema Funchess THE STORY BEHIND THE SITE ABOUT WE KNOW THE W The numbers. The history. The people who make the game matter. MEET THE CREATOR I’m Shakeema Funchess. You can call me Shak. I’m an author, educator, creative learning facilitator, and doctoral student in education with a focus on social-emotional learning. Through Adventures in Zen, my work centers representation, belonging, and making room for people to see themselves in a story. We Know the W brings that same attention to women’s basketball. I built this space to connect the parts of the game that too often live in separate places: a player’s numbers, her team’s history, the culture around the court, and the life she is building beyond basketball. I wanted a place where following a question could become a whole afternoon of discovery. Start with a box score, meet a player, trace a franchise, learn a play, and find the women who made today’s game possible. That curiosity is the heart of We Know the W. Shakeema “Shak” Funchess · Creator OUR MISSION Make the W easier to explore. Give its stories room to grow. Bring statistics, history, analysis, and culture together in an accessible, connected home for women’s basketball. Meet the players → WHO THIS SPACE SERVES There’s room for you here. We Know the W is for longtime fans, first-time viewers, students, educators, writers, and curious people who want to understand more than the final score. You do not need to know every roster or remember every championship to belong here. Bring your questions. The basketball vocabulary can come with time. From Live Stats and The Stat Kitchen to The W Vault , The Film Room , and Herstory , the goal is to make research feel connected and learning feel inviting. EDITORIAL PHILOSOPHY Bring receipts. Keep the humanity. Facts deserve a source. Our standard is to ground factual coverage in identifiable sources, prioritize primary records where available, and distinguish confirmed information from reports or uncertainty. Automated feeds can lag or conflict. Missing data should not be presented as zero. Opinion should own its perspective. Rankings, grades, Starting Five selections, Bench Mob rotations, and Snack Shak commentary reflect this site’s editorial judgment. They are not official league awards. Evaluations should explain their criteria and distinguish career achievement from a single season. Players are people. We aim to discuss performance honestly without reducing athletes to a stat line, a rumor, or a stereotype. Identity, community, education, and life beyond the court deserve thoughtful coverage alongside basketball. History belongs in the conversation. Current stars do not exist in a vacuum. We connect today’s game to retired players, earlier teams, and the women who expanded what professional basketball could be. Comparisons across eras should acknowledge differences in opportunity and context. Corrections make the work stronger. Readers can flag inaccurate statistics, broken links, missing images, accessibility barriers, or other problems by emailing books@adventuresinzen.com . Reports are reviewed against available evidence; substantive editorial corrections should be clearly identified in the affected story. Credit and transparency matter. Sources and image credits belong with the work they support. Any sponsored coverage should be labeled, and any AI-generated illustration should be identified as such. Illustrations must not be presented as documentary photographs of real events. INDEPENDENT BY DESIGN A fan-created publication with its own voice. We Know the W is an independent website created by Shakeema Funchess. It is not affiliated with, sponsored by, or endorsed by the WNBA, the NBA, their teams, players, or other leagues covered here. League and team names, logos, trademarks, photographs, and other third-party materials belong to their respective owners. Their appearance identifies the subjects of coverage and does not imply endorsement. For credit or rights concerns, please contact us. LET’S CONNECT Questions, corrections, or a story worth telling? Shakeema Funchess · Creator, We Know the W books@adventuresinzen.com www.weknowthew.com For site errors, factual corrections, feedback, general inquiries, or credit concerns, email books@adventuresinzen.com directly.

items.title: The Race Is Real. The Trophy Is A’ja’s to Lose. | Food for Thought
items.keywords: Food for Thought: the 2026 WNBA MVP race, a dynamic five-candidate case board, and why A’ja Wilson enters the final week with the strongest two-way MVP argument. We Know the W home Official WNBA headshot of Las Vegas Aces center A’ja Wilson The Race Is Real. The Trophy Is A’ja’s to Lose. | Food for Thought FOOD FOR THOUGHT · 2026 MVP RACE · PLAYOFF UPDATE · OCTOBER 3 THE RACE IS REAL. THE TROPHY IS A’JA’S TO LOSE. The regular-season MVP argument built the case. The playoffs are adding the exclamation point. Wilson answered a deciding Game 3 with 36 points, 10 rebounds and 2 blocks, sending Las Vegas back to the semifinals. Open the case board Read the argument PLAYOFF UPDATE · LAS VEGAS ADVANCES 2–1 · GOLDEN STATE NEXT A’ja Wilson enters the final week leading the league in scoring average and blocks while anchoring a top-three Aces team. SCORING 26.1 PPG RIM PROTECTION 2.0 BPG REBOUNDING 9.4 RPG ON/OFF NET SWING +26.3 PIE 21.3 DASHBOARD · THE FIVE-PLAYER MVP BOARD Five résumés. Five different definitions of value. The official WNBA MVP check-in on September 17 listed Wilson, Olivia Miles and Kelsey Mitchell as its top three. The board expands to five using the current BetMGM market order, where Caitlin Clark and Paige Bueckers round out the next two spots. Stats below are a September 19 snapshot; team records refresh live from We Know the W. Read this board correctly: market order is context, not a vote. The dashboard is designed to show the shape of each case, not turn basketball into one mystery number. \n One important definition note: the September 15 market makes Paige Bueckers the fifth name on this board. WNBA editorial coverage on September 14 instead described Breanna Stewart as part of the five-player group pacing the race. Stewie is not being erased; the dashboard simply needs one consistent rule for who occupies card No. 5. DASHBOARD · LENS LAB Change the question. Watch the race move. MVP arguments get messy because people are often answering different questions. Pick a lens and the board will surface the candidate whose résumé speaks loudest in that category. SCORING VOLUME Who owns the scoreboard? FOOD FOR THOUGHT The problem with A’ja Wilson’s MVP case is that dominance can become background noise. When greatness repeats itself long enough, we start grading it on a curve. A new record feels exciting. A rookie leading the league’s best team feels historic. A generational passer makes every possession look like an argument. Meanwhile, A’ja Wilson is doing the basketball equivalent of holding up the ceiling, and because we have watched her do it before, there is a temptation to treat the ceiling like architecture instead of labor. Start with the hardest combination in the race. Wilson is not simply piling up points. She is carrying elite offensive volume while remaining one of the league’s most consequential defenders. The WNBA’s September 17 MVP analysis had her leading the league in scoring, blocks, usage rate and points in the paint. That is an absurd overlap of responsibilities. Most stars bend a game in one direction. Wilson bends both. That matters because “valuable” is not the same word as “spectacular,” “historic” or “best story.” Those can all be part of an MVP case, but the award asks a bigger question: how much of a team’s identity depends on this player being on the floor? THE NUMBER I CANNOT GET PAST +26.3 Las Vegas’ net rating swing with Wilson on the court versus off, according to the WNBA’s September 17 MVP analysis. The Aces do not just get better with her. They become a different team. With Wilson on the floor, Las Vegas had a 116.6 offensive rating and a +12.1 net rating in the WNBA’s latest MVP check-in. With her off, the offense fell to 94.7 and the net rating cratered to -14.2. That is a 26.3-point net-rating swing. You can debate the noise inside any on/off statistic, but a gap that large is not whispering. That is the spine of the “hers to lose” argument. Wilson has the counting stats. She has the efficiency. She has the rim protection. She has the team success. Then the impact data says the Aces’ entire ecosystem tilts when she steps across the scorer’s table. And then Kelsey Mitchell kicked the door in. Mitchell’s September 18 performance made the race more interesting, not less. She scored 33 against Toronto, pushed her season total to 1,034 points and broke Wilson’s WNBA single-season points record. She has now produced one of the great scoring seasons the league has seen. But total points and the scoring title are not the same thing. Mitchell reached the record in her 41st game of a 44-game schedule. Wilson’s old mark came in 38 games in 2024, and Wilson still leads the 2026 scoring race by average at 26.1 points per game to Mitchell’s 25.2. The record is a massive piece of Mitchell’s case. It is not, by itself, the whole MVP case. Olivia Miles owns the cleanest counterargument. If the ballot starts with “best player on the best team,” Miles has a serious answer. The rookie leads Minnesota in scoring and assists, the Lynx sit atop the standings, and she has done it with veteran-level efficiency and control. The scale of that achievement is easy to understate because she makes running an elite team look normal in Year 1. The separation comes on defense and individual burden. The WNBA’s own breakdown notes that Minnesota has defended better with Miles off the floor, while Wilson’s value survives the two-way test. Miles can still close that gap with a spectacular final stretch, but right now her case asks voters to emphasize team position and rookie history more heavily than Wilson’s broader individual impact. The Fever have two MVP cases, which is both a flex and a complication. Caitlin Clark remains the most devastating creator in this group. Her passing changes geometry, she carries enormous playmaking responsibility, and Indiana is 27–14. Mitchell, however, now owns the historic scoring record and the WNBA’s latest MVP ladder identifies her as Indiana’s most impactful player by on/off net rating. If voters are deciding who has been the Fever’s most valuable player, the existence of two legitimate answers can make it harder for either to overtake a candidate whose team’s case points overwhelmingly to one person. Paige Bueckers is the “do not blink” candidate. Bueckers has followed a Rookie of the Year season with another efficient, high-level year while Dallas climbed into the postseason. Her balance matters: scoring, playmaking and shot quality without needing the ball to dominate every second. The limitation is not that her season lacks value. It is that the top of this ballot has produced seasons that demand historical language. So why is it A’ja’s to lose? Because every route into the debate eventually runs into something Wilson already does at an elite level. Want scoring? She leads by average. Want efficiency? She is doing it without sacrificing volume. Want defense? She leads the league in blocks and still deters shots that never become box-score events. Want team success? Las Vegas is third. Want direct value? The on/off swing is enormous. Want durability and nightly burden? Her usage sits at the top of the league. There are better individual arguments against her than there were a month ago. There is not yet a better complete argument. THE COMPLETE CASE A’JA WILSON Scoring leader by average. Blocks leader. Elite efficiency. Top-three team. Massive on/off swing. THE BEST-TEAM CASE OLIVIA MILES 19.7 PPG, 6.0 APG and the primary creator for the No. 1 Lynx as a rookie. THE HISTORY CASE KELSEY MITCHELL 1,034 points and counting, the new WNBA single-season scoring record. THE CREATION CASE CAITLIN CLARK 22.5 PPG and 8.4 APG in the WNBA’s current player snapshot. THE BALANCE CASE PAIGE BUECKERS 20.4 PPG with 5.8 APG and efficient shot-making for a playoff Dallas team. THE COUNTERCASES If you are voting for somebody else, this is the argument. A strong MVP column should be able to make the opposition’s best case before answering it. OLIVIA MILES “Best player, best record, historic rookie.” Minnesota is first at 31–10, Miles leads the Lynx in scoring and assists, and no rookie has carried this exact combination of team success and offensive responsibility since the league’s earliest MVP-level rookie seasons. What she needs: A closing week big enough to make team dominance outweigh Wilson’s two-way statistical edge. KELSEY MITCHELL “The scoring season became history.” Mitchell just broke the single-season points record, owns a 25-game streak of 20-point performances and has a +13.3 Indiana net-rating swing in the WNBA’s latest MVP analysis. What she needs: The scoring gap by average to narrow, Indiana to keep winning, and voters to treat offensive gravity as decisive despite the defensive gap. CAITLIN CLARK “Nobody creates more offense this way.” Clark’s scoring plus league-shaping passing gives Indiana a second elite offensive engine. Her strongest argument is not just assists; it is the number of defensive decisions she forces before an assist can even happen. What she needs: A huge finish and a clear answer to the question of whether she or Mitchell owns Indiana’s 2026 MVP case. PAIGE BUECKERS “Efficiency, control and a Dallas climb.” Bueckers combines 20-plus scoring with nearly six assists and has kept Dallas moving upward without turning every possession into high-usage survival basketball. What she needs: A closing burst that forces voters to reconsider the volume gap separating her from the leaders. PLAYOFF UPDATE · OCTOBER 3 The ballot case is written. Now Wilson is carrying it into October. Las Vegas survived Indiana in three games and now meets No. 2 Golden State in a best-of-five semifinal. Wilson’s deciding-game response turned the old final-week MVP debate into a postseason statement. GAME 3 RECEIPT: Wilson scored 36 points with 10 rebounds and 2 blocks as Las Vegas beat Indiana 94–83 to win the series 2–1. The Aces advanced to an eighth consecutive WNBA semifinal and will face Golden State, which eliminated Dallas 77–73 in its own deciding Game 3. 01 Wilson stalls while a challenger detonates. A quiet finish from A’ja paired with multiple signature games from Miles or Mitchell could change the final impression voters carry into the ballot. 02 Minnesota locks No. 1 with a Miles masterpiece. The stronger the Lynx finish, the easier it becomes to argue that a rookie running the league’s best team deserves extraordinary weight. 03 Mitchell turns the points record into a scoring-title fight. The closer Mitchell gets to Wilson in points per game while extending her record, the harder it becomes to separate “historic scorer” from “most valuable.” 04 The Aces slip out of the top tier. Team record is not everything, but an ugly closing stretch would weaken one of the clean supporting pillars under Wilson’s case. SHAK’S FOOD FOR THOUGHT The real MVP test is not “Who gave us the newest story?” It is “Whose absence changes the most basketball?” Right now, the numbers keep bringing that question back to No. 22 in Las Vegas. RECEIPTS Make the take. Show the work. The dashboard combines official league analysis and profiles with current standings and a postgame scoring-record report. items.title: A’ja Wilson's Name Is Written Into South Carolina's Nike Deal
items.keywords: South Carolina's 10 year Nike contract formally includes A'ja Wilson signature shoes, Wilson related marketing and cash alternatives worth millions if those benefits are not delivered. South Carolina and Nike partnership announcement A’ja Wilson's Name Is Written Into South Carolina's Nike Deal | We Know the W HERSTORY · BUSINESS MOVES · AUGUST 29, 2026 HER NAME IS IN THE CONTRACT South Carolina’s move to Nike is a university wide apparel agreement. What makes A’ja Wilson’s influence unusually concrete is that the contract itself assigns value to her signature line, her marketing connection to the Gamecocks and the gear tied to her name. By We Know the W Staff 5 minute read Home › Playerpedia › Herstory: Entrepreneurship A’ NIKE Courtesy of South Carolina Athletics · Photo source BOARDROOM LEVERAGE A’ja Wilson is not merely associated with the South Carolina Nike deal. Her signature product and marketing connection are written into its additional benefits. THE DEAL 10 years July 2026 through June 2036 $70M retail product allotment $5M cash compensation 15% royalty on net sales There is a difference between saying a superstar helped make a partnership attractive and showing where her value appears in the paperwork. In A’ja Wilson’s case, the paperwork is unusually loud. The whole university wears the Swoosh South Carolina’s 10 year Nike partnership took effect July 1, 2026. Nike became the official supplier of uniforms, footwear, apparel and equipment for all 21 Gamecocks athletic programs. The agreement includes $70 million in retail product allotment, $5 million in cash compensation, $2.5 million in supplemental product and a 15 percent royalty on net sales. That scale reaches well beyond women’s basketball. Football, baseball, softball and every other varsity program are part of the same department wide relationship. Then comes the A’ja Wilson integration The binding term sheet recognizes Wilson as an iconic South Carolina athlete and ambassador. Nike agreed to provide South Carolina basketball with Nike branded A’ja Wilson signature sneakers, including university specific colorways. The agreement also calls for exploration of Wilson branded travel and other team gear for the women’s basketball program. The contract assigns a $15 million cash alternative if Nike does not or cannot provide that Wilson integration benefit. A separate provision says Nike will feature South Carolina in A’ja Wilson related marketing during the term, with a $3 million cash alternative if that benefit is not provided. THE IMPORTANT DISTINCTION The public record does not prove Wilson singlehandedly caused South Carolina to choose Nike. It does prove her name, signature product and marketing power carry explicit contractual value inside the deal. That is what boardroom leverage looks like Wilson’s influence has moved past the usual alumni endorsement. Her signature shoe line gives South Carolina a product connection that can reach current players, recruits, fans and marketing campaigns while tying the university’s basketball identity to one of its most recognizable graduates. When a former player’s signature line becomes part of what a global apparel company promises an entire athletic department, the athlete has become part of the institution’s business infrastructure. That is bigger than a logo placement. It is a form of commercial gravity. The cultural circle closes in Columbia Wilson delivered a national championship to South Carolina as a player, built a professional résumé that includes MVPs, championships and Olympic gold, then became a Nike signature athlete. The university that helped launch that career now has her signature products woven into its next apparel era. That is the more defensible version of the argument that A’ja moved the boardroom. The contract does not say she made the deal happen. It says her value is important enough to be priced. A’JA INTEGRATION $15M cash alternative tied to non delivery of the signature shoe and related gear benefit. MARKETING $3M cash alternative tied to South Carolina being featured in A’ja Wilson related marketing. items.title: The Best Coaches in the W: Legends, Legacy & the 2026 Finals | Food for Thought
items.keywords: Food for Thought: a searchable WNBA coaching legacy board, a women's college basketball all-time board, and the 2026 Finals matchup between Karl Smesko and Natalie Nakase. We Know the W home The Best Coaches in the W: Legends, Legacy & the 2026 Finals | Food for Thought FOOD FOR THOUGHT · COACHING LEGACIES The best coaches in the W: legends, legacy & the 2026 Finals What makes a great coach: the winning percentage, the banners, the longevity, or the team that was supposed to be a year away? Two searchable boards put the records on the table. Then we get to the Finals question: was Karl Smesko robbed? WE KNOW THE W UPDATED OCT. 11, 2026 Food for Thought THE COACHING DEBATE There is no single kind of greatness. Winning a title is the loudest credential. It is not the whole résumé. Some coaches build dynasties; some change a franchise’s ceiling; some turn a first-year expansion team into a playoff team. We score those stories separately, and keep regular-season records, playoff records and championships visible beside every number. All grades use a shared 55–99 peer scale, with a separate comparison pool and career inputs for each board. The WNBA grade compares the selected WNBA coaches; the college grade compares the selected Division I coaches. They are not cross-league equivalents. OUR RULE Show the math. Keep the context. Editorial W Grades are peer-relative comparison tools, not official league statistics. 2026 WNBA FINALS · ATLANTA vs. GOLDEN STATE Two benches. Two very different paths. Atlanta’s Karl Smesko meets Golden State’s Natalie Nakase. The snapshot below is through Oct. 9, before the Finals; the 2026 Form grade includes the Finals trip but no championship result. 2026 playoff bracket ↗ 2026 Finals snapshot WNBA career so far How to read the finalist grades: Career W Grade (through 2025) and 2026 Form use the same 55–99 peer-percentile scale as the full Coaches dashboard, comparing the 15 coaches tracked there. PROV indicates fewer than two prior 44-game WNBA regular seasons or a small playoff sample; the pre-2026 game count appears with the grade. Missing career dimensions are omitted and remaining weights are rebalanced, so lack of Finals opportunity is not scored as zero. The historical WNBA and college boards below use that scale within their own selected pools, with their league-specific career inputs. Grades are relative to those pools, not absolute or cross-league quality rankings. See the full current-coach dashboard for the complete method. THE PRO GAME · CAREER RESUMÉS The WNBA legacy board A selected group of title winners and career leaders. Sort by W Grade, wins, titles or either win percentage; search a coach’s name to find a résumé quickly. THROUGH OCT. 9, 2026 Find a coach Filter All selected coaches Two or more titles Three or more titles Sort by W Grade Regular-season wins WNBA titles Regular-season win % Playoff win % Selected WNBA coaching legacies and peer-relative W Grades Rank Coach Regular season Playoffs WNBA titles Legacy W Grade · /99 WNBA legacy base score = career regular-season win percentage × 40 + playoff win percentage × 40 + 5 points per WNBA title, capped at 20. The published W Grade converts that base score to a 55–99 mid-rank percentile within the 10 coaches shown. This is a selected historical group, not the full all-time WNBA coaching pool. The board focuses on coaches with at least 100 regular-season games; shorter résumés, including Smesko’s and Nakase’s, are featured above with provisional Career W Grades. Records include 2026 results where applicable. THE COLLEGE GAME · CAREER WIN LEADERS The women’s college coaching board Longevity carries weight here, because a career total tells a different story than a single tournament. The 2026 champion gets her place on the board, too. END OF 2025–26 SEASON 2026 NCAA CHAMPION Cori Close · UCLA UCLA finished 37–1 and won the program’s first NCAA title. Her College Legacy Grade includes accumulated career wins; it is not a grade of UCLA’s championship season. The published W Grade converts that base score to a 55–99 mid-rank percentile within the 11 coaches shown. This grade is relative to the selected Division I group and is not directly comparable with a WNBA grade. Records are through the completed 2025–26 season; career totals follow the cited college coaching records, while titles count NCAA Division I championships. First-round picks count unique players each coach coached as a head coach who were later selected in the WNBA first round, across career programs; a transfer may count for each coach who coached her. Includes the 1997 WNBA Elite Draft first round and selections through 2026. Draft totals are résumé context and do not affect the W Grade. Draft-count references: WNBA all-time draft archive · WNBA first-round school counts through 2026 . Coaching records: NCAA women’s basketball coaching records · NCAA Division I championship history · Texas record for Jody Conradt . ? THE FOOD FOR THOUGHT QUESTION Was Smesko robbed? 2025 COACH OF THE YEAR No. Nakase earned 53 of 72 votes; Smesko finished second with 15. In year one, Nakase took an expansion roster to a 23–21 record and the Valkyries became the first expansion team to reach the playoffs in its inaugural season. That was a historic award case, not a bad call. 2026 COACH OF THE YEAR Overlooked? Yes. Robbed? Debatable. The official ballot gave Reeve 40 votes, Nakase 20 and Sydney Johnson 14. Those 74 votes leave Smesko with none, despite Atlanta’s 30–14 regular season. That is a fair snub argument. Reeve still had the league’s best record at 33–11, while Nakase went 32–12. The Finals run came after the regular-season award was decided, so it cannot be the evidence for changing that ballot. Our call: Nakase was the right 2025 winner. In 2026, Smesko deserved a place in the conversation; “robbed” depends on whether you think Atlanta’s 30-win season should have earned him some share of the 74 votes. FOOD FOR THOUGHT What should count most in a coaching legacy? Make the playoffs. It is the minimum test of a regular-season builder. Win the games that get harder. Postseason results deserve their own column. Change the ceiling. A first-year expansion playoff berth and a fourth title are not the same achievement, but both can be extraordinary. Who belongs above the numbers: the dynasty builder, the best tactician, or the coach who changed what a franchise could be? items.title: DeWanna Bonner Leaves Phoenix for One More Title Run
items.keywords: DeWanna Bonner and the Phoenix Mercury agreed to a contract buyout, giving the 17-year veteran a chance to pursue a third championship in what could be one of her final postseason runs. DeWanna Bonner holding a basketball in a Phoenix Mercury uniform DeWanna Bonner Leaves Phoenix for One More Title Run | We Know the W PLAYER MOVEMENT · AUGUST 24, 2026 ONE MORE RUN DeWanna Bonner is leaving Phoenix through a contract buyout, not because the relationship broke, but because the Mercury gave a franchise great room to chase a third championship while the clock still offers one more postseason. By We Know the W Staff 8-minute read DB 24 DeWanna Bonner during her 2026 return to Phoenix. Photo via Phoenix Mercury . THE BONNER FILE 39 years old 17 WNBA seasons 2 championships 8,000+ career points The Phoenix Mercury and DeWanna Bonner have agreed to a contract buyout that allows the 17-year veteran to pursue a roster spot with a championship contender. Phoenix is out of the 2026 playoff race, while Bonner is staring at a postseason window that may not open many more times. The move The Mercury announced the agreement Monday, August 24. General manager Nick U’Ren described the decision as an act rooted in the organization’s relationship with Bonner, giving her an opportunity to chase another title in what could be her final postseason. Bonner expressed the same uncertainty about the road beyond 2026. She did not announce her retirement. She did acknowledge that this could be “one of my final postseason opportunities,” which makes the timing of the move the story inside the story. THE BOTTOM LINE Phoenix is protecting a relationship. Bonner is protecting one last chance. Why the buyout makes sense A buyout lets both sides tell the truth about where they are. The Mercury cannot reach the playoffs, so keeping a decorated veteran through the final games would preserve continuity but not create a postseason. Bonner still has enough game, experience and ambition to help a team that will be playing after Phoenix packs up. This is also a rare example of the business of basketball bending toward the human side. Phoenix did not have to erase Bonner’s importance to make a basketball decision. The organization recognized that a player who helped hang two championship banners deserved the chance to pursue another one. What Bonner still brings Bonner is not being evaluated as the 20-point scorer she was at her peak. She is being evaluated as a 6-foot-4 veteran wing who has played every kind of playoff possession, can rebound her position, disrupt passing lanes and score without needing an offense built around her. Through 37 games this season, she averaged 10.6 points, 6.1 rebounds and 1.2 steals. Those numbers make her more than a ceremonial addition. For the right contender, she can steady a second unit, close certain matchups and bring championship experience into a locker room where every late-game decision becomes heavier. A Phoenix story, even when she leaves The Mercury selected Bonner fifth overall in the 2009 WNBA Draft. She won three consecutive Sixth Player of the Year awards to begin her career and helped Phoenix capture championships in 2009 and 2014. After ten seasons with the Mercury, she joined Connecticut in 2020 and helped the Sun reach the 2022 Finals. Her path eventually curved back to the desert. Bonner returned to Phoenix during the 2025 season after a brief stop in Indiana, then re-signed for 2026. This summer she crossed 8,000 career points, another marker in a career that already places her among the league’s most productive and durable players. The buyout does not rewrite that history. If anything, it underlines it. Phoenix is not sending away a stranger. It is opening the door for family. What happens next No destination had been confirmed when this story was published. The next team will need more than a recognizable name. It will need a real role, a roster opening and a belief that Bonner’s playoff experience can solve a specific problem. The cleanest fit will be a contender looking for size on the wing, defensive flexibility, rebounding and a veteran who will not be surprised by the speed or pressure of a postseason series. Bonner’s next jersey remains unknown. Her purpose does not. The landing spot board: watch New York Sports Illustrated identified Atlanta, Minnesota and New York as the three most logical destinations. Atlanta has the cleanest cap situation, Minnesota offers a proven championship system, and New York has the combination that makes this prediction especially interesting: available money, a playoff berth and an immediate opening for experienced frontcourt depth. The Liberty have $129,904 in available cap space, according to Sports Illustrated’s analysis. Satou Sabally is also away from the team indefinitely while dealing with lingering effects of a head injury. Her health comes first, but her absence leaves New York without the versatile size it expected to carry into the postseason. WE KNOW THE W PICK · 1 New York Liberty The Liberty can afford Bonner, have already clinched a playoff berth and need dependable length behind Breanna Stewart and Jonquel Jones. New York can offer a defined role without asking her to carry the offense. Why it feels real: need + money + title path 2 · CLEANEST FIT Atlanta Dream Atlanta reportedly has $190,663 in cap space and a natural defensive role beside Rhyne Howard, Allisha Gray and Angel Reese. The Dream may be the easiest transaction to complete. Why it works: cap room + scheme 3 · SYSTEM FIT Minnesota Lynx Minnesota can use another long veteran wing, and Cheryl Reeve has a record of maximizing experienced players. The obstacle is structural because the Lynx would need to create room first. Why it works: coaching + contender status Our read: Atlanta may be the simplest fit on paper, but New York is the team to watch. The Liberty have a clearer immediate need, enough cap space and the kind of veteran core that lets Bonner contribute without pretending she must still be the first option. No agreement with New York or any other team was confirmed at publication. Bonner must first pass through waivers before she can sign as an unrestricted free agent. The bigger meaning There is a difference between leaving and being discarded. Bonner’s exit feels closer to a franchise handing one of its legends the ball with the clock running down. Maybe this becomes the final chapter. Maybe Bonner writes another one after it. For now, she is choosing possibility, and the Mercury are letting one of their own chase the only ending that could make a farewell feel less like goodbye: one more run, one more postseason and one more shot at a ring. 2026 PRODUCTION 10.6 PPG 6.1 RPG 1.2 SPG 37 games with Phoenix PHOENIX LEGACY 2009 and 2014 champion Three-time Sixth Player of the Year Fifth pick in the 2009 Draft Open the Phoenix Mercury hub → SOURCE DESK How this story was checked We separated the confirmed buyout and career record from any speculation about Bonner’s next team. Seven high draft picks who didn't live up to WNBA expectations. Seven overlooked talents who proved the league wrong. And why international careers complicate the word bust. We Know the W · Published October 11, 2026 · 14 player profiles Sydney Taylor · Photo: WNBA player media ← All Food for Thought · Snack Shak Every April, families celebrate and franchises introduce tomorrow's cornerstones. The WNBA Draft is a prediction, though, not a promise. A No. 1 pick can be gone in two seasons. An undrafted guard can rewrite the rookie record book. Who gets labeled a bust? The player whose college dominance never translated? The front office that picked her? Or a development system with too few roster spots and too little patience? The global game provides an essential second opinion. 7 Draft picks below WNBA expectations 7 Surprise success stories 5 Undrafted players among the surprises How we're judging: Draft disappointment measures WNBA return against selection cost, not whether a player has talent, value as a person, or a successful career overseas. Injuries, player development, championships and national-team accomplishments all matter. All 14 7 draft disappointments 7 surprises PART ONE · THE HIGH PICKS Big Draft Capital. Small WNBA Returns. Not all seven situations are alike. Some players were given little time; others suffered serious injuries. Several turned their careers around abroad. The draft positions, however, still invite scrutiny. Photo: WNBA player media DRAFT DISAPPOINTMENT Charli Collier 2021 · No. 1 · Dallas Wings 45 games · 2.9 PPG Dallas drafted the Texas standout to anchor its frontcourt. Her All-Rookie selection offered an encouraging start, but she averaged only 2.9 points and 2.5 rebounds across two WNBA seasons. A franchise-defining pick never became a franchise-defining player. Where are they now? Her basketball story continued overseas. After professional stops in Italy, Israel, Poland, China and Australia, she joined Melikgazi Kayseri in Turkey for 2025–26 and İstanbul Gençlik Spor for 2026–27. A clear No. 1-pick disappointment, not the end of a pro career. Player / reporting source ↗ Photo: WNBA player media DRAFT DISAPPOINTMENT Evelyn Akhator 2017 · No. 3 · Dallas Wings 15 games · 0.9 PPG Akhator barely got started in Dallas: 15 appearances and only 61 WNBA minutes. No. 3 overall was an enormous investment for that return. Yet judging this Nigerian international by her WNBA box score alone would miss most of her résumé. Where are they now? She joined BOTAŞ in Turkey for 2026–27 after competing in Spain and France. Akhator averaged 12.6 points and 9.0 rebounds at the 2018 FIBA Women's World Cup for Nigeria and has been an important AfroBasket contributor. The draft pick failed. The international player did not. Player / reporting source ↗ Photo: WNBA player media DRAFT DISAPPOINTMENT Lauren Cox 2020 · No. 3 · Indiana Fever 41 games · 2.9 PPG The Baylor champion was expected to provide size, defense and passing. Instead, injuries and limited opportunities kept Cox from securing a sustained WNBA role in Indiana or Los Angeles. Where are they now? She later played productively with the Townsville Fire in Australia's WNBL, including double-doubles in 2024–25. A knee injury interrupted 2025–26; a new 2026–27 team has not been verified. An injury-affected lottery disappointment, not a fair case for blaming talent alone. Player / reporting source ↗ Photo: WNBA player media DRAFT DISAPPOINTMENT Kysre Gondrezick 2021 · No. 4 · Indiana Fever 24 games · 1.7 PPG Indiana's surprise top-four selection never secured a regular rotation role. Gondrezick made 19 appearances for the Fever and five more for Chicago in 2024, with little statistical return from a valuable lottery pick. Where are they now? She has pursued fashion, entertainment and a basketball comeback. Athletes Unlimited announced her for 2026, but a serious Achilles injury affected her return. No current WNBA or overseas club contract has been verified. An especially costly scouting gamble for Indiana. Player / reporting source ↗ Photo: WNBA player media DRAFT DISAPPOINTMENT Chelsea Dungee 2021 · No. 5 · Dallas Wings 14 games · 0.6 PPG Dungee scored 22.3 points per game as an Arkansas senior. Dallas selected her fifth, then played her for approximately 65 total WNBA minutes. Was that a failed evaluation, a failed developmental fit, or both? Where are they now? After professional basketball in Turkey and Australia, Chelsea Dungee-Artberry moved into college coaching. For 2026–27 she is at Alabama in player development, recruiting operations and an assistant-coaching role. A poor draft return, followed by a promising second act in coaching. Player / reporting source ↗ Photo: WNBA player media DRAFT DISAPPOINTMENT Alaina Coates 2017 · No. 2 · Chicago Sky 95 games · 2.7 PPG A foot and ankle injury disrupted the South Carolina star's WNBA launch. Coates never averaged the kind of production expected from the second overall pick, though she later earned a championship ring with Las Vegas in 2023. Where are they now? She played in the 2026 Athletes Unlimited season. Overseas stops include Hungary, China, Turkey, Israel and Italy; at Nesibe Aydın in 2021–22 she averaged 17.9 points and 12.9 rebounds. Underwhelming lottery return; meaningful global longevity. Player / reporting source ↗ Photo: WNBA player media DRAFT DISAPPOINTMENT Kaleena Mosqueda-Lewis 2015 · No. 3 · Seattle Storm 157 games · 5.1 PPG One of UConn's most accomplished shooters did not become the offensive centerpiece Seattle hoped for. Across her WNBA career, her three-point accuracy was 33.7%, well below the reputation she carried into the draft. She did, however, win the 2018 title with Seattle. Where are they now? She continued her career in Europe and returned to Toulouse Métropole Basket in France in early 2025 after a reported retirement. A 2026–27 club has not been confirmed. A below-expectations No. 3 pick, not a total career failure. Player / reporting source ↗ PART TWO · THE HIDDEN GEMS Passed Over. Never Counted Out. Some went undrafted. Others were selected late and had to wait years for opportunities. Every one of these careers shows why draft-night rankings aren't destiny. Photo: WNBA player media OVERRATED THE DRAFT Sydney Taylor Undrafted · 2024 · Chicago Sky 2026: 504 points · 13.6 PPG No draft-night phone call. Taylor instead played in Lithuania and Poland, developing an experienced scorer's game. She earned a 2026 Chicago training-camp invitation and became an AP All-Rookie selection. Where are they now? She finished the 2026 season with Chicago as the highest-scoring undrafted rookie in WNBA history: 504 points in 37 games, with two game-winning go-ahead threes. She is a proven WNBA scorer entering her next career decision. A historic undrafted rookie season. The headline of the other side of this debate. Player / reporting source ↗ Photo: WNBA player media OVERRATED THE DRAFT Becky Hammon Undrafted · 1999 · New York Liberty 6× All-Star · Hall of Fame The league let the Colorado State star go unpicked. New York signed her, and she became a six-time WNBA All-Star, earning four All-WNBA honors across a 16-season career. Where are they now? After starring internationally in Russia and winning an Olympic bronze for Russia in 2008, Hammon became Las Vegas Aces head coach. She led titles in 2022, 2023 and 2025 and entered the Basketball Hall of Fame in 2023. From undrafted to Hall of Fame: the gold standard. Player / reporting source ↗ Photo: WNBA player media OVERRATED THE DRAFT Erica Wheeler Undrafted · 2013 · Rutgers 2019 All-Star Game MVP Wheeler took the overseas route before breaking into the WNBA in 2015. She built herself into Indiana's starting point guard and became the first undrafted player to win WNBA All-Star Game MVP. Where are they now? She played for the Los Angeles Sparks in 2026, averaging 9.0 points and 5.0 assists. Her time in overseas leagues was a bridge to the WNBA, not the consolation prize. An All-Star whose story no draft board predicted. Player / reporting source ↗ Photo: WNBA player media OVERRATED THE DRAFT Kayla Thornton Undrafted · 2014 · UTEP 2024 champion · 2025 All-Star Defense, rebounding, energy and adaptability are easy to underprice on draft night. Thornton turned those traits into a title with the New York Liberty in 2024 and became Golden State's first All-Star in 2025. Where are they now? Thornton helped lead the Valkyries into the 2026 WNBA Finals. International work includes Australia, Israel, Italy, Puerto Rico, Russia, Turkey and South Korea, where she won league honors. The kind of cornerstone that costs zero draft capital. Player / reporting source ↗ Photo: WNBA player media OVERRATED THE DRAFT Alysha Clark 2010 · No. 17 · San Antonio 3× champion · Sixth Player of the Year Being picked in the second round did not guarantee Clark a job. San Antonio waived her twice. Seattle eventually gave her a role, and she evolved into an elite defender and championship contributor in 2018, 2020 and 2023. Where are they now? Clark played for Dallas in 2026, scoring 21 in its September 30 playoff win over Golden State. Her long international career has included Israel, Turkey, Poland and France. Three rings and a Sixth Player award from a discarded second-rounder. Player / reporting source ↗ Photo: WNBA player media OVERRATED THE DRAFT Pauline Astier Undrafted · France · New York Liberty 2026: 9.3 PPG · 3.3 APG Undrafted did not mean inexperienced. Astier came to New York in 2026 with years of high-level European club basketball behind her and a silver medal with France at the 2024 Olympics. Where are they now? After contributing 10.2 points and 5.6 assists in EuroLeague for USK Praha in 2025–26, she became a useful Liberty guard during the 2026 WNBA season and playoff run. An American draft miss, not an international scouting mystery. Player / reporting source ↗ Photo: WNBA player media OVERRATED THE DRAFT Marine Fauthoux 2021 · No. 29 · New York Liberty Oct. 7 playoffs: 20 points The Liberty chose Fauthoux late in the third round in 2021 and waited five years for her WNBA debut. She spent that time building a serious professional résumé in Europe and with the French national team. Where are they now? Fauthoux joined New York in 2026. Her four threes and 20 points against Atlanta on October 7 illustrated why patience and a third-round investment can pay off, even if a definitive WNBA career verdict is premature. The long-view draft-and-develop success worth watching. Player / reporting source ↗ Was the 2021 Draft the Ultimate Warning? Dallas drafted Charli Collier first and Chelsea Dungee fifth; Indiana took Kysre Gondrezick fourth. Those three combined for just 83 WNBA games. That return on three top-five choices is difficult to defend. But it doesn't automatically invalidate the entire 2021 class. The point is what teams do after the announcement. Was the skill evaluation wrong? Was the system a poor fit? Were there enough minutes to develop an answer? These are decisions a general manager must own. The International Game Is Not a Footnote Evelyn Akhator's Nigerian national-team work and Turkish career tell a dramatically different story than her 15 WNBA games. Charli Collier, Lauren Cox and Alaina Coates also found playing opportunities outside the United States. Overseas leagues give some players extended roles, a different pace and the chance to build confidence that an 11th or 12th WNBA roster spot rarely affords. And that road also runs in reverse. Sydney Taylor developed in Lithuania and Poland before her historic 2026 Chicago season. Erica Wheeler built her base internationally. Pauline Astier arrived in New York as an experienced European professional, not an inexperienced prospect. Kayla Thornton turned years of global hoops into championship credentials. So Who Really Missed? Charli Collier has a strong case as the biggest modern No. 1 disappointment. Evelyn Akhator presents the most extreme gap between WNBA draft cost and minutes. The injury histories of Lauren Cox and Alaina Coates call for nuance. On the other side, Becky Hammon remains the historical standard for an undrafted WNBA success, while Sydney Taylor delivers the newest example. Draft position tells us what a team believed in April. A career tells us what the player became. WE KNOW THE W VERDICT: The scouting report isn't the final report. And a player's story does not end when a team stops calling. Research: WNBA official player and team profiles; FIBA; international league and club records; Basketball-Reference; university athletics departments. Player portraits link to official WNBA photo media. The photography is not AI-generated. Image rights remain with their respective owners.

items.title: The Dream Beat the Lynx. Now Minnesota Has a Pattern Problem.
items.keywords: Atlanta beat Minnesota 89-81, handing the Lynx a second straight loss as Allisha Gray, Jordin Canada and Angel Reese exposed a different version of the pressure points Golden State found six days earlier. The Dream Beat the Lynx. Now Minnesota Has a Pattern Problem. | We Know the W FOOD FOR THOUGHT · GAME REACTION · AUGUST 30, 2026 THE DREAM BEAT THE LYNX. NOW MINNESOTA HAS A PATTERN PROBLEM. Atlanta did not copy Golden State's blueprint. It translated it, then handed Minnesota an 89 to 81 loss, a second straight defeat and a very long film session heading into the World Cup break. By We Know the W Staff 7 minute read August 30, 2026 Home › Snack Shak › Food for Thought › Dream 89, Lynx 81 MINNESOTA LYNX 31 and 9 FINAL 81 · 89 Atlanta wins season series 2 to 1 ATLANTA DREAM 26 and 14 TEAM Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4 FINAL MIN 21 20 21 19 81 ATL 26 26 19 18 89 HALFTIME CONTROL 52 to 41 Atlanta won each of the first two quarters and made Minnesota chase the game. THREE POINT MATH 13 to 6 Made threes. That is a 21 point Atlanta advantage from behind the arc. GLASS EDGE 37 to 32 Atlanta won the rebounding battle, with Angel Reese grabbing 11. SECOND STRAIGHT L2 Minnesota also lost 80 to 66 to Golden State on August 24. Two games ago, Minnesota could call it one ugly night. After Atlanta's 89 to 81 win Sunday, that explanation has officially expired. The Dream took the rubber match of the season series, 2 to 1, improved to 26 and 14, and sent the league leading Lynx into the World Cup break at 31 and 9 with consecutive losses for the first time since early July. Minnesota is still Minnesota. It still owns the best record. Nobody needs to hit a panic button. But somebody should probably move the button within reach. Because the most interesting part of this two game slide is that Golden State and Atlanta did not beat the Lynx the same way. Atlanta won this one before halftime The Dream opened with a 26 to 21 first quarter, then repeated the pressure with another 26 points in the second. By halftime, Atlanta led 52 to 41. Minnesota actually won the second half 40 to 37. That is the sort of detail that can make a final score look more competitive than the game felt. The Lynx spent the night trying to repair damage that had already been done. THE GAME IN ONE NUMBER Atlanta made seven more threes than Minnesota. Seven extra makes from deep equals 21 points of scoreboard leverage in an eight point win. The Dream did not copy Golden State. They translated the idea. Our last Lynx film piece asked whether Atlanta could take pieces of Golden State's pressure blueprint and make them fit its own personnel. The answer was yes, but the box score makes an important distinction. Golden State beat Minnesota by speeding up decisions and forcing 18 Lynx turnovers. Atlanta did almost the opposite in the turnover column. The Dream committed 18 turnovers themselves while Minnesota had only 11. If this were simply a copy and paste job, Atlanta should have lost. Instead, the Dream attacked different pressure points. They stretched the floor, won the rebounding battle and made Minnesota's best rookie scorer operate more like an isolated scorer than the connective playmaker who usually organizes the Lynx offense. THE BOX SCORE BALANCE 43% FG% 46% 32% 3PT% 36% 32 REB 37 17 AST 21 11 TO 18 Allisha Gray controlled the temperature Allisha Gray finished with 23 points and 11 rebounds, hit six of her 11 three point attempts, added three steals and finished plus 17. Every time Minnesota threatened to make the game small again, Atlanta had a perimeter answer available. Jordin Canada added 16 points and 10 assists. Rhyne Howard scored 16 with three assists and no turnovers. That matters because Minnesota's defense still created chaos. Atlanta just had enough creation across multiple guards to survive it. ALLISHA GRAY 23 points · 11 rebounds 6 made threes 3 steals +17 JORDIN CANADA 16 points · 10 assists 6 of 12 FG 2 made threes double double ANGEL REESE 15 points · 11 rebounds 29th double double 3 OREB +15 OLIVIA MILES 21 points · 5 rebounds 0 assists 2 turnovers minus 19 Miles scored. Atlanta disconnected the rest. Olivia Miles led Minnesota with 21 points. That is the good news. The number sitting beside those 21 points is the one Atlanta will probably circle in red during film review: zero assists. Miles entered Sunday averaging 6.1 assists per game. Against the Dream, she did not record one. That does not mean she played poorly. She shot 7 of 14, got to the line seven times and kept attacking. It means Atlanta made her scoring live separately from the easy creation Minnesota usually gets around it. Napheesa Collier and Kayla McBride each scored 17. Natasha Howard filled the stat sheet with nine points, seven rebounds and seven assists. But Minnesota finished with only 17 team assists, while Atlanta had 21. The Lynx had production. The Dream had flow. Angel Reese put a record inside the win Reese finished with 15 points and 11 rebounds, giving her 29 double doubles this season. She entered the game tied with Alyssa Thomas at 28 for the WNBA single season record. Now the record belongs to Reese alone. And this was not history detached from winning. Atlanta outrebounded Minnesota 37 to 32. Reese had three offensive rebounds, eight defensive rebounds, two steals and a block. She helped make sure Minnesota's defensive possessions actually ended. That is the Atlanta version of the blueprint. Golden State manufactured extra possessions through pressure. Atlanta created its advantage with spacing, shooting and the glass. AUGUST 24 Golden State 80, Minnesota 66 18 Lynx turnovers, a season low 66 points and a pressure defense that delayed Minnesota's offense. → AUGUST 30 Atlanta 89, Minnesota 81 13 Dream threes, a plus five rebounding margin and zero Olivia Miles assists. The second straight loss changes the conversation Back to back losses do not erase a 31 win season. They do, however, create better playoff questions. Golden State showed that Minnesota can be pushed out of its preferred timing. Atlanta showed that the Lynx can also be made to chase a game when an opponent has enough shooting and rebounding to punish every slow start. Those are two different routes to the same destination. The Dream also won the season series 2 to 1. Atlanta took the opener 91 to 90, Minnesota answered 96 to 81 in May, and Sunday's win gave the final word to the Dream before the break. OLIVIA MILES HEALTH WATCH Concern, yes. Diagnosis, not yet. There was late concern around Miles' health, but no new official postgame diagnosis was available when this article was published. That distinction matters. Miles recently twisted her left ankle against Golden State on August 19 and did not return to that game, then returned to action afterward. Until Minnesota provides an update from Sunday, this belongs in the monitor column, not the confirmed injury column. Now Minnesota has to sit with it The timing might be the most uncomfortable part. The WNBA pauses for the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup, so Minnesota does not get an immediate chance to wash this taste out with another game. The Lynx are scheduled to return September 18 against New York. That also gives Cheryl Reeve and her staff something valuable: time. Time to look at the Golden State tape next to the Atlanta tape. Time to decide which problems are noise and which are becoming repeatable. Time to get healthier. Food for thought Minnesota is still the team everybody has to catch. But being the best team over 40 games and being the hardest team to beat four times in a playoff series are related questions, not identical ones. Golden State made Minnesota uncomfortable by shrinking its time. Atlanta made Minnesota uncomfortable by stretching its defense and winning the math from three. Two teams, two methods, two straight losses. That is not a collapse. It is a scouting report getting thicker. items.title: AU Expansion & Evolution
items.keywords: Athletes Unlimited Expansion and Evolution tracks five seasons of league growth, 2026 team branding and the confirmed 2027 pause. AU Expansion & Evolution | We Know the W EXPANSION WATCH · ATHLETES UNLIMITED GROWTH WITHOUT FRANCHISES AU’s basketball model does not expand like the WNBA or UPSHOT. Its story is structural: deeper player pools, weekly redrafts, permanent team identities in 2026 and a confirmed 2027 pause while the league evaluates what comes next. Home › Expansion Watch › Athletes Unlimited 2022 → 2026 Five seasons of changing the container. AU kept its player-first leaderboard and weekly draft at the center while changing location, roster composition, presentation and finally the names fans used for the four weekly teams. 5 2022 YEAR ONE AU Pro Basketball debuts with one player pool, four weekly drafted teams and an individual champion. 2023 THE MODEL RETURNS The captain draft and individual leaderboard remain the competitive spine rather than permanent franchises. 2024 SEASON THREE The format continues to build a recognizable winter stage for established pros and emerging WNBA players. 2025 NASHVILLE The league moves into its Nashville era while teams are still commonly identified by captains during each weekly draft. 2026 NAMED IDENTITIES Gold Rush, Glow, Rhythm and Eclipse give fans four stable team names even though the player rosters still reset each week. 2027 OFFICIAL PAUSE AU announces there will be no 2027 basketball season while it evaluates the competition’s long-term future. THE 2026 CHANGE The colors finally got names. Permanent team branding was the closest AU came to franchise-style expansion. The key difference: the names stayed, the rosters did not. GOLD Gold Rush One of four permanent names introduced for Season 5. ORANGE Glow A stable identity applied to a roster that was still redrafted weekly. BLUE Rhythm The team name remained from week to week even as its captain and players changed. PURPLE Eclipse AU’s fourth named identity completed the new 2026 team set. Why Playerpedia says “2026 Week 4” AU assignments are temporary by design. Playerpedia stores the final-week team snapshot rather than implying a player belonged to one AU team for the entire season. JULY 31, 2026 A pause is part of the history too. Athletes Unlimited officially announced that Pro Basketball will pause during the 2027 season while the organization evaluates how the property can make its greatest long-term impact. CONFIRMED No 2027 AU basketball season The site will not manufacture a schedule, roster or champion for a year AU has explicitly paused. Official update ↗ ARCHIVE Five completed seasons stay visible Champions, leaderboard history, team evolution and Playerpedia affiliations remain part of the W’s broader pro ecosystem. Open AU history → STATUS Reimagination, not speculation Any return date, new format or new ownership structure belongs here only after AU makes it official. WHAT TO WATCH If AU basketball returns, what changes? FORMAT Does the weekly draft survive? The captain-led redraft is AU basketball’s clearest competitive signature. IDENTITY Do Gold Rush, Glow, Rhythm + Eclipse return? The 2026 names created continuity AU had not previously emphasized. PLAYER POOL Who comes back? items.title: Expansion Draft 101
items.keywords: Expansion Draft 101 explains how WNBA expansion teams can build inaugural rosters, using Golden State's 2024 draft as a recent example. Expansion Draft 101 | We Know the W ROSTER BUILDING · EXPLAINED EXPANSION DRAFT 101 How does a brand-new team get players? Protect. Select. Trade. Draft. Sign. Build. Expansion Watch Protected players Available pool Trades + rights Free agency + draft THE BIG IDEA An expansion draft creates a starting point, not a finished roster. The league sets special rules that let a new franchise select from players or rights held by existing teams. The exact rules can change from one expansion cycle to another, so this page uses Golden State's 2024 Expansion Draft as a recent real-world example — not a promise of what Cleveland, Detroit or Philadelphia will receive. League sets the rules The WNBA determines roster lists, protection limits, eligibility and trade windows for that specific expansion draft. Teams protect players In Golden State's 2024 example, each existing team could protect up to six players. Expansion team selects Golden State could acquire a contract or negotiating rights to one available player from each existing team and was not required to choose from every team. Trades shape the board The expansion team could make agreements involving selecting — or not selecting — certain available players. The roster keeps growing Free agency, the college draft, trades, waivers and camp competition continue the build after the expansion draft. VISUAL MAP Protected → Available → Selected. Important: protection counts, selection limits, unrestricted-free-agent rules and draft positioning are not universal forever. The WNBA will publish the rules that apply to each future expansion team or expansion cycle. WHY FANS SHOULD CARE Expansion changes every team's roster math. DEPTH Good benches become vulnerable When protection spots are limited, teams have to decide which role players and developing talent they can risk exposing. OPPORTUNITY Roles can get bigger A player buried on one roster can become a starter, veteran anchor or featured defender for a new team. STRATEGY Front offices matter Expansion drafts reward contract knowledge, rights management, scouting and creative trades — not just star chasing. GOLDEN STATE CASE STUDY What happened in 2024? 6 Maximum protected players per existing team The remaining players and rights on the submitted roster list formed the available pool, subject to the specific 2024 rules. 1 Opportunity to select from each existing team Golden State could take one available contract or set of rights from each of the 12 teams, but could skip a team. 11 Players ultimately selected The Valkyries selected 11 players and then continued building through free agency and the 2025 WNBA Draft. ← Philadelphia Past Expansion Waves → Expansion Watch → Recent rule example: WNBA Golden State Expansion Draft FAQ ↗

items.title: WNBA Expansion Watch
items.keywords: WNBA Expansion Watch: Houston's 2027 relocation, Cleveland, Detroit, Philadelphia, roster building and past expansion waves. WNBA Expansion Watch | We Know the W EXPANSION WATCH · THE W THE W GETS WIDER The official growth map now has two different kinds of movement: Houston returns in 2027 through the Connecticut Sun relocation, then Cleveland, Detroit and Philadelphia add new franchises on the road to 18 teams. Home › Expansion Watch › The W 2027 · RELOCATION, NOT EXPANSION Houston Comets: the dynasty returns. The WNBA and NBA Boards of Governors unanimously approved the sale and relocation of the Connecticut Sun to Houston for the 2027 season. The Comets will play at Toyota Center under Fertitta Entertainment. Because an existing franchise is moving, the league remains at 15 teams in 2027. Open the Houston Comets team page → 2027 Why this matters to Expansion Watch The market changes, but the team count does not. The Sun finish 2026 in Connecticut, then the franchise moves to Houston. Connecticut says Houston receives the rights to any player and coach contracts still held at handoff, so there is no separate Houston expansion draft. THE ROAD TO 18 Three new franchises follow Houston's move.
