GABBY WILLIAMS · FRANCE LEONIE FIEBICH · GERMANY SEMIFINAL 01 · FRANCE vs GERMANY Can Germany make France play one possession at a time? France has spent this tournament removing oxygen. It is shooting 61.4 percent on twos and 45.7 percent from three while holding opponents to 27.6 percent beyond the arc. When Gabby Williams turns one mistake into transition and Marine Johannès stretches the defense another step, the opponent can lose the game in a two-minute blur. Germany’s counter is not to win a track meet. It is to refuse to donate possessions. The hosts average only 9.8 turnovers, own a 46.2 to 39.5 rebounding advantage over France, and have won four straight since Spain beat them by 30 on opening day. Leonie Fiebich can control a game without dominating shots; Frieda Bühner supplies efficient scoring; Nyara Sabally just punished Belgium with 16 points and 12 rebounds. THE PRESSURE POINT France wants multiplication. Germany wants preservation. If the hosts keep the possession count clean and the crowd engaged, the favorite has to execute instead of simply overwhelm. SEMIFINAL 02 · SPAIN vs USA Can Spain keep USA from becoming an avalanche? USA’s 108 to 56 quarterfinal win was not merely a response to the close call against Italy. It was a warning. Five players reached double figures, the team produced 31 assists, and the score became the highest ever in a Women’s World Cup quarterfinal. USA also poured in 59 first-half points, a quarterfinal record. It does not need one scorer to own the night because the next lineup can change the terms. Spain cannot trade runs. FIBA’s semifinal preview gives USA a 17.3 to 8.8 edge in fast-break points and a 48.8 to 29 advantage in bench scoring. Spain’s route is deliberate: protect the ball, make the game live in the half court and trust Martin and Fam to create without feeding USA’s transition. The underdog does not need forty perfect minutes. It needs forty connected ones. THE PRESSURE POINT Spain wants a negotiation. USA wants a landslide. The longer the score stays tight, the more each empty American possession starts to feel expensive. Germany has the best upset ingredients against a high-speed favorite: few turnovers, superior rebounding and a home crowd that has already watched one giant fall. Spain has the best upset blueprint against USA: shrink the possession game, keep the ball out of transition and make the favorite solve pressure late. items.title: Gold Is Earned Twice | USA 97, France 79
items.keywords: A dashboard-driven Food for Thought analysis of USA's 97-79 comeback victory over France in the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup final. Jackie Young and Kahleah Copper celebrate World Cup gold Gold Is Earned Twice | USA 97, France 79 Food for Thought • FIBA World Cup Final Gold Is Earned Twice. France won the opening argument. Team USA won the adjustment. A 14-point hole became an 18-point championship victory because experience did not panic when pressure arrived. UNITED STATES WORLD CHAMPIONS 97–79 FRANCE WORLD SILVER World Cup celebration · WNBA.com. Photo source The final was two different games. For roughly a quarter and a half, France looked like the team that had solved the tournament. The spacing was clean, the threes were falling, and Gabby Williams powered a 21–2 burst that pushed the lead to 14. Then the United States stopped chasing the game and started controlling it. Largest USA deficit 14 France turned early rhythm into real scoreboard pressure. Halftime 43–45 Clark's buzzer-beating three made the comeback feel inevitable before it was complete. Decisive quarter 30–12 USA flipped the final with an 18-point advantage in the third. Quarter-by-quarter dashboard Team Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4 Final USA 17 26 30 24 97 France 20 25 12 22 79 Glass dashboard 36–27 USA's nine-rebound advantage created the extra possessions France could not afford to surrender. Momentum map 17–20 France leads after Q1 21–2 French run creates separation 43–45 USA closes before halftime 73–57 USA owns the third quarter Who carried the weight? USA scoring leaders Stewart 22 Young 18 Copper 15 Gray 12 Clark 12 Captain's line 22 + 9 Breanna Stewart paired a game-high 22 points with nine rebounds, one board shy of a championship double-double. France scoring leaders 41 Dominique Malonga scored 21 and Gabby Williams added 20. Together they produced more than half of France's points. Primary creator 7 AST Williams paired her scoring with seven assists, carrying both creation and finishing responsibility. USA table-setters 5 + 5 Chelsea Gray and Jackie Young each recorded five assists while adding 30 combined points. What went right, and what went wrong? USA: What went right No panic. The veterans answered France's 14-point lead possession by possession instead of trying to erase it with one shot. The halftime bridge. Clark's three at the horn cut the deficit to two and changed the emotional temperature of the game. The starting group took command. Stewart, Young, Copper and Gray combined scoring with steady decision-making. Rebounding traveled. A 36–27 edge gave USA second chances and helped prevent France from restarting its transition attack. The defense adjusted. France scored only 12 in the third as USA disrupted the rhythm that fueled the early run. USA: What went wrong The opening defense was reactive. France found driving lanes, kick-outs and early threes before USA established its physicality. Ball security wobbled. Clark finished with four turnovers, including early possessions where pressure held the ball in one place too long. The rotation tightened sharply. The veteran core carried heavy minutes while several young players had only brief opportunities. Free throws left points available. Reese's misses were part of an uneven night at the line that could matter in a closer rematch. France: What went right The game plan worked early. France spaced the floor, attacked decisively and landed the first true punch with a 21–2 run. Williams bent the defense. Her 20 points and seven assists forced USA to account for both her scoring and playmaking. Malonga kept growing into the moment. The 20-year-old center finished with a team-high 21 points and scored through the final stretch. France proved it belongs. Its first World Cup final ended with the nation's best finish, not a failed tournament. France: What went wrong The offense became harder to reproduce. The early shotmaking did not survive USA's defensive adjustment. The third quarter broke the structure. A 30–12 period erased the lead and forced France to play from urgency rather than flow. The glass tilted the possession count. France lost the rebound battle by nine and could not consistently end USA possessions. The supporting scoring thinned. Williams and Malonga combined for 41, but the rest of France produced only 38. Food for Thought France showed that USA can be moved. USA showed that moving a champion and finishing one are still two different assignments. The 97–79 score looks comfortable. The path was not. That is what made this final useful: USA's crown is intact, but the world is no longer waiting politely outside the throne room. Four playoff teams took the floor after the FIBA break. Four won. Atlanta, Washington, Dallas and Las Vegas combined to win by 131 points. The postseason did not start early, but somebody forgot to tell them that. See the return board Playoff pressure Connecting to the 2026 W feed Return-night spotlight: Jackie Young scored a career-high 35 in Las Vegas' win at Seattle. Image via WNBA.com. WIN MARGIN 32.8 DASHBOARD · BERLIN → THE W Apparently, Berlin was the warmup. Several Team USA players went from a World Cup title in Berlin on September 13 straight back into WNBA playoff positioning four nights later. Their club roles changed. The production did not disappear. 01 LVA · GOLD MEDALIST Jackie Young 35 PTS · 5 AST · 4 3PM Twenty-two points in the first quarter tied the WNBA record for points in a quarter. She finished with a new career high. 02 ATL · GOLD MEDALIST Angel Reese 30 PTS · 10 REB Her 30th double-double extended her single-season WNBA record, and Atlanta needed fewer than 25 minutes from her to get it. 03 DAL · GOLD MEDALIST Paige Bueckers 19 PTS Dallas won its fifth straight and tied the franchise single-season wins record while Bueckers shifted immediately back into a primary club role. 04 WAS · GOLD MEDALIST Kiki Iriafen 18 PTS · 11 REB Washington's young frontcourt returned from Berlin and helped turn a road game into a 30-point win. 05 ATL · GOLD MEDALIST Rhyne Howard 10 PTS · 8 AST · 4 STL Her 129th three of the season broke the WNBA single-season record even on a night when her shot was not the main reason Atlanta won. From Berlin back to club basketball: Paige Bueckers returned to Dallas for a fifth straight Wings win. Image via WNBA.com. FOOD FOR THOUGHT Return night did not settle the race. It made it louder. There was a reasonable question hanging over September 17: what would the playoff teams look like after the World Cup break? Atlanta, Washington, Dallas and Las Vegas answered it with a combined 424 points and not one close finish. Atlanta did not return quietly. Angel Reese needed less than 25 minutes to put up 30 points and 10 rebounds in a 103–59 win over Connecticut. Rhyne Howard missed her first eight attempts from three and still found the shot that mattered historically: No. 129, the new WNBA single-season record. Atlanta also got a franchise scoring record from Allisha Gray. The larger playoff point is not that every Dream star shot perfectly. It is that Atlanta won by 44 without needing perfection from any one of them. Jackie Young brought the gold-medal heat home. Las Vegas saved the loudest closing statement for Seattle. Young scored 22 in the first quarter and 35 for the game as the Aces won 114–77. A'ja Wilson added 29 points, seven rebounds and five assists. If the concern was whether the international turnaround would dull Las Vegas' edge, the first quarter answered before most people had settled into the late window. Las Vegas at Seattle, September 17, 2026. Scott Eklund/NBAE via Las Vegas Aces game gallery. Washington's young core looked ready for the next assignment. The Mystics beat Chicago 110–80 behind 20 points from Shakira Austin and an 18-point, 11-rebound double-double from Kiki Iriafen. Washington's value here was not just the margin. It was the shape of the win: five starters in double figures, efficient offense and a defense that turned Chicago mistakes into immediate pressure. Dallas keeps removing the word “surprise.” The Wings beat Los Angeles 97–77 for a fifth straight win. Paige Bueckers scored 19, while Jessica Shepard posted 13 points, 11 rebounds and 12 assists for her fifth triple-double of the season. Dallas tied the franchise single-season wins record. At some point, a hot streak becomes a basketball identity, and Dallas is getting very close to that line. Phoenix and Portland gave the night its thriller. The only game without a playoff team was also the only game decided by one possession. Phoenix beat Portland 94–91 behind 22 bench points from Shay Ciezki and an 18-point, eight-rebound, six-assist line from Alyssa Thomas. Those teams are out of the postseason race, but September still matters when a franchise is deciding which habits and players belong in the next version of itself. The real takeaway Return night was not proof of what will happen in the playoffs. It was proof that the teams with postseason business did not need a grace period. Atlanta, Washington, Dallas and Las Vegas all scored at least 97. Three reached 100. None won by fewer than 20. The FIBA medals are already handed out. Now the currency is seeding, home court and rhythm. THE NIGHT IN ONE NUMBER +131 Combined point differential for the four playoff teams that played. ATLANTA +44 The largest win of the night. LAS VEGAS 114 The highest team score of the night. DALLAS 5 Consecutive wins after beating Los Angeles. Golden State kept the pressure on at the top, Dallas stretched its winning streak to six, Atlanta created a little room in the home-court race, and Minnesota answered Sunday by moving to 32–10. Here is the We Know the W guide to the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup, who matters, what changes when W players put on national-team jerseys, which games deserve an alarm, and why winning your group is worth more than bragging rights. By We Know the W Published September 3, 2026 Updated for final World Cup rosters Home › No Offseason › FIBA World Cup › Watcher's Guide THE 30-SECOND BRIEFING No passport required. An alarm clock helps. Berlin is six hours ahead of Eastern time. The tournament runs September 4 through 13, expands to 16 teams for the first time, and squeezes 36 games into 10 days. Group winners earn a direct trip to the quarterfinals, which makes every early result matter. WHEN Sept. 4–13 Group play ends Sept. 7. Qualification games are Sept. 8–9, quarterfinals Sept. 10, semifinals Sept. 12, medals Sept. 13. WHERE Berlin Games are staged at Berlin Arena and Max-Schmeling-Halle in Germany. FIELD 16 teams Four groups of four, expanded from the 12-team field used in 2022. THE PRIZE One less game Finish first in your group and skip the single-elimination qualification round. Why the group winner matters: second and third place do advance, but they have to survive an extra elimination game. In a compressed tournament, winning the group buys the rarest luxury in Berlin: rest. SET YOUR ALARM · TEAM USA Three group games, three very different clocks. Every Team USA game is on TNT and streams on HBO Max. TNT/truTV carry 17 of the tournament's 36 games, while HBO Max streams all 36. Courtside 1891 on DAZN also carries the World Cup live or on demand, subject to local availability. Hungary turns Dorka Juhász into a featured star, Nigeria brings AfroBasket pedigree, and Korea can punish teams that lose shooters. GROUP C Belgium · Australia · Türkiye · Puerto Rico 🇧🇪 Belgium 🇦🇺 Australia 🇹🇷 Türkiye 🇵🇷 Puerto Rico The read: This is the group to circle in ink. Belgium's movement and Emma Meesseman meet Australia's size, experience and Sandy Brondello. Türkiye has Kennedy Burke, while Puerto Rico has the freedom of a team nobody should overlook. GROUP D USA · China · Italy · Czechia 🇺🇸 USA 🇨🇳 China 🇮🇹 Italy 🇨🇿 Czechia The read: USA is the favorite, but China gives the group serious interior size and Italy arrives with EuroBasket continuity plus Cecilia Zandalasini. Czechia's job is to make the favorites uncomfortable enough for one result to rearrange the bracket. PHOTO BOARD · MEDAL RADAR Six teams worth learning before the ball goes up. These are real team and tournament photos pulled from official FIBA coverage. The first five are also FIBA's latest subjective Smart Power Rankings top five. Germany gets the sixth spot here because the host crowd changes the temperature of the whole event. SMART POWER RANK · 1 🇺🇸 USA Eleven World Cup titles, four straight, and enough depth to remain No. 1 even after A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum withdrew. Photo / team source ↗ SMART POWER RANK · 2 🇫🇷 France Gabby Williams, Marine Johannès, Dominique Malonga and a roster built to finish the job that ended one point short in Paris. Photo / team source ↗ SMART POWER RANK · 3 🇪🇸 Spain Megan Gustafson, Maria Conde, Awa Fam and Raquel Carrera give Spain size, skill and a real podium ceiling. Photo / team source ↗ SMART POWER RANK · 4 🇧🇪 Belgium The Belgian Cats already own back-to-back EuroBasket titles. Emma Meesseman and Julie Allemand are trying to turn continental dominance into a first global medal. Photo / team source ↗ SMART POWER RANK · 5 🇦🇺 Australia Alanna Smith, Ezi Magbegor and Steph Talbot keep the Opals dangerous even after a pre-tournament roster hit. Photo / team source ↗ HOST NATION 🇩🇪 Germany Leonie Fiebich, Luisa Geiselsöder and home-court noise make Germany the team most capable of turning a normal group game into an event. Photo / team source ↗ WNBA PASSPORT STAMP The W is everywhere in Berlin. The WNBA's Sept. 3 primer counted 51 current WNBA players, 23.5% of the league's 217 rostered players, across 14 of 15 WNBA teams and 15 of the 16 World Cup nations. Final-roster movement can change counts at the margins, so We Know the W treats FIBA's confirmed roster tracker as the live authority. 51 WNBA players in the WNBA primer The United States supplies 12. France has eight. Australia has seven. Spain has six. Germany has four. Belgium has three. Italy and Nigeria have two each. China, Czechia, Hungary, Japan, Korea, Mali and Türkiye each have one in the WNBA count. USA 12 France 8 Australia 7 Spain 6 Germany 4 Belgium 3 THE CLUB STORY New York sends the biggest suitcase. The WNBA primer counted seven Liberty players headed to Berlin, representing six countries. Minnesota followed with six, Portland with five, and Atlanta, Golden State, Las Vegas and Seattle with four apiece. Chicago is the only WNBA team without a player in that primer, but Sky assistant Rena Wakama is still in Berlin as Nigeria's head coach. Open the WNBA primer ↗ Translation: if you already know the WNBA, you already know a lot of this tournament. The trick is recognizing that the same player may have a completely different job once the jersey changes. SAME PLAYER · DIFFERENT JOB National-team basketball changes the menu. A WNBA fifth option can become the whole offense. A 34-minute WNBA star can become a 20-minute specialist. That role change is one of the best reasons to watch FIBA. 🇭🇺 DORKA JUHÁSZ From Lynx role player to Hungary centerpiece She averaged 18.0 points and 9.0 rebounds in qualifying, opened with 35 points, and made the All-Star Five while helping Hungary reach its first World Cup in 28 years. 🇯🇵 MAI YAMAMOTO Bench spark in Vegas, engine for Japan Yamamoto led Japan in qualifying scoring, threes and steals, then earned All-Star Five honors. Watch how often the ball is in her hands compared with her Aces role. 🇫🇷 JANELLE SALAÜN Golden State weapon, France tournament MVP Salaün led France's qualifying team in scoring, rebounding and made threes, earning qualifying tournament MVP honors with outrageous efficiency. 🇺🇸 RHYNE HOWARD WNBA workhorse, USA luxury piece Howard leads the WNBA in minutes per game, but Team USA can spread creation and defense across 12 elite players. Less usage does not mean less importance. TEAM USA · DRIVE FOR FIVE New generation, same gold standard. USA is chasing a fifth consecutive World Cup title. A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum are out for health reasons, and Sonia Citron plus Kiki Iriafen have joined the final 12. Only five players from the 2024 Olympic team return, which makes this roster both overwhelmingly talented and unusually new. THE ANCHOR Breanna Stewart The veteran who keeps a roster with nine World Cup debutantes from feeling young. Playerpedia → THE CONNECTOR Napheesa Collier Defense, rebounding, cutting and lineup flexibility, all without needing the offense built around her. Playerpedia → THE TABLE SETTER Chelsea Gray The safest organizer when a young lineup needs the game slowed down and put in the right order. Playerpedia → THE DEBUT Caitlin Clark Qualifying MVP meets her first World Cup, with less required usage than she sees in Indiana. Playerpedia → THE DEBUT Paige Bueckers A secondary creator who can score without monopolizing possessions, ideal for a roster this deep. Playerpedia → THE PAINT Aliyah Boston Without Wilson, interior finishing, screens and defensive positioning become even more valuable. Playerpedia → THE GLASS Angel Reese Rebounding can swing short tournaments. Reese owns a skill that travels without needing a play called. Playerpedia → THE TWO-WAY KNIFE Jackie Young Guard bigger players, space the floor, attack a closeout, then do it again in another lineup. Playerpedia → THE LATE CALL Sonia Citron Defense and off-ball intelligence are useful when there is almost no time to install a new role. Playerpedia → THE LATE CALL Kiki Iriafen Already part of the qualifying program, she brings an athletic frontcourt option after Wilson's withdrawal. Playerpedia → GAMES TO CIRCLE Watch beyond the USA box. Opening weekend is packed with games that can decide who earns the quarterfinal bye and who gets dropped into the qualification-round traffic. 01 USA vs. China · Sept. 4 USA's speed and depth versus China's size. It is the first look at how Lawson redistributes the frontcourt after Wilson's withdrawal. 02 Spain vs. Germany · Sept. 4 A top-three Smart Power Rankings team versus the host. If Germany wants to turn Berlin into a run, this is the temperature check. 03 Belgium vs. Türkiye · Sept. 4 Belgium needs to establish control of Group C before the Opals game. Türkiye gets the first chance to make that group messy. 04 Hungary vs. France · Sept. 4 France's depth against Dorka Juhász in full national-team-star mode. 05 USA vs. Italy · Sept. 6 Italy brings continuity and Zandalasini's shotmaking. USA gets a European-style spacing and execution test. 06 Belgium vs. Australia · Sept. 7 The game most likely to decide Group C's direct quarterfinal ticket. 07 Japan vs. Spain · Sept. 7 Japan's pace and guard play versus Spain's size and half-court structure. 08 USA vs. Czechia · Sept. 7 The final Group D game, potentially the difference between a clean quarterfinal bye and extra bracket work. WATCH LIKE IT'S FIBA One rule wrinkle you will notice immediately. This World Cup is still played under the 2024 FIBA rules. The new 2026 rule changes do not take effect until October 1, after the tournament. RIM Once the ball hits the rim, it is live. Under FIBA basket-interference rules, players can tip or knock the ball after it touches the rim in situations that would still be protected by the imaginary cylinder in WNBA/NBA play. If a rebound suddenly looks like somebody swatted a ball off the iron, your eyes are not lying to you. WNBA MINDS ON FIBA SIDELINES The coaching crossover is deep too. AUSTRALIA Sandy Brondello The Toronto Tempo head coach leads the Opals. GERMANY Olaf Lange Toronto associate head coach leads the host nation. USA Kara Lawson + WNBA staff Stephanie White, Natalie Nakase and Nate Tibbetts are assistants. Jose Fernandez serves as scout coach. NIGERIA Rena Wakama The Chicago Sky assistant is D'Tigress head coach. BELGIUM Mike Thibault The three-time WNBA Coach of the Year leads the Belgian Cats. JAPAN Corey Gaines The 2009 WNBA champion coach leads Japan. THE RECEIPTS Where this guide came from. The WNBA primer was the starting point. One drought. One trophy. USA has not lost a World Cup game since 2006. France has never played in a World Cup final. Paris gave us a one point Olympic gold medal game. Berlin gives us the rematch. By We Know the W September 12, 2026 Dashboard refreshes from FIBA connected results Home › Snack Shak › USA vs France Final CHAMPIONSHIP GAME FINAL SET USA 11 WORLD TITLES VS SEP 13 · 20:00 BERLIN 2:00 PM ET FRA FIRST WORLD CUP FINAL Counting down to the title game… Official FIBA game center ↗ USA · DEFENDING CHAMPIONS THE REMATCH USA vs FRANCE PARIS 2024 WAS 67 TO 66 FRANCE · FIRST TIME FINALIST REAL IMAGERY ONLY · All player portraits are official FIBA images and all action photos are real tournament photography. No AI imagery is used on this page. THE QUICK BITE The crown has history on one side and pressure on both. USA owns the streak. France owns the most explosive scoring profile of this tournament. Something has to give. The United States walks into Sunday carrying 35 consecutive World Cup wins, four straight world titles and a 71 game winning streak across World Cup and Olympic play. The last World Cup loss came in 2006. Since then, the program has turned global pressure into routine, at least from the outside looking in. France is the opposite kind of story. This is its first World Cup final and its first guaranteed medal since taking bronze at the inaugural tournament in 1953. Yet nothing about this run feels accidental. France is 5 and 0, averages 96.2 points and has outscored opponents by 35.6 points per game. USA is also 5 and 0, but at 87.6 points per game and a plus 27.8 average margin. Then there is the memory neither team needs explained. The 2024 Olympic final ended USA 67, France 66. One point separated gold from heartbreak. Two years later, Gabby Williams and France get another shot at the same flag, this time for a trophy the country has never lifted. SHAK'S BITE USA is trying to extend an era. France is trying to end one, and begin its own. 35 STRAIGHT USA WORLD CUP WINS 71 STRAIGHT WORLD CUP + OLYMPIC WINS 11 USA WORLD TITLES 73 YEARS SINCE FRANCE'S LAST WORLD CUP MEDAL LIVE COUNTRY DASHBOARD Same record. Very different road. The team cards pull the latest completed World Cup results from the We Know the W FIBA feed. If the final goes live, the game card above can update with it. Statistics are through the semifinals. 🇺🇸 USA 🇫🇷 France Official FIBA headshots only. The photographs above are not generated images. WORLD CUP HISTORY One program owns the record book. The other is writing a new page. Tap either country to move between its all time World Cup résumé and the history at stake Sunday. USA HISTORY FRANCE HISTORY WHAT DECIDES IT Three questions, forty minutes. The final is not really USA depth versus France shooting. It is whether either team can force the other to abandon what has made it comfortable. 01 Can USA make Gabby Williams work for every touch? Williams enters the final as France's engine, scorer, connector and defensive disruptor. She had 22 points, five rebounds, five assists and four steals in the semifinal. USA has enough bodies to change the matchup possession by possession. The question is whether the changes slow her down or simply give her a new problem to solve. 02 Can France turn this into another one possession game? Spain showed the route. Slow USA's early offense, make the half court crowded and keep the score close enough that every late decision becomes heavy. France has more offensive firepower than Spain and already knows what a one point championship game against USA feels like. 03 Which version of USA's depth arrives? Breanna Stewart led the semifinal with 16 points. Jackie Young has been the team's leading scorer across the tournament, Caitlin Clark leads the assists, and Rhyne Howard has supplied the ball pressure. USA does not need one superhero. It needs its waves to stay connected. THE PICK IS NOT THE POINT USA should be favored because history, depth and late game defense have survived every test. France, however, has been the more explosive team by scoring margin. This is the rare final where calling the favorite obvious would ignore what the tournament has actually shown. USA is still the favorite, but this is no longer the same twelve-player team that was announced in August. Losing A’ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum removes an elite interior anchor and a veteran pressure guard just days before tipoff. Adding Kiki Iriafen and Sonia Citron keeps the talent level high, but it makes chemistry, role clarity and adjustment time even more important. 01 THE ROSTER CHANGE Two stars out, two Mystics in USA Basketball announced that Wilson and Plum will miss the World Cup for health reasons. Plum's calf has not fully healed, while Wilson is taking needed recovery time after a heavy WNBA workload. Washington teammates Iriafen and Citron step into the twelve-player group together. The names still scream favorite. The question is how quickly a changed roster can sound like one team. 02 THE BACKCOURT Citron changes the guard puzzle Caitlin Clark and Paige Bueckers arrive for their first World Cup alongside Chelsea Gray, Jackie Young and Rhyne Howard. Citron adds another versatile guard and wing who can defend, move without the ball and play within lineups that do not require every touch to run through her. Without Plum's downhill pressure, USA may lean even more on pace, spacing and multiple playmakers sharing creation. 03 THE FRONTCOURT Wilson's absence reshapes the paint Wilson was the 2022 World Cup MVP and the most outstanding player of the Paris 2024 Olympics. Her absence changes both ends of the floor. Breanna Stewart, Napheesa Collier, Aliyah Boston and Angel Reese now carry more of the interior burden, while Iriafen gives USA another athletic forward who already has experience with this year's national-team program. Watch who closes games at the five, who protects the rim and whether USA can still dominate the glass without Wilson. 04 THE GROUP First place is worth more than bragging rights The winner of each group moves directly to the quarterfinals. Second and third place teams have to play an extra qualification game. That makes the three Group D games more than a warm up. USA has the depth to survive an extra game, but there is no reason to volunteer for one. The clean path is simple: win Group D, rest, then make somebody else survive the extra round. 05 GROUP D SWING GAME China and Italy could decide the shape of the group FIBA has circled China against Italy as the pivotal game behind USA. China has the interior size. Italy returns to the World Cup after a 32 year wait and arrives with confidence from its EuroBasket bronze. Czechia enters with injury concerns, which makes every result in the middle of the table matter even more. USA should control the top of Group D. China and Italy may decide who gets the better road behind them. 06 MEDAL RADAR The real pressure is waiting outside Group D FIBA's newest power ranking has USA first, France second, Australia third, Spain fourth and Belgium fifth. France came within one possession of taking Olympic gold in Paris. Australia has experience and size. Belgium can carve teams apart with passing. Spain has a path that could build confidence before the medal rounds. USA remains the favorite, but removing two experienced Olympic guards and forwards from the original roster makes the medal rounds less automatic than they looked a day ago. MY READ USA should still win Group D, but the margin for sloppy chemistry just got smaller. Wilson and Plum brought championship experience, late-game certainty and established roles. Iriafen and Citron bring youth, versatility and the advantage of already playing together in Washington. The talent remains overwhelming. The new test is how quickly this version of Team USA becomes connected enough to make that talent feel overwhelming on the floor. items.title: The Film Room
items.keywords: Learn basketball positions, offense, defense, strategy and how to watch WNBA film with illustrated coaching boards from We Know the W. We Know the W home The Film Room | We Know the W THE W VAULT · LEARN THE GAME THE FILM ROOM Basketball education without assuming you already know the language. Learn the roles, see the actions on the clipboard and discover what is really happening before the ball reaches the rim. Home › The W Vault › The Film Room TODAY'S FILM Read the floor. O = offense · X = defense → = movement · ⇢ = pass START WITH THE WHY The shot is the ending. The story starts earlier. A screen changes an angle. A defender tags the roller. A shooter relocates. One extra pass turns a crowded possession into an open look. The Film Room helps you follow that chain instead of watching only the ball. 1 Shape Where are the ten players spaced? 2 Action What screen, cut or matchup starts the play? 3 Reaction How does the defense answer? 4 Advantage Where does the offense find two-on-one? 01 · POSITIONS Five starting spots. Far more than five jobs. Traditional positions are a helpful starting point, but modern lineups are fluid. A forward may initiate the offense, a guard may screen, and a center may stretch the floor or make decisions from the elbow. Positionless does not mean jobless. It means the lineup can assign ballhandling, screening, spacing, rebounding and defensive responsibilities by skill rather than height alone. 02 · OFFENSE Create an advantage. Make the defense choose. Good offense is not just making hard shots. It uses spacing, pace, screens and quick decisions to force two defenders to guard one action—then moves the ball before the defense can recover. SPACING Give the action room Keep help defenders far enough away that every double-team creates an open teammate. PAINT TOUCH Collapse the defense A drive, roll or post catch inside the lane can pull defenders inward and unlock kick-out passes. SECOND SIDE Attack the next rotation If the first action bends the defense without producing a shot, reverse the ball and attack before everyone resets. 0.5 DECISIONS Shoot, pass or drive Fast decisions keep an advantage alive. Holding the ball gives the defense time to recover. 03 · DEFENSE Protect the paint without surrendering the arc. Every coverage is a tradeoff. The defense decides what it can live with, communicates the plan, helps on time and finishes the possession with a rebound. 1 Contain Keep the ball in front. → 2 Help Stop the immediate danger. → 3 Rotate Cover the helper's player. → 4 Rebound End the possession. 04 · STRATEGY Every game is a set of choices. Coaches balance lineup strengths, opponent tendencies, foul trouble, pace, score and time. A strategy is not automatically good or bad; it is a bet on which tradeoff favors your team. 01 Pace control Run after misses and turnovers, or slow the game to protect possessions and organize half-court execution. Ask: Who benefits from more possessions? 02 Matchup hunting Use screens and movement to place the preferred defender in the action—or force a switch the offense wants. Ask: Who is being made to defend repeatedly? 03 Possession math Three-point volume, free throws, offensive rebounds and turnovers shape how efficiently a team uses its chances. Ask: Where are the extra possessions coming from? 04 Lineup geometry Shooting stretches the floor, size protects the rim, speed increases pressure and versatility expands coverage choices. Ask: What did the substitution change? 05 Foul and timeout economy Late-game choices depend on team fouls, remaining timeouts, advance-the-ball rules and who can be protected. Ask: What resources remain? 06 Two-for-one Near the end of a quarter, a quick first shot may create time for one more possession after the opponent attacks. Ask: Did the first shot leave enough clock? STYLE SHORTCUTS Memorable names for what you see These are Film Room teaching labels—not official team nicknames. The Track Meet Run, pressure and turn every rebound into a race. The Boa Constrictor Shrink space, force late-clock decisions and wear an offense down. Paint the Town Attack the rim, post mismatches and own the offensive glass. Mismatch Hunting Season Screen until the preferred matchup appears, then clear a side. 05 · WATCH LIKE A COACH Watch one possession twice. First follow the ball. On the replay, ignore it. Track the screener, the low defender and the player in the weak-side corner. That second viewing is where the hidden work appears. YOUR FILM LOG Four lines are enough Lineup: Who is on the floor? Action: What starts the possession? Coverage: How does the defense respond? Result: What shot or turnover follows—and why? Try tracking five straight possessions instead of one entire game. Patterns get loud very quickly. KEEP THE GLOSSARY OPEN Hear a term you do not know? The expanded Basketball Dictionary translates coaching language into plain English, includes what to watch for and filters the full glossary by topic. Open the Basketball Dictionary →

items.title: Front Office 101 | The W Vault
items.keywords: Front Office 101 explains WNBA contracts, salary caps, hardship deals, waivers, free agency, core designations, roster limits, draft lotteries, expansion drafts, trade rules and the labor history behind the 2026 CBA in plain language. Front Office 101 | The W Vault | We Know the W THE W VAULT · BUSINESS OF THE GAME FRONT OFFICE 101 Contracts, cap space, roster spots, waivers, free agency, drafts and trades without the legal-language headache. Learn what the transaction means before deciding whether your team won the move. START HERE · 2026 RULES SNAPSHOT The front office board. The rules below reflect the 2026 WNBA framework and are written for fans, not cap lawyers. When the CBA or league procedures change, this page should change with them. 2026 Why this page is date stamped The 2026 season brought a new salary structure, developmental roster spots and a two-team expansion draft. Treat these numbers as the current-season rules, not permanent league history. TEAM SALARY CAP $7.0M The 2026 team payroll ceiling announced with the new CBA framework. STANDARD ROSTER 12 players The normal 2026 standard roster, with league exceptions available in specific situations. DEVELOPMENTAL SPOTS 2 players Separate development positions used for practice, growth and limited game activation. 2026 TRADE DEADLINE Aug. 2 3:00 p.m. ET. After the deadline, normal in-season trades are closed. LABOR HISTORY · HOW THESE RULES GOT HERE The Union Behind the Deal The CBA is not just a rulebook. It is the result of players organizing, bargaining and voting on the terms of their work. NNEKA + THE WNBPA Meet the players who secured the 2026 CBA Nneka Ogwumike led publicly, but the bargaining work included Kelsey Plum, Napheesa Collier, Breanna Stewart, Alysha Clark, Elizabeth Williams, Brianna Turner, 26 team player representatives, union staff and the broader membership. Read the Herstory feature → THE UNION PROCESS How collective bargaining works The WNBPA negotiating committee represents the full spectrum of the league, players receive updates and opportunities to participate, and the membership votes on the final agreement. Open the WNBPA CBA desk ↗ CONTRACT LANGUAGE What exactly did she sign? “Signed” can mean very different things. The contract type tells you how much control the team has, how long the player may stay and whether the deal uses a standard roster spot. 01 Contracts, in plain English A player contract is the agreement that gives a team the right to employ a player under league and CBA rules. Salary, years, guarantees, options, roster status and special designations determine what happens next. Think of it this way: “Signed” tells you she joined the organization. The contract type tells you how permanent, expensive and flexible that move is. STANDARD Regular WNBA contract Counts toward the standard roster and team salary rules. ROOKIE SCALE Drafted-player structure Young players enter under the league’s rookie contract system, with the 2026 scale substantially increased. DEVELOPMENTAL Development pipeline Two spots per team, outside the standard salary cap, with practice access and limited game activation. HARDSHIP Temporary roster relief Used when league-approved circumstances make the normal roster impractical because players are unavailable. QUALIFYING OFFER Free-agency control tool A team can preserve certain negotiating or matching rights by making the appropriate qualifying offer. CORE OFFER Veteran control designation A one-year fully guaranteed supermax qualifying offer tied to the Core designation. 02 Salary cap The salary cap is the team payroll limit, not a maximum salary for one player. Teams have to fit their standard contracts within the league’s cap rules while still filling the required roster. 2026: the league announced a $7.0 million team cap, a $1.4 million maximum salary level and minimum salaries ranging from $270,000 to $300,000 based on service. Why it matters: A team can love a player and still be unable to add her unless the contract, roster slot and cap math work together. 03 Guaranteed vs. flexible money Not every contract has the same protection. Guarantee language affects how much salary remains owed or charged if a player is waived. Fan translation: A guaranteed deal is harder to simply erase. A more flexible deal gives the front office more room to change the roster. Watch the transaction wording: “waived,” “released,” “signed,” “converted” and “rest-of-season” are clues that the contract status changed. ROSTER MATH Why a team can need a player and still not have a spot. A front office is managing people, money and roster categories at the same time. “How many players are on the team?” is no longer answered by one number alone. 04 Roster limits For 2026, the WNBA says teams can roster 12 standard players and can also carry two developmental players. If a team drops below 12 standard players during the regular season, the league’s 2026 free-agency guidance says it generally has 72 hours to fill the spot. Plain English: The 12 standard spots are the main roster. Developmental contracts are a separate lane. Important: hardship and other league-approved exceptions can temporarily change the normal headcount. 05 Developmental contracts The 2026 system allows two developmental roster spots. These players can practice with the team, receive stipends and benefits, and can be activated for up to 12 games. Think “in-house pipeline,” not full standard roster spot. A developmental signing lets a team keep working with a player without treating the contract exactly like a normal standard deal. Site connection: We Know the W keeps developmental status visible in Playerpedia and Player Movement so the player does not disappear from the roster story. 06 Hardship deals A hardship mechanism gives a team temporary roster relief when enough players are unavailable and the league approves an exception. That can allow a team to add a replacement even when normal roster limits would otherwise block the move. Plain English: The league is saying, “You do not have enough healthy or available players to operate normally, so you may temporarily add help.” Why the contract can be short-lived: hardship relief exists because of the unavailable players. When the underlying hardship changes, the replacement player’s roster situation can change too. That is why a hardship signing and a later waiver can both be logical front-office moves. FREE AGENCY Free agent does not always mean completely free. Years of service and the team’s qualifying offer determine how much control the previous team keeps. 07 Restricted free agent Under the 2026 rules, a player who is out of contract with four years of WNBA service can become a restricted free agent if her team sends the required Restricted Qualifying Offer. Plain English: She may negotiate with another team, but her previous team gets the right to match a multi-year offer sheet. If the old team matches: the player stays on the offer-sheet terms. If it does not match, she joins the new team. 08 Reserved player A player with three years of service or fewer can become Reserved if her previous team extends a Reserved Qualifying Offer. Plain English: This is more restrictive than RFA. The prior team holds the exclusive negotiating rights unless it declines to make the qualifying offer. Why fans miss this: a player can be “out of contract” but still not have the freedom of a veteran unrestricted free agent. 09 Core designation A team can have at most one veteran free agent under the Core designation at a time. The Core Qualifying Offer is a fully guaranteed one-year supermax offer, and the designating team controls where the player can directly sign during free agency. Closest translation: It functions somewhat like a franchise tag, but the WNBA’s rules are their own system. Movement is still possible: the player and team can agree to a sign-and-trade. Starting in 2027, players with seven or more years of service cannot be designated as Core Players. 10 Unrestricted free agent An unrestricted free agent can negotiate and sign with another team, subject to league rules, cap space and any special status that may apply. Plain English: Her old team does not have RFA matching rights just because she used to play there. But: “UFA” does not mean every team can afford the same offer or has the same roster opening. DRAFT ROOM Lottery luck, expansion strategy and rights. The college draft and an expansion draft solve different problems. One assigns incoming talent. The other helps a new franchise acquire existing league players and rights. 11 WNBA Draft Lottery The lottery determines the earliest first-round picks among eligible non-playoff teams. For the 2026 Draft Lottery, five teams participated. Fourteen numbered balls generated combinations for the No. 1 and No. 2 picks, then the remaining lottery teams were ordered at Nos. 3 through 5 by their cumulative two-season records. Plain English: Being the worst team does not automatically guarantee the first pick. The lottery adds chance at the top, while recent record still matters. Trade wrinkle: the team in the lottery is not always the team that owns the pick. Previously traded first-rounders can move lottery chances to another franchise. 12 Expansion Draft An expansion draft lets a new franchise select players or rights from existing teams before its first season. In 2026, the 13 existing teams could protect up to five players for the Portland Fire and Toronto Tempo expansion draft. 2026 format: Portland and Toronto alternated over two rounds, each with up to six selections per round. No existing team could lose more than two unprotected players, up to one per round. Not just active players: the submitted roster lists could include active, suspended, draft-list/reserved, core and retired-list rights. Open the full Expansion Draft 101 → 13 Draft picks can be assets before they become players WNBA teams can trade draft picks. For the 2026 Draft, the league said picks could be traded until the night before the draft. Once a selection was actually made, the selected player could then be traded during or after the draft. Plain English: “Pick No. 8” is an asset. After the name is called, the asset becomes the rights to that drafted player. That is why draft-night graphics can change fast: a team can select a player for another team as part of an agreed transaction. TRANSACTION DESK Trades and waivers are different exits. A trade sends a contract or basketball rights to another team as part of an exchange. A waiver removes a player from the roster and exposes her to the league’s waiver process. 14 Trade rules Teams can exchange players, contracts, rights and eligible draft assets when the transaction satisfies league rules. The 2026 in-season trade deadline was August 2 at 3:00 p.m. ET. Plain English: A trade is not just “Player A for Player B.” Cap space, roster spots, draft rights and contract status can all be part of the math. Special case: a Core player can still move through an agreed sign-and-trade. Expansion-draft teams could also make pre-draft agreements about selecting or not selecting players. 15 Waivers When a team waives a player, it removes her from its active roster and places her into the league’s waiver process. Another team may be able to claim her under the applicable rules. If she clears waivers, her next status depends on her contract and rights situation. Plain English: “Waived” does not mean retired, erased or permanently out of the league. 2026 playoff note: August 24 was the league’s waiver date tied to playoff eligibility. That is one reason late-season waiver timing matters. 16 Follow the transaction from headline to roster A move is not fully understood until you answer four questions: What happened to the player? What did the old team give up or gain? What rights does the new team now have? What changed in the roster/cap picture? STEP 1 Transaction Signed, waived, claimed, traded, cored or converted. STEP 2 Contract Standard, rookie, developmental, hardship or free-agent rights. STEP 3 Roster Standard spot, developmental spot or exception. STEP 4 Cap + rights Salary impact, matching rights, draft rights or future assets. STEP 5 Basketball impact Who plays, who becomes available and what the rotation gains or loses. HEADLINE TRANSLATOR Transaction decoder. Use this when Player Movement posts a new line and you want to know what the verb actually means. Term What it means What to check next Signed The player and team entered a contract. Contract type, length, roster category and whether another player had to move. Re-signed The player stayed with the same organization on a new agreement. Free-agent status, term and whether rights such as RFA/Core affected the deal. Waived The team removed the player from its roster and sent her through waivers. Claim, free-agent status, guarantee/cap impact and Playerpedia status. Claimed Another team acquired the player through waivers. New team, roster spot and contract status. Traded Player, contract, rights or draft assets moved between teams in an approved exchange. Every incoming/outgoing asset and the new cap/roster picture. Restricted The player may seek an outside multi-year offer sheet, but the prior team can match. Who holds matching rights and the offer-sheet window. Reserved The prior team holds exclusive negotiating rights after the proper qualifying offer. Years of service and whether the qualifying offer was made. Cored The team used its Core designation and controls direct free-agent negotiations. Core offer, potential sign-and-trade and future core eligibility. Developmental The player joined one of the team’s two 2026 developmental spots. Activation count, standard-roster openings and later conversion/signing possibilities. Hardship League-approved temporary roster relief allowed the team to add a player. Which unavailable players triggered the exception and when the hardship can end. USE THE LESSON Go from rulebook to real roster. Front Office 101 is designed to sit beside the live parts of We Know the W, so a definition can immediately connect to an actual player, move, team or draft. TRANSACTION WIRE Player Movement See signings, waivers, claims, trades and developmental deals in real time. Open the wire → ROSTER CONTEXT Availability See the injury and availability situations that can create hardship needs. Check availability → PLAYER STATUS Playerpedia Follow active, free-agent and retired status without losing transaction history. Search players → DEEPER DRAFT FILE Expansion Draft 101 Go deeper on protection lists, selection strategy and expansion rights. Open the file → OFFICIAL RECEIPTS Where these rules come from. 2026 CBA FRAMEWORK WNBA/WNBPA announcement covering the $7.0M 2026 salary cap, salary levels, rookie scale changes and the 2027 Core eligibility change. Read the official release ↗ FREE AGENCY WNBA 2026 Free Agency: Decoded explains RFA, Reserved players, Core designations, 12 standard roster spots and two developmental spots. Read the official explainer ↗ EXPANSION DRAFT The official 2026 Expansion Draft FAQ explains protection lists, two rounds, selection limits and potential unrestricted free agents. Read the official FAQ ↗ DRAFT LOTTERY The league’s 2026 lottery FAQ explains the five-team field, combination drawing and two-season record ordering. Read the lottery FAQ ↗ SEASON DEADLINES The official 2026 key dates provide the trade deadline, waiver playoff-eligibility date, roster cut-down dates and postseason calendar. NEW PRIMARY ICON · REVEALED OCTOBER 29, 2026 Four stars for four titles. A comet streaking toward Houston's next chapter. The Houston Comets return for the 2027 WNBA season after the league approved the sale and relocation of the Connecticut Sun to Houston. The refreshed red, navy and silver identity carries the name into its next era. Behind the name Around the W Expansion Watch 2027 tip-off Toyota Center Fertitta Entertainment BEHIND THE NAME Space City gets its Comets back. A name made for Houston Comets joined Houston’s space-themed sports vocabulary alongside the NBA’s Rockets when the WNBA launched in 1997. The name fits Space City, but Houston’s women built a legacy all their own: the original Comets won the first four WNBA championships, from 1997 through 2000. Read the naming history ↗ 1997 ORIGINAL · 2027 RETURN One returning name. A connected franchise trail. The original Comets played from 1997 to 2008 and won the league’s first four championships. Houston’s official return announcement says their records and history carry forward into this next chapter. The relocating organization began as the Orlando Miracle, became the Connecticut Sun in 2003, and returns as the Comets for 2027. Name trail: Houston Comets legacy (1997–2008) · Orlando Miracle → Connecticut Sun (through 2026) → Houston Comets (2027 return). The primary icon pairs an upward-slanted H with a basketball comet forming its crossbar. Four stars honor Houston’s four consecutive WNBA championships from 1997 through 2000. Three stars are silver, and the fourth is white for Texas. The official color guide names Comets Red, Houston Comets Blue and Houston Comets Silver: Pantone 186 C, 289 C and 422 C. RETURN APPROVED · MAY 13, 2026 The dynasty returns through relocation. The WNBA and NBA Boards of Governors unanimously approved Tilman J. Fertitta's purchase of the Connecticut Sun and the team's move to Houston beginning with the 2027 season. The Comets will be owned and operated by Fertitta Entertainment and play at Toyota Center. Important: this is not a new expansion franchise. Houston replaces Connecticut on the league map in 2027, so the WNBA remains at 15 teams until Cleveland joins in 2028. items.title: Kelsey Mitchell Becomes the WNBA's First 1,000 Point Guard
items.keywords: Kelsey Mitchell became the first guard in WNBA history to score 1,000 points in a single season, reaching 1,001 points for Indiana on August 28, 2026. Kelsey Mitchell Becomes the WNBA's First 1,000 Point Guard | We Know the W MILESTONE MOMENT · AUGUST 29, 2026 THE 1,000 POINT GUARD Kelsey Mitchell crossed a scoring line no WNBA guard had reached before. Her 34 point night against Connecticut pushed her to 1,001 points for the season and into a two player club with A’ja Wilson. By We Know the W Staff 4 minute read Home › The W Vault › Milestone Moments KM 1001 THE MILESTONE First guard in WNBA history with 1,000 points in one season. AT THE CROSSING 1,001 season points after Aug. 28 40 games played 25.0 points per game 34 points vs. Connecticut Kelsey Mitchell did not merely reach four digits. She changed who can be pictured when we talk about a 1,000 point WNBA season. The first guard through the door Mitchell scored 34 points in Indiana’s August 28 win over Connecticut, lifting her 2026 total to 1,001. That made her the first guard in league history to score at least 1,000 points in a single season and only the second player at any position to do it. A’ja Wilson established the 1,000 point season club in 2024. Mitchell joining her matters because the routes are different. Wilson created history from the frontcourt. Mitchell reached the same threshold as a 5 foot 8 guard whose scoring is built on pace, pull ups, three point volume, movement and relentless pressure on defenses. Volume without giving away efficiency At the moment she crossed the mark, Mitchell had played 40 games and was averaging 25.0 points while shooting 51.3 percent from the field and 45.5 percent from three. Reaching 1,000 is a volume achievement, but those percentages show why this season is more than accumulation. Her August 28 line fit the larger pattern. Mitchell made 12 of 19 shots against Connecticut, scored 34, and helped Indiana turn an early deficit into a 111 to 91 win. The record is still moving The 1,001 total is a milestone snapshot, not a final season number. Mitchell’s 2026 scoring total will continue to change as Indiana plays. What will not change is the first: no WNBA guard had ever crossed 1,000 points in one season before her. That is why this belongs in Milestone Moments, not only in a nightly box score. Mitchell moved the scoring ceiling for her position. WHY IT MATTERS 2 players have reached 1,000 points in a WNBA season, A’ja Wilson and Kelsey Mitchell. items.title: Legendary Duos: Ranking 30 WNBA Seasons
items.keywords: One defining WNBA duo from every season, 1997 through 2026, ranked by team success, combined excellence, postseason impact and basketball fit—with honorable mentions for the last five years. Maya Moore Seimone Augustus Legendary Duos: Ranking 30 WNBA Seasons | We Know the W SEASON 30 · WNBA HISTORY TWO BY TWO One defining duo from every WNBA season, then all 30 pairings ranked against each other. Championships matter. Awards matter. The playoffs matter. So does the way two games fit together. By We Know the W Staff 14-minute read Updated August 26, 2026 2× 30 MAYA MOORE + SEIMONE AUGUSTUS The 2013 Lynx pairing that inspired this journey finished a perfect 7–0 in the postseason. Player portraits via WNBA. THE RANKING FILE 30 seasons · 1997 to 2026 30 yearly duo selections 4 championship eras represented * 2026 remains provisional THE STORY BEFORE THE LIST Thirty seasons taught me that partnership is its own basketball skill. I did not rank careers, reputations or the two biggest names on a roster. I ranked the season-specific version of each partnership: how completely two players shaped winning together, how their games answered one another and what remained when the possessions became heaviest. That is why Cynthia Cooper and Sheryl Swoopes in 2000 sit at No. 1. Cooper still owned the close, Swoopes had become both MVP and Defensive Player of the Year, and Houston finished a four-peat with two different kinds of control. One player could decide the possession with the ball; the other could decide it before the ball ever arrived. Their trophies were not separate arguments. They were evidence that the partnership worked at both ends. The first dynasties established the language. Houston created the original model: pressure, poise and a ruthless understanding of who should take over. Los Angeles answered with Lisa Leslie as the center of gravity and guards and wings who made the entry pass, the extra pass and the championship shot. Sacramento’s Yolanda Griffith and Ticha Penicheiro proved a duo could dominate without looking like a scoring contest—one controlled the paint, the other controlled time. Detroit complicated the formula again. Deanna Nolan and Katie Smith were interchangeable problems: both could score, defend and survive a physical series. Seattle then found the cleanest inside-out marriage of the era in Lauren Jackson and Sue Bird. Jackson stretched the floor without surrendering the paint; Bird read the second defender before it moved. Their 2010 perfect postseason earns the No. 2 position because the fit was as overwhelming as the record. Minnesota made repetition a measure of greatness. The Lynx dynasty is where this exercise becomes hardest. Maya Moore appears with Seimone Augustus and Sylvia Fowles because her greatness translated across different partnerships. Augustus gave her another three-level scorer. Fowles changed the geometry at the rim. The repeat marker beside a player’s name is intentional: it recognizes the rare stars whose game could create more than one championship-level relationship. The 2013 Moore–Augustus team inspired this project and went 7–0 in the postseason, yet it lands ninth overall. That is not a slight. It is the cost of comparing one flawless run with thirty years of MVPs, Finals MVPs and dynasties. The top of the board rewards the pairings that combined a perfect answer on the court with the largest historical consequence. The modern game widened the definition of a duo. A’ja Wilson and Chelsea Gray did not simply divide inside and outside in 2022. They bent coverage from different places, then punished the adjustment. Breanna Stewart and Jonquel Jones gave New York two centers of gravity in 2024. The best contemporary pairings can screen, handle, facilitate and defend across positions, which means their value is often the number of choices they remove from an opponent. Napheesa Collier and Olivia Miles are my provisional 2026 selection because Minnesota has paired an MVP-level two-way forward with a rookie guard already organizing a championship-level team. Their place is deliberately last for now: a season in progress should not leap finished championship evidence. The postseason can move them. The argument is part of the pleasure. A ranking asks whether a perfect postseason outweighs a dominant regular season, whether overlapping stars can be greater than a cleaner stylistic fit and how much a championship should decide. I made those choices below, but the film leaves enough room for you to make your own. DYNASTY ECHOES Houston appears in all four championship seasons. Seattle places four title pairings on the board. Minnesota supplies five seasons across its dynasty and new era. Las Vegas owns three selections in four seasons. Follow every champion in The Trophy Room → Meet the legends in Playerpedia → THE FULL 1–30 The story settles into the board. The top ten receive the spotlight treatment. For 2022–2026, the honorable mentions sit beside the winning selection so each season can be read in one place. items.title: Love & Basketball: The Teammate Couples Tournament
items.keywords: Love & Basketball meets the WNBA: an eight pair teammate couples tournament with We Know the W scores, a live 2026 player grade dashboard and an interactive head to head matchup lab. We Know the W home Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd in Dallas Wings uniforms DeWanna Bonner and Alyssa Thomas together in Connecticut Sun uniforms Gabby Williams and Marine Johannes together in France uniforms Love & Basketball: The Teammate Couples Tournament | We Know the W FOOD FOR THOUGHT · LOVE & BASKETBALL LOVE. BUCKETS. BRACKET. What happens when your person was also your teammate? Eight WNBA connected couples enter a head to head tournament built on what they did in the same uniform, how their games fit and what survived the biggest stage. By We Know the W Staff 10 minute read September 16, 2026 Open the bracket Build a matchup Paige + Azzi Dallas, 2026 DeWanna + Alyssa Connecticut Gabby + Marine France FIRST, THE RULES This is not a ranking of anybody's relationship. Love is not a stat. Basketball is. So the tournament only asks one question: which publicly reported couple built the strongest basketball résumé while they were teammates? That distinction matters. Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd have already asked people to keep the private part private while they handle the basketball part professionally. The same respect applies here. We are grading shared titles, shared peaks, fit, longevity and big stage impact. No points for matching outfits, anniversary captions or who remembers to take the trash out. The field is WNBA connected rather than WNBA teammate only. Both players must have WNBA experience or a current WNBA connection, and the pair must have shared a real basketball roster somewhere. That keeps Gabby Williams and Marine Johannès eligible through France, and Breanna Stewart and Marta Xargay eligible through Dynamo Kursk, even though neither pair shared a WNBA roster. W SCORE · PAIR EDITION 35 Shared team success 25 Collective peak 20 Basketball fit 10 Teammate longevity 10 Big stage impact 100 points total. Editorial basketball model, separate from the live individual W Score. LIVE 2026 DATA The current W Score travels with the story. Active players pull from We Know the W's current player grade model. Retired players stay labeled as legacy so a 2026 grade is never invented for them. Connecting to the 2026 W Score feed… Current player grades use the site's existing league relative model. Pair scores use the teammate résumé model above. THE LOVE & BASKETBALL TOURNAMENT Eight pairs. Three rounds. Basketball receipts only. The higher Pair W Score advances. Tap any pair to open the scouting card beneath the bracket. SCOUTING THE FIELD Why each pair is here. Every card uses a basketball photo from the WNBA, FIBA or an established editorial source. Photo credits link back to the original page. HEAD TO HEAD LAB Make your own matchup. Choose any two pairs and the dashboard compares every scoring lane. This is where the bracket becomes an argument at the group chat table. Pair A VS Pair B FOOD FOR THOUGHT The tournament says something bigger than who advances. The W has always made room for players to be whole people. The basketball history is richer because some of those people built their careers beside the person they loved. Diana Taurasi and Penny Taylor are the measuring stick because the shared basketball evidence is almost rude. Three Mercury championships, 2007, 2009 and 2014, with both players central to the same winning ecosystem. Taurasi supplied the pressure and shot creation. Taylor connected lineups, defended across roles and punished the space Taurasi created. Their Pair W Score does not win because they are an iconic couple. It wins because the same uniform produced three banners. Courtney Vandersloot and Allie Quigley make the final because their fit may be the cleanest in the field. One bent the defense with passing, one bent it with shooting, and Chicago eventually turned that geometry into the 2021 championship. They were also the league's first married teammates, which makes the history important, but the bracket advances them because the basketball held up. DeWanna Bonner and Alyssa Thomas are the pair that can break this model if Phoenix adds a championship chapter. They already have years of Connecticut contention, a 2022 Finals run, completely different offensive profiles and a shared appetite for difficult possessions. The Pair W Score rewards what is finished. Their story may not be. Then come the challengers. Paige and Azzi own the most obvious ceiling because they already have the 2025 NCAA title, years of shared reps and now a Dallas chapter. Gabby and Marine might be the purest style pairing here, downhill force meeting improvisational shooting. Their France tape looks like two players who understand where the other wants the next pass before it leaves the hand. That is the real Love & Basketball lesson. Chemistry is not magic. It is accumulated information. You learn where somebody wants the ball, what silence means after a bad possession, when to clear a side and when to cut behind the help. Most great teammates spend years learning that language. Some of these pairs happened to take it home with them. TOURNAMENT CHAMPION DIANA TAURASI + PENNY TAYLOR 99 · PAIR W SCORE Three shared WNBA titles are the tiebreaker nobody else in this field can match. Try to knock them off → SOURCE DESK Receipts behind the bracket Relationship references are limited to public reporting. items.title: So, About That Lynx Blueprint... Atlanta Added a Chapter
items.keywords: Atlanta gave the Lynx blueprint a second chapter. Minnesota had Courtney Williams back and still lost, showing there is more than one way to make the league leaders uncomfortable. So, About That Lynx Blueprint... Atlanta Added a Chapter | We Know the W FOOD FOR THOUGHT · PLAYOFF FILM · SEPTEMBER 2, 2026 SO, ABOUT THAT LYNX BLUEPRINT... Golden State showed one way to bother Minnesota. Atlanta just showed another, and this time Courtney Williams was back. By We Know the W Staff 5-minute read September 2, 2026 Home › Snack Shak › Food for Thought › Lynx Blueprint I wanted to see Minnesota against Atlanta before getting too comfortable with the idea of a Lynx playoff blueprint. We got the test, and Atlanta gave the conversation a second chapter. The Dream beat Minnesota 89–81 on August 30. More important than the final score, Courtney Williams was back. That matters because her absence was the biggest asterisk hanging over Golden State's 80–66 win. The Lynx had another ball handler again and still couldn't take control of the game. Atlanta didn't copy Golden State That's probably the most useful part of this result. Golden State bothered Minnesota with ball pressure, delayed offense and turnovers. Atlanta found another route. The Dream won the rebounding battle 37–32. Angel Reese finished with 15 points and 11 rebounds. Jordin Canada had 16 points and 10 assists. Atlanta kept Minnesota defending, moved the ball and found enough offense from different places that the Lynx couldn't simply load up on one player. THE NEW FILM NOTE You don't have to beat Minnesota one specific way. You have to keep taking comfortable possessions away from them. Extra possessions come in different packages Golden State stole possessions with turnovers. Atlanta stole them on the glass. The box score calls those different things, but in a playoff game the effect is pretty similar. Minnesota gets fewer clean chances to settle into its offense, while the opponent gets another opportunity to score. That's why the rebounding piece keeps moving higher on my list. If you're not a team built to hound the ball for 40 minutes, you can still make Minnesota work by extending possessions and making the Lynx defend again. Then Atlanta made the math hurt The Dream hit 13 threes. Minnesota made six. That's a 21-point swing from behind the line in a game Atlanta won by eight. Allisha Gray made six of them and scored 23. Rhyne Howard scored 12 of her 16 points in the fourth quarter. That last part is worth remembering. Minnesota doesn't just need to be uncomfortable early. Somebody has to make the Lynx pay late. Howard did. The Courtney Williams asterisk got smaller Williams returned from her right-foot sprain and scored 11. Her presence didn't magically erase the problems we've been watching. That changes the conversation. The Golden State lesson was never supposed to be “pressure Olivia Miles because Williams is missing.” The better version is broader: make Minnesota defend multiple points of attack, keep the Lynx from controlling possession after possession, and force their offense to work later into the clock than it wants to. There is a new availability question, though. Miles took a hard fall late against Atlanta. Until Minnesota provides something definitive, I'm not turning that into an injury diagnosis. It is simply something to watch as the postseason gets closer. Two different losses, one bigger picture Golden State gave us the defensive version. Pressure the guards. Create turnovers. Get real production from the bench. Make Minnesota spend time just trying to begin its offense. Atlanta gave us the possession version. Rebound. Move the ball. Make the Lynx guard several creators. Get into the paint enough to move the defense, then punish the rotations from three. And when the fourth quarter arrives, have somebody who can actually finish the job. The scary playoff opponent is the team that can do some of both. Food for thought Minnesota is still 31–9 and still sitting on top of the league. Two losses don't erase months of evidence that the Lynx are very, very good. But the question has changed. We aren't asking whether one weird Golden State night exposed something. Now we've seen two different opponents make Minnesota uncomfortable in two different ways, including one with Williams back in the lineup. Pressure the ball when you can. Win the glass. Create extra possessions. Get something from the bench. Touch the paint. Make Minnesota rotate. Hit the open three. And if you're lucky enough to still have the game in front of you late, you better have somebody ready to take it. Golden State gave the league the first page. Atlanta just wrote in the margins. items.title: Milestone Moments | The W Vault
items.keywords: Milestone Moments is a curated WNBA timeline of historic firsts, record setting performances, social impact and league growth. Milestone Moments | The W Vault THE W VAULT · FIRSTS + BREAKTHROUGHS MILESTONE MOMENTS The plays, people and decisions that moved the line forward. This is a curated timeline of league firsts, barrier breakers and chapters that changed what came next. 1996 to 2000 Foundation 2002 to 2010 New ground 2014 to 2024 Player power 2025 to 2026 New map FOUNDATION FIRSTS The opening years established the language of the league. 1996 The league is approved On April 24, the WNBA concept received approval. Val Ackerman became the first president, while Sheryl Swoopes and Rebecca Lobo became the first announced signees. 1997 First game, basket, MVP and champion Penny Toler scored the first basket. New York won the first game. Cynthia Cooper became the first MVP. Houston became the first champion. 1999 The first All Star Game Madison Square Garden hosted the inaugural All Star Game on July 14. The West won 79 to 61 and Lisa Leslie earned MVP honors. 1999 The first triple double Sheryl Swoopes posted 15 points, 14 rebounds and 10 assists against Detroit on July 27. Foundation sources: WNBA History Timeline ↗ · Pioneers of the WNBA ↗ NEW GROUND The game kept finding places it had never been. 2002 Lisa Leslie throws down the first dunk On July 30, Leslie completed the first dunk in WNBA game history against the Miami Sol in Los Angeles. 2003 A new ownership path The Connecticut Sun became the first independently owned and operated WNBA franchise, separating team ownership from the original NBA team model. 2008 Basketball moves outdoors New York and Indiana played the first regular season outdoor game at Arthur Ashe Stadium on July 19. 2010 Cynthia Cooper enters Springfield Cooper became the first WNBA player inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame. New ground sources: Lisa Leslie Through the Years ↗ · Liberty 2008 history ↗ · WNBA pioneers ↗ POWER BEYOND THE BOX SCORE Players expanded their influence from the bench to the boardroom. 2014 2015 Former WNBA players enter NBA coaching Becky Hammon and Nancy Lieberman became the first two women to serve as full time NBA assistant coaches, extending WNBA experience into another professional coaching pipeline. 2020 A season dedicated to social justice Players centered Black Lives Matter and the Say Her Name campaign, using the season to honor women affected by racial violence and to make civic engagement part of the league’s public work. 2021 Renee Montgomery reaches the ownership table Montgomery became the first former WNBA player to hold both a team ownership stake and an executive role when she joined the Atlanta Dream ownership group. 2024 Leaguewide charter travel begins The WNBA instituted a full charter flight program, phased in from the beginning of the 2024 regular season. Player power sources: 2020 social justice season ↗ · Atlanta ownership approval ↗ · 2024 charter program ↗ THE MAP OPENS AGAIN Seventeen years without a new team ended in a rush. 2025 Golden State breaks the expansion drought The Valkyries became the first new WNBA franchise since Atlanta entered in 2008, then became the first expansion team to reach the playoffs in its inaugural season. 2026 Toronto crosses the border The Toronto Tempo became the WNBA’s first franchise based outside the United States. 2026 Portland lights the Fire again Professional women’s basketball returned to Portland under the revived Fire identity. Portland and Toronto entered as the league’s 14th and 15th franchises. What counts as a milestone? This exhibit focuses on firsts and breakthroughs that changed the league’s direction. Complete statistical records live in the Trophy Room, while future franchise developments stay in Expansion Watch until they actually happen.
