items.title: The W Is Changing Hands | Scouting the Next WNBA Commissioner
items.keywords: Cathy Engelbert is retiring at the end of 2026. We Know the W examines her legacy and scouts seven possible candidates to become the WNBA's next commissioner. Cathy Engelbert holding a WNBA basketball Swin Cash in a white blazer Sarah Mensah wearing a black suit Bethany Donaphin standing beside a basketball trophy Golden State Valkyries president Jess Smith Nneka Ogwumike in her Los Angeles Sparks uniform Renie Anderson holding an NFL football Condoleezza Rice in a blue blazer The W Is Changing Hands | Scouting the Next WNBA Commissioner FOOD FOR THOUGHT · LEAGUE BUSINESS · SEPTEMBER 5, 2026 THE W IS CHANGING HANDS Cathy Engelbert helped build a bigger WNBA. The next commissioner must build a better relationship with the people inside it. By We Know the W 12 minute read September 5, 2026 Home › Snack Shak › Food for Thought › The W Is Changing Hands Photo: Jennifer Pottheiser, via Georgetown University 2019 Engelbert appointed The WNBA names its first commissioner. 15 Teams in 2026 Expansion is scheduled to reach 18 teams by 2030. 2024 Full charter travel A league wide program changes the player experience. 2026 Historic CBA A new compensation era arrives before her exit. Cathy Engelbert is retiring at the end of 2026, and the WNBA is not the league she inherited in 2019. That sentence is both the strongest argument for her legacy and the clearest warning for whoever follows her. The WNBA announced Engelbert's retirement on September 4 , bringing an end to more than seven years under the league's first commissioner. Before Engelbert, the WNBA's top executive held the title of president. She arrived from Deloitte with a business résumé, a growth plan, and the difficult assignment of convincing the sports world to stop treating the WNBA like a promising side project. She leaves behind a league with 15 teams, plans to reach 18 by 2030, charter air travel, larger audiences, soaring franchise values, and a new collective bargaining agreement capable of producing the first million dollar salaries in league history. THE LEGACY IN ONE LINE Engelbert helped move the WNBA into a different neighborhood. The next commissioner must make sure the players feel at home there. What Engelbert built Her first full season arrived during a global pandemic. The 2020 Wubble kept the league playing while giving its athletes a national platform for racial justice and civic engagement. The Commissioner's Cup followed in 2021. In 2022, Engelbert led a $75 million capital raise intended to support marketing, digital development, international growth, and league operations. Charter flights eventually became standard. The Finals expanded. The regular season grew to 44 games and will increase to 50 in 2027. Golden State, Toronto, and Portland expanded the league's footprint, with Cleveland, Detroit, and Philadelphia scheduled to bring the WNBA to 18 teams by 2030 . The new seven year collective bargaining agreement may become Engelbert's most important closing achievement. The agreement established a $7 million salary cap for 2026, projected an average salary of approximately $583,000, and created a path toward contracts worth more than $1 million per season. It also codified charter travel, improved facilities and benefits, and expanded support for families and retirees. The part of the legacy that cannot be placed on a revenue chart Engelbert's relationship with players became the central weakness of her leadership. Players repeatedly criticized the league for reacting too slowly to concerns involving officiating, online abuse, personal safety, and accountability. Napheesa Collier's public criticism in 2025 turned private frustration into a league wide conversation about whether WNBA leadership truly listened to its players. Engelbert later acknowledged that the league needed to do better if players did not feel appreciated or heard. The new CBA proved that the league and union could still complete historic work together, but it did not magically repair every relationship. Both parts of Engelbert's record deserve space. She helped create the strongest business foundation the WNBA has ever had. She also showed that a commissioner cannot lead this particular league through financial strategy alone. The next commissioner's assignment The WNBA's next commissioner must speak two languages fluently. She must understand the economics of owners, media companies, and corporate partners while respecting the experiences of the athletes whose talent, personalities, and advocacy created the product being sold. The next commissioner does not need to be the players' best friend. Commissioners work for ownership. She does, however, need enough trust to disagree with players without making them feel dismissed. That is the assignment. Here is the early scouting board. EARLY BOARD · SEPTEMBER 2026 Seven candidates, seven different versions of the job These names are potential candidates, not confirmed finalists. The search may include executives who have not yet been publicly identified. Photo via PlayersTV LEAD CANDIDATE A + Swin Cash President, Women's Sports Foundation · Hall of Famer · Former WNBA and NBA executive Cash offers the most complete bridge between the court, front office, and ownership suite. She played 15 seasons in the WNBA, won three championships, and later gained NBA basketball operations experience with the New Orleans Pelicans. In 2026, she became president of the Women's Sports Foundation. Cash was also among the investors in the WNBA's 2022 capital raise. Any ownership interest would need to be reviewed and properly addressed before she became commissioner. Best trait Credibility across players, executives, sponsors, and fans. The question Has she managed an organization with the financial, legal, and operational complexity of an entire league? Verdict The strongest all around profile on the early board. Photo via Nike THE SCALE CANDIDATE A Sarah Mensah President, Jordan Brand · Former Portland Trail Blazers chief operating officer Mensah may be the strongest pure business operator in the group. She leads Jordan Brand's global strategy, marketplace, and business portfolio. Before joining Nike, she spent 19 years with the Portland Trail Blazers and eventually oversaw revenue strategy, marketing, communications, digital operations, community impact, and facility operations. Best trait Basketball business scale and global brand leadership. The question Can she quickly build authentic player relationships and master labor and basketball operations? Verdict If ownership wants an executive who can scale the business, Mensah belongs near the top. Photo via WNBA THE CONTINUITY CANDIDATE A − Bethany Donaphin Head of WNBA League Operations · Former WNBA player Donaphin knows how the league actually works. Since becoming head of league operations in 2018, she has overseen on court operations, rules, scheduling, scouting, conduct standards, and venue compliance. She would enter the job understanding the personnel, systems, and daily pressures that an outside candidate would need months to learn. Best trait Immediate command of the league's daily machinery. The question Can an established league insider become the face of meaningful change? Verdict The safest operational choice, although not necessarily the cleanest cultural reset. Photo via The San Francisco Standard THE EXPANSION BUILDER A − Jess Smith President, Golden State Valkyries · Former Angel City FC revenue executive Smith has already built something the rest of the league wants to copy. Golden State's launch turned the Valkyries into a ticketing, sponsorship, and community success. Her work earned the WNBA's inaugural Business Executive Leadership Award. Best trait Modern expansion instincts and proof that women's sports can become an event and a community. The question Is leading one WNBA franchise enough preparation to govern an entire league and answer to every ownership group? Verdict The fastest riser on the board, and future commissioner material even if this search comes early. Official player image via WNBA THE PLAYER TRUST CANDIDATE B + Nneka Ogwumike WNBPA president · Retiring as a player after the 2026 season No candidate would arrive with more immediate credibility among players. Ogwumike has served as WNBPA president since 2016 and helped represent players through two collective bargaining agreements. She understands compensation, benefits, working conditions, league politics, and the personal consequences of executive decisions. Best trait Player trust, policy fluency, and a decade of labor leadership. The question Can the league's leading player advocate become the owners' chief executive without weakening the trust that makes her candidacy attractive? Verdict A powerful possibility, although an empowered player strategy role may be the better first step. Photo via NFL THE REVENUE SPECIALIST B Renie Anderson NFL executive vice president and chief revenue officer Anderson knows how the biggest sports league in the country turns attention into durable revenue. She oversees partnerships, sponsorships, consumer products, new business, and media sales. Best trait Major league commercial expertise and a deep sponsor network. The question Can she combine revenue skill with the player relationships and cultural fluency this league urgently needs? Verdict The business sleeper, especially if she arrives prepared to listen before rebuilding the machine. Photo via Southern Methodist University THE POLITICAL WILDCARD B Condoleezza Rice Stanford professor · Former United States secretary of state · WNBA equity investor Rice's WNBA connection is much deeper than her title in a candidate graphic suggests. She became an equity partner in the league's 2022 capital raise. At Stanford, she served as Chiney Ogwumike's faculty mentor , advising her as she balanced basketball, academics, and plans beyond the court. Rice also chaired the NCAA's Commission on College Basketball, which examined relationships among schools, athletes, agents, apparel companies, and outside basketball organizations. That gives her significant experience in governance, negotiation, crisis management, and institutional reform. Her political prominence is also the largest strike against her candidacy. The WNBA's players have placed civil rights, voting rights, and social justice at the center of the league's public identity. Rice's service in a Republican administration would invite every constituency to view her decisions through a partisan lens, even when the issue is basketball or business. The question is not whether players must share a commissioner's politics. It is whether her appointment would turn the commissioner's office into a political story before she had the chance to build trust. Best trait Governance, diplomacy, institutional strategy, and the ability to command difficult rooms. The question Can she earn broad player trust when her political identity could overshadow her WNBA investment and sports governance experience? Verdict A serious governance candidate, but probably too politically polarizing for the cultural reset the league needs. Her experience may fit better on an advisory board than in the commissioner's chair. The We Know the W pick Swin Cash is the best fit today. She has lived the WNBA from nearly every angle: player, champion, executive, entrepreneur, advocate, nonprofit leader, and investor. She offers the clearest opportunity to preserve Engelbert's business momentum while repairing the emotional distance between the league office and its players. Sarah Mensah may be the strongest outside executive. Bethany Donaphin would provide the smoothest operational transition. Jess Smith has already demonstrated how quickly a women's sports property can become an event, a community, and a thriving business. Condoleezza Rice is the most fascinating wildcard because her relationship with the WNBA, Stanford athletes, and sports governance is real. The ultimate answer may not be one perfect résumé. The WNBA may need a commissioner with Swin Cash's basketball credibility, Sarah Mensah's business scale, Jess Smith's expansion instincts, Nneka Ogwumike's player trust, and Condoleezza Rice's ability to navigate powerful institutions. Unfortunately, creating that candidate in a laboratory would probably violate the new CBA. Engelbert leaves the next commissioner a stronger league. She also leaves a harder job. Expectations are higher, the money is larger, the scrutiny is louder, and players are no longer willing to accept being treated as supporting characters in the story their labor created. The next commissioner must understand that the WNBA does not need to be rescued. It needs to be respected, protected, and led into the future it has already earned. TOP BUSINESS OPERATOR SARAH MENSAH Global scale, brand leadership, and nearly two decades of NBA front office experience. WHAT THE JOB REQUIRES Player trust Owner alignment Labor fluency Media strategy Expansion discipline Global ambition Basketball credibility

items.title: One Possession From Overtime | 2026 FIBA World Cup
items.keywords: Puerto Rico and Italy came one possession from overtime in the FIBA Women's World Cup. We break down what cost them, Trinity San Antonio's defensive case and the three leading defenders still alive. We Know the W home Trinity San Antonio walking toward the court in her Puerto Rico uniform Isobel Borlase smiling with Australia teammates after a World Cup game Gabby Williams in her France uniform Angel Reese in her USA uniform Rhyne Howard in her USA uniform One Possession From Overtime | 2026 FIBA World Cup | We Know the W FOOD FOR THOUGHT · FIBA WORLD CUP One Possession From Overtime Puerto Rico and Italy lost by five combined points. The last shot will get remembered, but both losses were built earlier, one inside the paint and one inside a 26 point hole. By We Know the W Published September 9, 2026 Data through September 9 9 minute read QUALIFICATION TO QUARTERFINALS 🇵🇷 PUR 72 FINAL 75 CHN 🇨🇳 22 lead changes. One last chance. QUALIFICATION TO QUARTERFINALS 🇮🇹 ITA 80 FINAL 82 AUS 🇦🇺 Down 26. Tied with 1:09 left. Home › Snack Shak › Food for Thought › One Possession From Overtime Trinity San Antonio made the loudest exit in Berlin. She finished the China game with 24 points, 9 rebounds, 7 assists and 5 steals. Photo and report: FIBA ↗ Isobel Borlase built the cushion Australia needed. Her 30 points kept the Opals alive when Italy erased almost all of a 26 point deficit. Photo and report: FIBA ↗ THE OPENING READ Five points changed the entire bracket. China survived Puerto Rico by three. Australia survived Italy by two. Both favorites advanced, but neither result felt safe until the clock finally removed the alternative. These were not identical near upsets. Puerto Rico stayed close from the opening tip, creating a game with 22 lead changes and 10 ties. Italy spent most of the night looking buried, fell behind by 26 in the third quarter, then delivered a 31 to 13 fourth quarter that turned a runaway into a possession game. That distinction matters. Puerto Rico lost a forty minute negotiation. Italy lost the first thirty minutes and nearly won the final ten loudly enough to erase them. In both cases, one more clean possession could have purchased five extra minutes and shifted every ounce of pressure onto the favored team. Overtime would not have guaranteed two upsets. It would have guaranteed that China and Australia had to survive each game twice. COMBINED MARGIN 5 Two elimination games were separated by five total points. LEAD CHANGES 22 Puerto Rico and China traded control all night. ITALY, FOURTH QUARTER 31–13 The comeback arrived with almost no room left. SAN ANTONIO STEALS 5.0 Her tournament average remains the field’s best by a mile. PUERTO RICO 72, CHINA 75 The upset lived. The paint collected the bill. Puerto Rico made the game uncomfortable enough to win. China made the most valuable shots inside the arc and the biggest one beyond it. Pamela Rosado tied the game at 66 with 3:38 remaining. China answered immediately. Xu Han stepped out for a three with 2:56 left, then China completed a 6 to 0 run that created the only real separation of the closing stretch. The deciding gap was not effort. It was two point efficiency. China shot 57.1 percent inside the arc, while Puerto Rico finished at 40.4 percent. Puerto Rico made more of its threes by percentage and shot 90 percent at the line, but China kept finding cleaner value closer to the rim. Xu Han produced 21 points and 11 rebounds. Shuyu Yang added 15 points and 11 assists. Ziyu Zhang scored 13 points in only 9:26 and made five of six two point attempts. Puerto Rico had to solve size, touch and playmaking at the same time. That is a long defensive checklist for any team, especially one that could not afford an empty possession late. What hurt Puerto Rico most was that its best defensive work did not always become points. Between 4:17 and 1:40, both teams committed two turnovers and neither reached the line. The game became frantic, but China’s late run supplied order. Puerto Rico created the chaos it wanted, then China found the shot it needed. THE DIFFERENCE China won the valuable geography. 2PT FG 40.4% to 57.1% OVERALL FG 40% to 48% LATE SWING 0–6 Puerto Rico had the defensive activity. China had the more efficient interior answers. ITALY 80, AUSTRALIA 82 Italy’s comeback was real. So was the hole. A 31 point fourth quarter can change how a game feels. It cannot refund the first three quarters. THE DIFFERENCE Australia banked the game early. LARGEST LEAD 26 TIME LEADING 37:06 BORLASE 30 PTS Italy won the ending. Australia had already accumulated just enough beginning and middle. Australia led 48 to 33 at halftime and 69 to 49 after three quarters. The Opals built a 26 point lead twice in the third. They were in front for 37:06. When a team controls that much of the night, the opponent’s margin for late error becomes microscopic. Italy still made the impossible look available. A 10 to 0 run erased a 77 to 67 deficit. Costanza Verona’s three tied the score at 77 with 1:09 left. Italy had the crowd, the rhythm and the emotional weight of the game leaning in its direction. Then Zitina Aokuso scored at the rim with 24 seconds remaining. That one response mattered because it forced Italy to chase the score again instead of choosing the final shot from a tie. The comeback had used nearly every available possession. Australia only needed enough composure to make the next one count. Isobel Borlase was the reason there was still a cushion to protect. She scored 30 points, including 23 in the first half, and made 14 of 16 free throws. Italy shot 39.1 percent from three, well above Australia’s 27.3 percent, but the Opals shot 51 percent overall and 57.5 percent on twos. Italy’s defense became suffocating late. It needed to arrive much earlier. THE FIVE MINUTES WE DID NOT GET Overtime would have moved the pressure. The favorites still would have had talent, size and experience. The underdogs would have owned the emotional terms of the restart. 🇵🇷 PUERTO RICO San Antonio had become the game’s organizing force. She was scoring, creating and turning defense into extra possessions. In overtime, China’s size would remain a major advantage, but Puerto Rico would begin those five minutes knowing it had already dragged China into exactly the kind of game it wanted. 🇮🇹 ITALY The momentum was wearing blue. Italy had just won the fourth quarter by 18 and erased a 26 point deficit against a short handed Australia team. The Opals had the stars to recover, but Italy would have entered overtime with the fresher confidence and the louder belief. An almost upset is not the same as an upset. Still, these games showed exactly why the extra five minutes can feel like a new contest instead of an extension of the old one. THE DEFENSIVE PLAYER CASE Trinity San Antonio may have left before her argument did. Elimination shortened her stage. It did not make the work disappear. TOURNAMENT STEALS 5.0 PER GAME 20 steals across four games San Antonio’s case begins with separation. She averaged 5.0 steals per game. The next names on FIBA’s leaderboard sat at 2.7. This was not a narrow statistical lead. She nearly doubled the field while carrying a major offensive and playmaking load. Against China, she delivered 24 points, 9 rebounds, 7 assists and 5 steals, becoming the first player since 1994 to post at least 20 points, 5 rebounds, 5 assists and 5 steals in a Women’s World Cup game. Her efficiency rating of 35 was the best single game mark of the tournament at the end of qualification play. If Puerto Rico had reached overtime and then advanced, San Antonio would have received another game, another high visibility matchup and another chance to make the award feel inevitable. Team success often becomes the invisible tiebreaker in individual awards. That is the part of her case elimination may hurt. But if Best Defensive Player means the defender who changed the most possessions, not simply the best defender on a semifinalist, San Antonio should remain in the conversation. She made ballhandlers look over their shoulders for four straight games. That is a tournament identity. THE RACE STILL PLAYING The top three defenders left in the bracket. With Puerto Rico eliminated, these are the three highest remaining players in the We Know the W Defensive Impact Rating entering the quarterfinals. W DEF 96 1 · FRANCE Gabby Williams 2.7 STL 0.3 BLK 4.3 DREB Williams owns the strongest remaining blend of pressure, recovery and foul discipline. She can take the first assignment, switch onto size and turn one deflection into a French avalanche. San Antonio’s exit makes Williams the clearest active favorite on our board. W DEF 92 2 · USA Angel Reese 1.3 STL 1.0 BLK 3.0 DREB Reese is producing across every defensive activity category in only 17.2 minutes per game. Her path to the award is opportunity. More knockout minutes would give her switchability, rebounding and second effort defense room to become the story instead of a powerful piece of USA’s committee. W DEF 90 3 · USA Rhyne Howard 1.7 STL 0.3 BLK 1.0 DREB Howard’s defensive production is compressed into 14.8 minutes per game. Her length closes passing windows quickly, and her steals rate gives USA another lineup changing defender. Like Reese, she needs a signature knockout stretch that voters can attach to the numbers. How W DEF works Steals, blocks, defensive rebounds and foul control are adjusted per 40 minutes, then standardized within the 16 player candidate field. It is an independent We Know the W measure, not an official FIBA rating. SHAK’S FINAL READ San Antonio leaves with the loudest defensive résumé. Williams inherits the clearest path. Puerto Rico and Italy did not lose because they lacked belief. Puerto Rico lost because China converted more efficiently where size matters most. Italy lost because a brilliant fourth quarter could not completely erase three quarters of damage. Both teams were one make from changing the emotional math of the night. San Antonio’s team is gone, but 5.0 steals per game should stay on every award ballot. Among the players still alive, Gabby Williams has the most complete case today. Angel Reese and Rhyne Howard have the defensive tools and the team runway to catch her. The quarterfinals will decide whether this award follows the best tournament defender or the best defender whose team survived long enough to be seen. THE QUESTION Should elimination remove San Antonio from the award race, or did four games of historic disruption already say enough? THE RECEIPTS Scores, statistics and photography. The live FIBA dashboard will continue moving. This article freezes the qualification round and Defensive Impact Rating after completed games on September 9. items.title: Past Expansion Waves
items.keywords: Past Expansion Waves maps the WNBA's growth from the original eight teams through the modern expansion boom. Past Expansion Waves | We Know the W THE W KEEPS REDRAWING THE MAP PAST EXPANSION WAVES Expansion is not one straight line. The WNBA grew fast, contracted, relocated, paused, and is now in its biggest modern growth era. 1997 Original 8 1998–2000 Rapid growth 2006 Chicago 2008 Atlanta 2025–2030 Modern boom WAVE ONE Eight teams became sixteen in four seasons. The WNBA launched in 1997 with eight charter teams. Then it expanded aggressively: Detroit and Washington in 1998, Minnesota and Orlando in 1999, and Indiana, Miami, Portland and Seattle in 2000. 1997 The Original Eight Charlotte Sting, Cleveland Rockers, Houston Comets, Los Angeles Sparks, New York Liberty, Phoenix Mercury, Sacramento Monarchs and Utah Starzz. Charlotte Cleveland Houston Los Angeles New York Phoenix Sacramento Utah 1998 Detroit + Washington The Shock and Mystics pushed the league to ten teams. Detroit Shock Washington Mystics 1999 Minnesota + Orlando The Lynx and Miracle continued the early expansion sprint. Minnesota Lynx Orlando Miracle 2000 Four more cities Indiana, Miami, Portland and Seattle brought the league to 16 teams. Indiana Fever Miami Sol Portland Fire Seattle Storm Early expansion history: WNBA history archive ↗ WAVE TWO + THE LONG PAUSE Growth slowed, but it did not stop. 2006 Chicago Sky Chicago joined as a new expansion franchise and became one of the league's early independently operated teams. 2008 Atlanta Dream Atlanta joined for the 2008 season. The league would not add another expansion franchise for 17 years. 2009–2024 Expansion pause The map still changed through relocations and franchise transitions, but no brand-new expansion team entered after Atlanta until Golden State. Important distinction: relocation is not the same as expansion. Detroit's old Shock franchise eventually became today's Dallas Wings; the 2029 Detroit team is a separate new expansion franchise. THE MODERN BOOM The drought ended — then the floodgates opened. 2025 Golden State Valkyries The Valkyries became the first new WNBA expansion franchise since Atlanta in 2008. 2026 Toronto Tempo + Portland Fire Toronto became the league's first team outside the United States, while Portland returned to the WNBA map with a revived Fire identity. 2028–2030 Cleveland → Detroit → Philadelphia The league's next approved wave takes the W to 18 teams, one new franchise per season across 2028, 2029 and 2030. ← Expansion Draft 101 Cleveland Sirens → Expansion Watch → Modern expansion: Golden State announcement ↗ · Cleveland/Detroit/Philadelphia announcement ↗

Our W composite ranks every player with a published grade on the eight clinched teams—and gives a league leader the edge when W scores are tied. By Shak · Shakeema Funchess August 27, 2026 112 roster entries · 105 ranked · 7 unranked 01 AW Las Vegas Aces A'ja Wilson 26.0 PPG · 31.8 PER 96 A+ · W score 02 OM Minnesota Lynx Olivia Miles 19.7 PPG · 22.9 PER 95 A+ · W score 03 AB Indiana Fever Aliyah Boston 17.0 PPG · 24.6 PER 94 A · W score All eight tickets are punched. Minnesota, Golden State, Las Vegas, Atlanta, Indiana, New York, Washington and Dallas have clinched. Records and positions below are the August 27 standings, not final playoff seeds . Current standings → Minnesota Lynx 31–8 · 1st Clinched View players Golden State Valkyries 27–11 · 2nd Clinched View players Las Vegas Aces 26–13 · 3rd Clinched View players Atlanta Dream 25–13 · 4th Clinched View players Indiana Fever 25–14 · 5th Clinched View players New York Liberty 23–15 · 6th Clinched View players Washington Mystics 23–15 · 7th Clinched View players Dallas Wings 23–16 · 8th Clinched View players Shak’s take The stars set the ceiling. The whole roster sets the terms. A season-production ranking for a field that has already clinched—not a prediction of a player’s next series. Once Dallas secured the final berth, the conversation changed. Eight teams could stop wondering whether they belonged in the postseason and start asking what they could do there. My first question is about the players: who has put together the strongest statistical season, and how much help does each contender have behind its biggest name? This board answers that with the same W composite used in Playerpedia. Reputation does not get an extra serving. Dallas’s clinching game A’ja Wilson sits first at 96 , followed by Olivia Miles at 95 . That is a striking opening: an established centerpiece beside a guard whose all-around production demands attention. The interesting arguments begin immediately behind them. Five players share 94, three share 93, and the league-leader rule changes the order of several crowded groups. A tied score now has a visible explanation. Read the full editorial Wilson earns the first seat Wilson’s lead starts with production, not name recognition. Her 31.8 PER and 61.9% true shooting sit alongside league leads in scoring and blocks. The composite rewards that combination: scoring matters, efficiency matters, and defensive events count too. Her leader badges do not manufacture first place—her 96 is already higher than every other score here. They make the breadth of that season easier to see. Miles at 95 is the board’s invitation to look past a points-only argument. Her 22.9 PER and 60.8% true shooting accompany a grade that also considers creation, rebounding, defensive activity and possession efficiency. Minnesota has Miles, Napheesa Collier and Natasha Howard in the first six. That concentration is part of what makes the Lynx so imposing: the statistical burden is spread across more than one player. The 94 group needs precision Aliyah Boston, Breanna Stewart, Collier, Howard and Paige Bueckers all receive 94. None leads one of this board’s nine qualified league-leader categories, so PER resolves their order: Boston’s 24.6 leads that group, followed by Stewart, Collier, Howard and Bueckers. Boston takes third overall. That is a consistent way to separate an exact score tie, not a claim that one roster role is automatically more valuable than another. Collier’s sample deserves attention: her grade covers 11 games. She clears the current minimum, but that remains far less evidence than Howard’s 39 games. Both numbers belong in the conversation. The board preserves the published composite and exposes games played instead of quietly giving the smaller sample a reputation bonus. A league lead has to mean something At 93, Jackie Young’s league-leading free-throw percentage puts her ahead of Jessica Shepard and Caitlin Clark. At 92, Rhyne Howard’s leads in steals and made threes break her tie with Jonquel Jones. At 91, Kelsey Mitchell’s three-point percentage gives her the first position in a group that also includes Veronica Burton, Kayla McBride and Sonia Citron. The 88 group shows the next layer. Angel Reese leads rebounding; NaLyssa Smith leads field-goal percentage. Both move ahead of Jordin Canada. Reese and Smith each own one leading category, so PER settles their remaining tie: 19.9 to 19.8. No category is counted twice as both a per-game lead and a total lead. And a postseason player does not inherit a crown from an eliminated team: Alyssa Thomas remains the assists leader even though Phoenix is outside this field. Eight rosters, not eight highlight reels The board continues beyond the stars because playoff possessions do. items.title: Standings Show the Record. Power Rankings Show the Temperature.
items.keywords: We Know the W compares its latest power rankings with the official WNBA standings through August 30, showing where momentum changes the order. Comparison of We Know the W power rankings with official WNBA standings through games played August 30, 2026 Standings Show the Record. Power Rankings Show the Temperature. | We Know the W SNACK SHAK BYTE · POWER RANKINGS · SEPTEMBER 1, 2026 THE STANDINGS SHOW THE RECORD. THE POWER RANKINGS SHOW THE TEMPERATURE. Minnesota owns the official table, but Golden State owns this week's apron. Here is where the latest We Know the W ranking agrees with the standings, and where momentum changes the order. By We Know the W Staff 3 minute read September 1, 2026 Home › Snack Shak › Snack Shak Bytes › Power rankings versus standings Green means We Know the W ranks a team higher than its official standing. Pink means lower. Gold means the positions match. OFFICIAL NO. 1 Minnesota Lynx The Lynx own the league's best record at 31 and 9. POWER NO. 1 Golden State Valkyries A four win week, including a 14 point win over Minnesota, earns the apron. BIGGEST SPLIT Minnesota, down three The Lynx sit first officially and fourth in the current power ranking. Standings are the résumé. Power rankings are the temperature check. Through games played August 30, Minnesota sits first at 31 and 9, Golden State follows at 29 and 11, and Las Vegas holds third at 27 and 13. That is the full season table. The latest We Know the W ranking asks a slightly different question: who is cooking right now? Golden State took the top spot The Valkyries went 4 and 0 during the ranking week, beat Minnesota by 14, held New York to 60 points and closed the week on a four game winning streak. That pushes Golden State one place above its official standing and into the No. 1 power position. Atlanta lands second in the power ranking despite sitting fourth officially. The Dream beat Minnesota, received a record setting rebounding performance from Angel Reese and looked more dangerous at the end of the week than their place in the table alone suggests. The teams running hotter than their records RANKED HIGHER Atlanta, Dallas, Los Angeles and Seattle Each sits two places higher in the We Know the W ranking than in the official standings. RANKED LOWER Minnesota drops three Back to back losses to Golden State and Atlanta create the largest gap on the board. EXACT MATCH Las Vegas, Indiana, Washington and Connecticut For these four teams, the power ranking and official standing tell the same story. Dallas rises to sixth on the strength of a four game winning streak. Los Angeles moves to ninth after winning two straight and three of four. Seattle remains last in the official standings, but a win over Toronto and promising production from its young core lift the Storm to 13th in the power ranking. Minnesota is still the team to catch Dropping the Lynx to fourth is not a claim that three teams have built better seasons. Minnesota still owns the best record. Power rankings are allowed to hold two thoughts at once: the Lynx have been the league's best team across 40 games, and Golden State, Atlanta and Las Vegas carried better momentum into the break. SHAK'S TAKE The playoff field is locked. The playoff temperature is not. The standings decide who earned the position. Power rankings help explain who opponents would least like to see right now. Same league, different measuring cup. items.title: Preseason Hype Has Homework: Who Really Looks Ready for 2026–27?
items.keywords: South Carolina leads ESPN’s Top 25, JuJu returns to USC, and UCLA starts at No. 13. The real debate is what each contender still has to prove. Joyce Edwards of South Carolina drives against UConn’s Sarah Strong Preseason Hype Has Homework: Who Really Looks Ready for 2026–27? | We Know the W FOOD FOR THOUGHT · CLASS IS IN SESSION Preseason hype has homework. South Carolina leads ESPN’s Top 25, JuJu returns to USC, and UCLA starts at No. 13. The real debate is what each contender still has to prove. We Know the W · October 13, 2026 · Editorial analysis Joyce Edwards and Sarah Strong in previously published game action. Image via ESPN’s preseason rankings feature . October crowns do not come with nets Preseason rankings are basketball’s seating chart. They tell us who gets the good table before anybody has served the food. ESPN’s October 13 list puts South Carolina, UConn and USC in the first three seats. That is a useful starting point. It is also an invitation to ask what would make those choices look smart in March. Our question is simple: are we ranking a program’s reputation, a roster’s ceiling, or the team we expect to trust when a close game turns ugly? Those can be three different answers. A roster can win the introduction and still need months to learn how to win the possession. The ranks below belong to ESPN, not an AP poll and not a We Know the W score. The watch questions and verdicts are our editorial analysis. Nobody has earned a 2026–27 regular-season résumé yet. ESPN RANK · OCT. 13, 2026 The preseason board ESPN’s editorial Top 25, with our film questions. These are preseason projections, not results or W scores. Conference filters describe 2026–27 membership. Find a team Conference All conferences ACC BIG EAST Big 12 Big Ten SEC 25 teams ESPN preseason Top 25 and We Know the W watch questions Rank Team Conference Our film question 1 South Carolina SEC Late-clock organization 2 UConn BIG EAST Second-side creation 3 USC Big Ten Shared creation and timing 4 Duke ACC Possession control 5 Michigan Big Ten Quality-opponent execution 6 Louisville ACC Reliable closing lineup 7 Iowa Big Ten Half-court adaptability 8 LSU SEC Defensive lineup balance 9 Texas SEC Scoring under pressure 10 North Carolina ACC Consistent shot quality 11 Vanderbilt SEC Supporting possessions 12 Washington Big Ten Road-game response 13 UCLA Big Ten Rebuilding continuity 14 Notre Dame ACC Off-ball contributions 15 Kentucky SEC Frontcourt versatility 16 Minnesota Big Ten Interior spacing 17 Ohio State Big Ten Creation burden 18 Maryland Big Ten Guard depth 19 TCU Big 12 Transfer fit 20 Illinois Big Ten Lineup availability 21 Oklahoma State Big 12 Interior and perimeter balance 22 Arizona State Big 12 Sustained defensive habits 23 Oklahoma SEC Shot selection 24 Ole Miss SEC Possession discipline 25 West Virginia Big 12 Pressure without fouling South Carolina: being the favorite means showing your work South Carolina at No. 1 is defensible. It should also invite the toughest examination. Our test for Dawn Staley’s team is the quality of its half-court possessions: who organizes the offense, who gets the ball to the right spot, and who creates a good shot after the first option disappears? A favorite does not need to look flawless in November. It needs workable answers. Watch late-clock decisions, spacing around the paint, and whether the same action can produce multiple reads instead of one predictable finish. Defensive pressure can create easy points; a championship opponent will try to take those away. The W verdict: keep South Carolina in the first tier. Make it earn separation through possession quality. The logo is an introduction; the execution is the argument. UConn: Sarah Strong is the foundation, not the entire building UConn enters with Sarah Strong, the reigning national player of the year and unanimous BIG EAST preseason player of the year. KK Arnold and Blanca Quiñonez also earned unanimous preseason all-conference selections. Those are real reasons to expect a contender, confirmed by the program’s October 1 announcement. Our film question is what happens when opponents load up on Strong. Can the next receiver attack the advantage before the defense resets? Can a second creator rescue a possession without turning it into a difficult solo shot? The supporting cast matters most when an opponent has spent a week designing a plan for the star. For WNBA scouting, Strong’s value is not confined to scoring. Track the speed of her reads, defensive coverage changes, and decisions against help. A prospect who makes the right play when the easiest play is unavailable is telling us something useful. USC: JuJu is back. The chemistry still has to arrive USC confirms JuJu Watkins is returning after missing 2025–26 through injury. Both conference coaches and media named her Big Ten preseason player of the year. Jazzy Davidson joins her on the preseason all-conference teams after leading USC in points, rebounds, assists, steals and blocks last season. That makes No. 3 understandable. It does not make cohesion automatic. A returning star and an established young creator need shared timing: when to initiate, when to cut, when to clear a side, and when to turn a touch into an advantage for somebody else. We should judge Watkins’ return through basketball evidence rather than demanding a highlight reel immediately. Watch how the offense functions across multiple games, how responsibilities are distributed, and how the group responds to physical defense. A preseason honor is recognition, not a medical clearance or a guarantee about workload. The W verdict: USC has an exciting ceiling. The first useful question is whether its talented players can make one another easier to guard less often. Talent gathers attention. Connected talent gathers wins. UCLA at 13: disrespect, or a different roster? The defending champion starting at No. 13 is the obvious debate starter. UCLA’s own draft announcement supplies important context: six Bruins were selected in April, including five in the first round. That is a record-setting professional pipeline and a substantial amount of college production walking out the door. Our read: the championship deserves full credit, while the new team deserves its own evaluation. It is reasonable to forecast uncertainty after that kind of departure. It is also reasonable to expect the coaching staff’s habits to carry over. Neither point settles what the next roster can accomplish. Watch rebounding responsibilities, communication in transition, and which combinations remain functional when starters sit. Those details will tell us whether the Bruins are rebuilding continuity quickly. Calling every lower ranking disrespect skips the roster question; treating the title as irrelevant skips the coaching question. The rest of the table can change the conversation Duke and Michigan complete ESPN’s top five. Louisville and Iowa sit sixth and seventh, ahead of LSU and Texas. North Carolina closes the top ten. Our challenge to that group is the same: identify the lineup you trust against a quality opponent, then show why it works. The lower half deserves more than a drive-by. A team ranked in the teens can become a serious threat if its complementary pieces fit faster than expected. Conversely, a top-ten roster can spend the winter working through a problem everyone politely ignored in October. For fans, the most useful early result is not always the biggest win. Watch what happens after a team’s preferred style gets disrupted. Can it defend without fouling, survive a cold shooting stretch, and finish a possession with a rebound? That is where preseason optimism starts becoming evidence. Who Got Next? Scout the job, not just the name This season is also a new chapter in the WNBA pipeline. Watkins and Strong deserve attention, but scouting should not become a contest to see who can repeat the most famous names. Every prospect has to show skills that fit a professional role. For a lead guard, watch decisions against pressure and the ability to manipulate help. For a wing, watch shooting preparation, closeout attacks and defensive assignments. For a big, watch screening angles, defensive positioning, finishing windows and passing when the paint is crowded. College ranking, individual awards and draft position answer different questions. A freshman can reshape a contender without being part of the next draft. A veteran can be a compelling prospect on a team outside the top ten. Draft eligibility and declarations should be verified separately; being on our radar is not a declaration. The Food for Thought takeaway: keep the rankings, keep the debate, and ask for the film. October gives us the hypothesis. The season gets to grade the homework. Source desk Rank order: Charlie Creme, ESPN, October 13. Return, honors and draft facts: the official program announcements below. Verdicts and watch questions: We Know the W. items.keywords: Team USA women's 3x3 basketball headquarters, covering the Olympics, FIBA 3x3 World Cup, Women's Series, AmeriCup and Champions Cup. Team USA 3x3 Basketball | We Know the W TEAM USA · HALFCOURT · EVERY POSSESSION LOUD 3x3 BASKETBALL One hoop, four players, ten minutes and a 12 second shot clock. This is not smaller 5x5. It is a separate national team discipline with its own stars, circuit and medals. Home › No Offseason › Team USA › 3x3 Basketball OCT 28–NOV 1, 2026 · SAN SALVADOR · QUALIFYING UNDERWAY USA’s title defense now has a first opponent. Aziaha James, Flau’jae Johnson, Aerial Powers and Sydney Taylor make up the confirmed four-player roster. Colombia won Qualifying Draw A, beating Brazil 18–16 and Uruguay 19–11. USA opens against Colombia at 5:50 p.m. ET, then faces Cayman Islands at 9:20 p.m. ET on October 31. Follow the official results and standings in the Watch Hub. OPEN 2026 WATCH HUB → WATCH FIBA 3x3 ↗ POOL B USA · Cayman Islands · Colombia FIRST TIP · ET Oct 31 · 5:50 PM HEAD COACH Christina Batastini 2026 FIBA 3x3 WORLD CUP CHAMPIONS Four players, one gold medal run. Joyce Edwards, MiLaysia Fulwiley, Mikaylah Williams and Sahara Williams won the 2026 world title in Warsaw after building chemistry together on the Women’s Series. The result put USA back on top of the senior women’s 3x3 world stage. READ THE OFFICIAL RECAP ↗ WORLD CUP TEAM HOME ↗ HOST CITY Warsaw, Poland WORLD CUP ROSTER 4 players FINISH Gold medal 2026 FIBA 3x3 U23 WORLD CUP · WUHAN The next wave brought home gold, too. McKinna Brackens, Dani Carnegie, Katie Fiso and Tori McKinney won the U23 world title in Wuhan, beating the Netherlands 21-17 in the quarterfinals, Spain 21-16 in the semifinals and Canada 15-10 for gold. It is the second U23 women’s world title for the United States after the 2024 championship. USA BASKETBALL RECAP ↗ FIBA CHAMPIONSHIP RECAP ↗ FINAL USA 15 · Canada 10 ROSTER Brackens · Carnegie · Fiso · McKinney TOURNAMENT MVP Tori McKinney · 30 PTS POOL PLAY USA got through Pool D. Wins over Japan, Slovenia and Kenya put the Americans into the knockout round. The Australia game was not played because of court conditions and was recorded as a forfeit. KNOCKOUT RUN Three wins, three different tests. Dani Carnegie scored eight in the quarterfinal. Every U.S. player scored a key basket in the semifinal. McKinney then had six points and six rebounds in the defensive final against Canada. MVP Tori McKinney owned the last day. FIBA named McKinney the women’s tournament MVP after 30 total points. In the final she added six rebounds and three blocks to her game-high six points. THE PATHWAY Nations League to world champions. The same four-player group won the 2026 Nations League Americas North Conference in Chile to qualify the United States for Wuhan, then finished the job on the world stage. FOLLOW THE U23 PIPELINE → Heating the official 3x3 numbers… THE 3x3 CHEAT SHEET Fast rules, fast decisions. The compact court changes the math. There is more space to defend, less time to think and no place to hide a mismatch. COURT ½ One basket on a halfcourt. GAME CLOCK 10:00 Or first team to 21 points. SHOT CLOCK 12 Seconds to create every possession. ROSTER 4 Three on the floor, one substitute. THE SENIOR 3x3 MAP More than one tournament. The Olympics and World Cup are the headliners. The Women’s Series, AmeriCup and Champions Cup build rankings, chemistry and pressure reps between them. GLOBAL TITLE FIBA 3x3 World Cup Twenty national teams per gender chase the senior world championship. OLYMPIC MEDAL Olympic 3x3 USA won gold in Tokyo and bronze in Paris across the event’s first two Games. SEASON CIRCUIT Women’s Series Tour stops let national and commercial teams collect elite halfcourt reps. CUP EVENTS AmeriCup + Champions Cup Continental and champion level events keep the USA player pool active. WHY 3x3 PLAYERS HIT DIFFERENT The skill set is exposed. Possessions turn over instantly. Every player screens, handles, rebounds and defends in space. The best lineups combine strength, quick processing and the stamina to play without a quiet corner. OFFENSE Space, contact, quick reads. Made baskets do not create a full reset. Teams clear the ball and attack again, which rewards players who can screen, slip, finish through contact and make the next read before the defense recovers. Inside the arc counts one point. Beyond the arc counts two. The first team to 21 wins if it gets there before time expires. DEFENSE No weak link survives long. With only three defenders, one lost assignment becomes an open rim or a two point shot. Switchability, rebounding and communication matter on every exchange. One screen can force a mismatch. Long rebounds start instant offense. Fouls become increasingly expensive late. THE OLYMPIC TRACK Qualification has its own road. Country ranking points, designated events and qualifying tournaments determine who reaches the Olympic field. A 5x5 résumé does not automatically create 3x3 eligibility. SEE HOW QUALIFYING FITS → THE PIPELINE The halfcourt path starts young. U18 World Cups, Nations League and U23 events develop the habits and ranking experience that senior 3x3 demands. Team USA Women's AmeriCup | We Know the W TEAM USA · 5 ON 5 · CHAMPIONSHIP OF THE AMERICAS WOMEN’S AMERICUP A continental title, a World Cup doorway and one of the best places to see the next wave earn real national team responsibility. Home › No Offseason › Team USA › Women’s AmeriCup 2025 CHAMPIONS · SANTIAGO, CHILE Young legs, grown result. USA erased a seven point third quarter deficit and beat Brazil 92–84 in the final. The victory delivered the program’s fifth Women’s AmeriCup title and a direct berth in the 2026 FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup. READ THE OFFICIAL RECAP ↗ USA AMERICUP HOME ↗ FINAL USA 92, Brazil 84 TOURNAMENT MVP Mikayla Blakes NEXT EDITION 2027 Heating the official AmeriCup numbers… 2025 TITLE RUN The numbers that opened the World Cup door. The final became the signature moment, but the value of the tournament was bigger than one night. A young group handled seven games, pressure possessions and a direct qualification prize. FINAL SCORE 92–84 USA over previously unbeaten Brazil. USA AMERICUP GOLD 5 Fifth continental championship. BLAKES IN THE FINAL 27 Points in her best scoring game of the event. WORLD CUP BERTH ✓ The championship secured a direct ticket to Berlin 2026. WHY THIS TOURNAMENT MATTERS The bridge between promise and pressure. The AmeriCup is a senior championship, but USA often uses it to give rising players meaningful roles before the biggest global stages. REPRESENT Play for a continental title National teams from the Americas meet with a trophy and regional standing on the line. DEVELOP Expand the senior pool College stars and young professionals get real tournament minutes, not exhibition cameos. QUALIFY Move toward the World Cup AmeriCup placement can create or improve a country’s route into the global championship. EVALUATE See who travels upward Decision making, defense and role acceptance become evidence for future senior assignments. THE WE KNOW THE W READ Do not call this the junior varsity. The jerseys say senior national team and the games count. The opportunity is developmental, but the assignment is a championship. THE BREAKOUT Mikayla Blakes owned the biggest game. Blakes scored 27 in the final and won tournament MVP. That is the AmeriCup’s value in one line: a young player can move from prospect conversation to senior national team proof in a week. THE CONNECTOR Olivia Miles controlled the final. Miles delivered nine assists against Brazil. Her creation helped USA turn the fourth quarter, showing how a player’s national team role can reveal a different layer than her club assignment. THE PAYOFF Gold became a ticket to Berlin. The 2025 title directly qualified the United States for the 2026 World Cup. The path from continental championship to global stage is exactly why this event belongs in the Team USA hierarchy. The next Women’s AmeriCup will bring another roster, another pressure test and another chance to see who can carry senior responsibility before the next global event. USA captured its 12th consecutive FIBA U18 Women’s AmeriCup title in June, then won a seventh FIBA U17 Women’s World Cup gold medal in July. Different age groups, same pressure to develop while competing for first place. U18 GOLD RECAP ↗ U17 GOLD RECAP ↗ 2026 U18 AMERICUP Gold, 12th straight 2026 U17 WORLD CUP Gold, 7th title NEXT DESTINATION College, WNBA, senior USA Heating the official junior team numbers… THE 5 ON 5 LADDER AmeriCup first, World Cup next. The junior calendar alternates by age group. U16 and U18 continental teams qualify the program for the following U17 and U19 global championships. STEP 1 U16 Women’s AmeriCup The first major 5x5 national team stage for the youngest junior group. STEP 2 U17 Women’s World Cup The qualified age group moves from the Americas to a global field. STEP 3 U18 Women’s AmeriCup Older prospects face a continental championship with U19 qualification attached. STEP 4 U19 Women’s World Cup The final junior 5x5 world stage before college stars move deeper into senior contention. 2026 U23 3x3 WORLD CHAMPIONS Wuhan turned the pathway into a podium. McKinna Brackens, Dani Carnegie, Katie Fiso and Tori McKinney carried their Nations League chemistry into the FIBA 3x3 U23 World Cup and won gold. USA beat the Netherlands 21-17, Spain 21-16 and Canada 15-10 across the knockout rounds. FINAL 15-10 USA over Canada for gold. WORLD TITLE #2 USA U23 women also won in 2024. MVP McKINNEY 30 tournament points and a 44.7 player value. QUALIFYING PATH NATIONS LEAGUE Americas North champions before Wuhan. THE 3x3 DEVELOPMENT LANE Halfcourt habits start early. USA’s 3x3 pathway includes U18 World Cups, Nations League and U23 competition. The format develops fast decisions, physical finishing and defensive accountability in space. U18 3x3 U18 World Cup A first global halfcourt championship and an introduction to FIBA 3x3 eligibility. U21 + U23 Nations League Multiple stops create repetitions, country points and a deeper player pool. U23 3x3 U23 World Cup A direct bridge from youth competition to the senior international game. SENIOR Women’s Series + World Cup The best prepared players can move into tour stops and senior medal assignments. WHAT TO SCOUT The box score is only the first page. Junior dominance can hide the details. The real evaluation is how a player’s tools project when the size, speed and role demands rise. DECISION MAKING Can the advantage travel? Watch how quickly a player reads help defense, moves the ball and adjusts when the first option disappears. Those habits transfer better than a scoring average alone. ROLE RANGE Can she help without being the star? Junior teams collect primary scorers from across the country. The players who defend, screen, rebound and connect lineups show a senior ready layer. items.title: No. 31 Rises at Home: Tina Charles Becomes a Sun Legend
items.keywords: Tina Charles returned to Connecticut to become a Sun Legend and see her No. 31 raised at Mohegan Sun Arena. We trace the full-circle career and community legacy behind the honor. Tina Charles with Connecticut Sun president Jennifer Rizzotti during the Sun Legends ceremony No. 31 Rises at Home: Tina Charles Becomes a Sun Legend | We Know the W LEGACY · AUGUST 26, 2026 NO. 31 RISES AT HOME Tina Charles began and ended her WNBA career in Connecticut. Now her number hangs above the same floor, preserving a record-breaking career and a relationship that became bigger than basketball. By We Know the W Staff 7-minute read TC 31 Tina Charles and Sun president Jennifer Rizzotti during the August 25 ceremony. Photo: David Butler II / Imagn Images, viewed via Reuters Connect . THE CHARLES FILE 31 raised at Mohegan Sun Arena 4,262 career rebounds · WNBA record 8,396 career points · second all time 2012 WNBA Most Valuable Player Before Connecticut hosted Chicago on Tuesday night, Tina Charles stood beside Sun president Jennifer Rizzotti, accepted a Sun Legends varsity jacket and watched No. 31 join the names already suspended above Mohegan Sun Arena. The ceremony did not introduce her greatness. It gave that greatness a permanent address. A full circle, not a straight line Charles arrived in Connecticut long before she wore a Sun uniform. At UConn, she anchored back-to-back undefeated national championship teams. The Sun then selected her first overall in the 2010 WNBA Draft, keeping one of the most decorated players in college basketball close to the place where she had already learned how to win. She was Rookie of the Year immediately. Two seasons later, Charles averaged 18.0 points and 10.5 rebounds, won league MVP and pushed Connecticut to a 25–9 record and the top seed in the Eastern Conference. She became the first Sun player to win the award. THE FULL-CIRCLE LINE Connecticut drafted the player, watched the legend travel, and welcomed the woman home. The years away made the return richer Charles left after the 2013 season and built a career broad enough to touch six WNBA franchises. She played for New York, Washington, Phoenix, Seattle and Atlanta, collecting scoring titles, All-WNBA selections and records that grew larger every season. When she returned to Connecticut in 2025, she was no longer the young center trying to establish herself. She was the league’s measuring stick for longevity. Charles led the Sun in scoring at 16.3 points per game, set a franchise single-season scoring record with 700 points and finished her career where it began. The record book has her fingerprints everywhere Charles retired in May as the WNBA’s all-time leader in rebounds with 4,262 and made field goals with 3,364. Her 8,396 points rank second in league history. Those totals explain the scale of the career, but they do not fully explain the consistency required to build it. Her game lasted because it evolved. Early Charles overwhelmed defenses with power, quick second jumps and touch around the rim. Later she expanded her range, learned how to create from different spots and continued to rebound even as her role and teammates changed around her. What Connecticut was really honoring The banner recognizes a player, but the timing made the night about place. The Sun are spending their final Connecticut home stretch celebrating the people who formed the franchise’s identity before the organization relocates to Houston. Charles belongs in that story twice: as one of its first transcendent stars and as the veteran who chose to return for the last complete season in Uncasville. She joined a 2026 Sun Legends class that includes Jonquel Jones, Alyssa Thomas, Jasmine Thomas and Curt Miller. No. 31 now hangs with the franchise’s other honored numbers, making sure the Connecticut chapter remains visible even after the team’s address changes. The legacy extends beyond the glass Charles also became a two-time recipient of the Dawn Staley Community Leadership Award. Through Hopey’s Heart Foundation, founded in memory of her aunt Maureen “Hopey” Vaz, she has helped place hundreds of automated external defibrillators in schools, recreation centers and underserved communities. In 2025, the foundation reached its 500-device milestone. The ceremony night also carried a distinctly Tina Charles detail: she used it to introduce “SUNSET,” a hazy IPA from her 78 Brewing Co. dedicated to the players, coaches and fans who built Connecticut Sun basketball. It was remembrance turned into entrepreneurship, another way of carrying the story forward. A banner as a promise Jersey honors often feel like punctuation. This one feels more like preservation. Connecticut is changing, the franchise is moving and Mohegan Sun Arena will soon hold memories instead of a WNBA schedule. Raising No. 31 promises that the history will not be flattened by the move. Charles once said that everything started for her in Connecticut. On August 25, the state answered: what she started there will remain. Filter the board by team or by verdict. Everyone Liberty Lynx Showed up Did not The Collier distinction: she did not disappear. She competed through a difficult matchup and a season shaped by double ankle surgery. But 14 points on 6-of-14 shooting with five fouls is not the takeover Minnesota needed from its franchise player. THE FALL OF THE LYNX Minnesota did not get upset. Minnesota got solved. An upset can be a hot shooting night, a strange whistle or one bad fourth quarter. This was not that. New York won both games by the same 16-point margin. The Liberty took Game 1 in Minneapolis, then led wire to wire in Game 2. The top seed had 80 minutes to change the story. It never found the edit. Jonquel Jones moved the series into the paint. Jones scored New York's first seven points in Game 2 and kept collecting the misses Minnesota needed to end possessions. Six of her 13 rebounds came on the offensive glass. The Liberty won paint points 44-28 and rebounds 36-29. Minnesota's guards kept meeting size at the rim, and Minnesota's bigs kept having to defend a second action after the first stop should have ended the trip. This was the matchup pressure behind Olivia Miles' nightmare. The unanimous Rookie of the Year went 1-for-8, finished with five points and one assist, and played only 17 minutes. Across the series, she scored 16 points with two assists while shooting 20 percent. That does not erase her brilliant season. It is also exactly the kind of film every contender will place on her desk next spring. New York's stars looked like stars. Breanna Stewart played all 40 minutes and filled every column that mattered: 21 points, five rebounds, four assists, two steals and two blocks. Sabrina Ionescu shook off an uneven season with 18 points, seven assists and four threes. Jones finished with 21 and 13. The trio scored 60 of New York's 87 points and scored or assisted on 70. Minnesota had one clear answer. Courtney Williams brought 18 points, eight rebounds and five assists. Kayla McBride gave the Lynx 14 points and three steals. But one good backcourt night cannot cover a frontcourt mismatch, a rookie point guard trapped in traffic and a franchise star unable to bend the game. The regular season built a résumé. The series demanded counters. Cheryl Reeve earned Coach of the Year by guiding a remade roster to 33 wins while Collier missed the first half of the season. That work is real. So is the failure to produce a playoff adjustment that changed the geometry. New York shot 52 percent from three in Game 1. The Liberty dropped to 31 percent in Game 2 and still won by 16 because Jones owned the extra possessions, Stewart controlled the pace and Minnesota scored fewer than 20 points in each of the last three quarters. The ugliest number is not 71. It is zero. Minnesota never led in Game 2. The league's best regular-season team spent its elimination night chasing. THE SHAK TAKE New York was an eighth seed by record, not by ceiling. Minnesota knew that before the series. It still played as if the better seed would eventually rescue the better season. This is more than a bad week. The Lynx lost the 2024 Finals, fell in the 2025 semifinals and just exited in the 2026 first round. Each season had its own context. Together, they create a direction. Minnesota is still a first-class organization with an elite coach, a foundational rookie and a superstar. But the postseason trend is moving backward while Collier's leverage is moving forward. THE SERIES 178-146 New York's aggregate score across two games. SECOND CHANCES 12 OREB New York offensive rebounds in Game 2. THE WALL 38.2% Minnesota's Game 2 field-goal percentage. LAST 3 QUARTERS <20 EACH Minnesota never reached 20 points in a quarter after the first. THE CORE THREE 60 PTS Jones, Stewart and Ionescu outscored every Lynx trio. PLAYOFF RIPPLE · OCTOBER 7 SNAPSHOT The bracket lost its favorite. Now New York is one loss from joining it. Atlanta leads the Liberty 2-0 after a 101-98 overtime win. Golden State and Las Vegas are playing Game 2 of the other best-of-five semifinal. 1 MINNESOTA · 8 NEW YORK NYL WINS 2-0 Historic upset complete. New York moves into a longer series where its star depth has more room to matter. 4 ATLANTA · 8 NEW YORK ATL LEADS 2-0 Atlanta can close the semifinal Friday in Brooklyn after surviving Game 2 in overtime, 101-98. 2 GOLDEN STATE · 3 LAS VEGAS GSV LEADS 1-0 The Valkyries won Game 1 by 11 and are hosting Game 2 at Chase Center. SEMIFINAL FORMAT FIRST TO 3 No WNBA team has rallied from 0-2 to win a playoff series. New York must make history to advance. 01 The “eight seed” label is camouflage. New York went 26-18, won the regular-season series against Minnesota and still carries the Jones-Stewart-Ionescu championship core. No remaining team should treat the Liberty like a traditional bottom seed. 02 Best-of-three rewards the first punch. The current 1-1-1 opening round leaves almost no recovery window. Minnesota lost its home opener and had to save the season in Brooklyn 48 hours later. 03 Atlanta has seized the wider road. The only 33-win team is gone, and the Dream have turned that opening into a 2-0 lead over New York. One more win sends Atlanta to the Finals. THE PHEE DECISION ROOM Will Napheesa Collier leave Minnesota? The honest answer is that nobody outside her circle knows. The important answer is that she can. WE KNOW THE W READ LEAN STAY Not a prediction of a signed contract. It is an editorial read of the basketball situation today. CONTRACT 2026: 1 YEAR · $1.4M The one-year supermax kept every 2027 option open. STATUS UNRESTRICTED FREE AGENT Collier can negotiate across the league after the season. TEAM CONTROL NO CORE TAG Under the new eligibility rules, Minnesota cannot use the core designation to block her market. Why she stays Why she leaves Our read BOTTOM LINE Do not turn a long postgame hug into a transaction. Collier has not requested a trade, announced a departure or publicly closed the door on Minnesota. She chose a one-year deal, called herself “focused on the now” and noted that contracts create “new opportunities every year.” The Lynx should hear that as leverage, not betrayal. MINNESOTA'S OFFSEASON BOARD What must change before the sales pitch begins. 01 Build a playoff offense, not just a winning offense. Minnesota needs counters when length closes the paint and opponents sit on Miles' first read. 02 Give Collier a frontcourt answer. Jones turned one miss into two possessions all night. Size, rebounding and interior physicality cannot be a one-player job. 03 Keep developing Miles without hiding the film. The rookie season was special. The series exposed the next syllabus: pressure reads, pull-up balance and passing over size. 04 Make the pitch before free agency. Collier already knows Minnesota's culture. The front office must show how the basketball plan will stop repeating the same ending. RECEIPTS The facts behind the thought.
