items.title: The Union Behind the Deal
items.keywords: How Nneka Ogwumike, the WNBPA executive committee, player representatives and union staff built the 2026 WNBA collective bargaining agreement, with the final deal checked against the signed CBA. The Union Behind the Deal | We Know the W HERSTORY · FRONT OFFICE 101 · LABOR THE UNION BEHIND THE DEAL Nneka Ogwumike became the public face of a historic CBA. The work behind it belonged to an entire union. Home › Herstory › The Union Behind the Deal The headlines told us the 2026 collective bargaining agreement was historic. The signed 409-page agreement shows exactly how. It raised the economic ceiling, but it also rebuilt the floor beneath the roster: minimum salaries, team spending requirements, retirement money, pregnancy protections, childcare, family planning, developmental jobs and formal ways for players to remain involved in league operations after bargaining ended. That is why this is not simply a story about stars getting paid. It is a labor story about the whole locker room. PRIMARY-SOURCE REVIEW · SEPT. 3, 2026 2026 CBA WNBPA LABOR HISTORY 2026 TEAM CAP $7.0M The exact 2026 Salary Cap in Article VII. SUPERMAX $1.4M 20% of the cap. The standard maximum is $1.19M. TEAM SALARY FLOOR $5.95M 85% of the cap must be reached by season’s end. LEGAL TERM Mar. 19, 2026 Effective through Jan. 15, 2033, subject to the negotiated early-out option. Primary-source correction: Earlier public summaries often used “$1.4 million maximum” as shorthand. The signed agreement is more precise. The Standard Maximum Salary is 17% of the cap, or $1.19 million in 2026 . The Supermax Salary is 20%, or $1.4 million , and only certain contracts qualify for it. Nneka was the captain. The union was the team. Nneka Ogwumike had already spent a decade as WNBPA president by the time the new agreement took effect. She helped lead the union through the 2020 CBA, the pandemic era, rapid commercial growth, expansion and a new level of attention around women’s basketball. By the time these negotiations arrived, players were bargaining inside a business that looked dramatically different from the one they had negotiated around five years earlier. Ogwumike’s role was enormous. She spoke publicly for the union, participated in negotiations, helped hold together a membership with very different career stages and economic interests, and carried strike authority after players overwhelmingly authorized the executive committee to use it if bargaining required it. But the final agreement itself reinforces the central idea behind her leadership: collective bargaining is bigger than any one player. The 2026 CBA is part of Nneka Ogwumike’s basketball legacy, but calling it “Nneka’s deal” would miss the lesson. The power was collective, and many of the most important gains are designed for players who will never sign the richest contract on the roster. The seven players with bargaining authority During the 2025 and 2026 negotiations, the seven player leaders on the WNBPA executive committee were Ogwumike, Kelsey Plum, Napheesa Collier, Breanna Stewart, Alysha Clark, Elizabeth Williams and Brianna Turner. Their union titles mattered because each role carried responsibility beyond being a recognizable player. PRESIDENT Nneka Ogwumike The principal elected player leader and the most visible voice of the union throughout the bargaining cycle. FIRST VICE PRESIDENT DURING BARGAINING Kelsey Plum A senior union voice during negotiations and one of the executive committee members empowered by the strike authorization vote. VICE PRESIDENT Napheesa Collier A prominent public advocate for a transformational economic model and one of the union leaders pressing the league on player value. VICE PRESIDENT Breanna Stewart A veteran union leader who remained publicly engaged through extensions, status quo bargaining and the final push toward an agreement. VICE PRESIDENT Alysha Clark Part of the executive committee carrying formal bargaining authority and an important veteran and role-player perspective inside the union. SECRETARY Elizabeth Williams A longtime player advocate whose union work included executive committee responsibility through the negotiation cycle. TREASURER Brianna Turner An executive committee member helping represent players whose value to the league cannot be reduced to star billing or maximum contracts. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR Terri Carmichael Jackson The union’s senior staff leader, supported by WNBPA staff and counsel through labor and collective bargaining work. The lineup changed after the bargaining period, so these titles are presented as part of the negotiation history. Union leadership is an office players hold for a period of time. The agreement belongs to the membership that authorized and ratified it. The less visible bargaining table The executive committee was only the top layer. Reporting during the talks described a typical player negotiating committee of at least 33 players, the seven executive committee members plus 26 team player representatives, with additional players able to participate. At the major 2025 All-Star bargaining session, more than 40 players attended. That matters because a reserve guard, a veteran forward, a player on a minimum contract, a mother, a rookie, an All-Star and a player fighting to keep a roster spot can experience the same CBA very differently. Team representatives connect the bargaining table to those locker-room realities. The final vote remained with the membership. Solidarity did not mean silence The negotiation was not a perfectly smooth march. Players debated strategy, revenue definitions, proposals and the pace of talks. That is not evidence of a weak union. It is evidence of a democratic one. Strong labor coalitions argue internally because different members carry different risks, then decide what they can stand behind together. In December 2025, 93 percent of players participated in a strike authorization vote and 98 percent voted yes. The vote did not automatically call a strike. It gave the executive committee authority to call one if bargaining required it. Once the new CBA became effective, Article XXXIX established the negotiated no-strike and no-lockout rules for the agreement’s term. The long nights before the signed pages OCT. 2024 Players opt out The WNBPA exercised its option to end the prior agreement early and bargain for a new economic framework. JULY 2025 All-Star solidarity becomes public More than 40 players attended an in-person bargaining session while the All-Stars used “Pay Us What You Owe Us” shirts to make the economic dispute visible. DEC. 2025 Strike authority is approved With 93 percent player participation, 98 percent voted to authorize the executive committee to call a strike if necessary. JAN. 2026 Status quo bargaining continues The parties continued bargaining after the prior agreement’s deadline without immediately stopping play or operations. MARCH 2026 Marathon negotiations Consecutive bargaining sessions pushed deep into the night as the parties worked through economics and working conditions. MARCH 19 The new agreement becomes effective The signed CBA itself defines March 19, 2026 as its effective date. MARCH 23–24 Ratification More than 90 percent of players participated and voted unanimously to approve the agreement. The league’s governors also ratified it. MAY 22 The long-form document is completed The parties announced execution of the final long-form CBA, the 409-page text that now governs the relationship. What the signed agreement actually changed The final CBA lets us move beyond headlines and read the machinery underneath them. The 2026 team salary cap is exactly $7 million. The minimum team salary is 85 percent of that cap, meaning a team that finishes below $5.95 million in Team Salary owes the shortfall to its players under a distribution method determined under the agreement. PLAYER MINIMUMS $270K to $300K in 2026 The minimum rises with years of service: $270,000 for zero years, $277,500 for one to three, $285,000 for four to six, $292,500 for seven to nine and $300,000 for ten or more. MAXIMUMS $1.19M standard · $1.4M supermax The standard maximum equals 17% of the cap. The supermax equals 20% and is reserved for the qualifying contract situations spelled out in Article V. ROOKIE SCALE No. 1 pick starts at $500K The signed 2026 rookie scale lists $500,000 for the first pick’s first season, with exact amounts for each first-round slot and later rounds. TEAM SPENDING FLOOR 85% minimum team salary This is one of the less glamorous but crucial protections. Teams cannot simply benefit from a higher cap while choosing not to spend a meaningful share of it. Revenue sharing is a formula, not a slogan The agreement defines Shared Basketball Revenue as the prior year’s League Revenue plus Team Revenue. The salary cap after 2026 is then connected to a defined share of those revenue buckets, after accounting for specified benefits and adjustments. For the 2027 Salary Cap Year, the agreement’s designated share uses 30.25 percent of 2026 League Revenue plus 12 percent of 2026 Team Revenue. The league-revenue share becomes 30.5 percent beginning with the next calculation, while the team-revenue share rises over the agreement from 12 percent to 13 percent. The cap itself is protected from extreme annual swings: 2027 cannot rise or fall by more than 13 percent from 2026, and later annual changes are generally limited to 10 percent. There is another protection hiding in the math. If the revenue formula would have produced a larger cap but the annual growth limit holds the cap down, the excess can create a Salary Cap Limit Shortfall. If aggregate player salaries finish below the aggregate salary-cap amount, that can create a Guarantee Shortfall. The CBA combines applicable shortfalls into a League Shortfall that must be paid to players who were on WNBA rosters during that regular season. In other words, the cap limiter is not simply a way to keep money away from the players. Why the role players matter A $1.4 million supermax makes the headline. A spending floor, minimum salary schedule, benefits after a waiver, retirement contributions, family protections and temporary replacement rules decide whether the agreement improves the career of the eighth, tenth, twelfth or developmental player too. The signed document makes that middle of the roster impossible to treat as an afterthought. The benefits tell the role-player story Some of the clearest evidence of what the union secured appears outside the salary tables. These provisions are not reserved for MVP candidates. They affect players building ordinary professional lives inside an unusually competitive labor market. 401(K) 140% employer match The plan adds a 140 percent employer match on eligible player deferrals. It also includes regular employer contributions equal to 2% of Base Salary at two years of playing service, 3% at three years and 4% at four or more years for eligible players. VETERAN RECOGNITION $30K · $50K · $100K Eligible current and retired veterans receive one-time recognition payments based on pre-agreement service. Retired players who previously won WNBA MVP receive the $100,000 tier regardless of service length. RETIRED PLAYER HEALTH Up to $1,250 annually Beginning in 2027, qualifying retired players with four or more years of service can receive a health reimbursement benefit for eligible preventative-care expenses, subject to the CBA’s coverage and employment conditions. PREGNANCY 100% salary protection A player who cannot render services because of pregnancy receives 100% of the applicable Base Salary she otherwise would have received, or the weekly stipend for a Developmental Player, for the period defined in Article X. CHILDCARE Up to $1,250 per month in 2026 The CBA provides qualifying childcare reimbursement and requires teams to accommodate eligible children and caregivers on team travel under the agreement’s rules. FAMILY PLANNING $20K per year · $60K career max Eligible players, spouses or domestic partners can receive reimbursement for specified adoption, surrogacy, egg-freezing and fertility or infertility costs not otherwise covered. NON-BIRTHING PARENT LEAVE Two paid weeks Standard Players who qualify as non-birthing parents receive two weeks of paid parental leave, which do not have to be taken consecutively. LIFE + CAREER PROGRAMS $700K life insurance The CBA maintains a $700,000 group life policy for non-developmental players and requires at least $250,000 per calendar year for qualifying education, training and career programs. Developmental players finally have a defined lane The two developmental spots per team are more specific than a generic “practice player” label. A Player Development Contract carries a base stipend calculated at $750 per week of the regular season, prorated when necessary, plus an Active Games Bonus for games in which the player is activated. A team may carry no more than two Developmental Players. An individual developmental player can be activated for the greater of 12 regular-season games or 25 percent of the scheduled season, rounded to the nearest whole number. The contract cannot exceed one season and does not carry Base Salary protection, but it contains a team option to convert the player to a Regular Contract at the applicable minimum if the team has cap room or an exception. Developmental salaries are excluded from Team Salary. That structure does not erase roster insecurity, but it creates an actual employment category, compensation rules and a path to conversion where the league previously had less formal room for development. Family, health and facilities are working conditions The agreement goes beyond checks. By the start of the 2027 season, teams must provide a safe family room at the home arena. Nursing mothers must have private accommodations that are not bathrooms, plus access to refrigeration for breastmilk. Practice-facility standards become enforceable beginning with the 2028 season, with reasonable-efforts expectations beginning in 2027. These provisions explain why collective bargaining cannot be reduced to one salary figure. A professional workplace includes where players train, how they recover, what happens when they become parents and whether their families can function around the demands of the job. Player voice did not end when bargaining did Article XXXVI creates a Player Advisory Panel to discuss league operations, improve player-league relations and foster the WNBA’s growth and success. The panel includes five players, the WNBPA Executive Director or designee, the Commissioner or designee and up to three team representatives. It must meet face to face at least once each offseason. That may sound less dramatic than a salary number, but it matters. The CBA does not treat player voice as something that exists only when a contract is expiring. It creates a formal place for that voice inside the life of the agreement. One legal detail worth remembering The CBA is effective as of March 19, 2026 and, absent use of the negotiated early-out provision, continues through January 15, 2033. Either the WNBA or WNBPA may give notice by January 15, 2031 to terminate it effective January 15, 2032. The agreement also explicitly says it is separate from the NBA/NBPA CBA and should be interpreted on its own terms. That is why Front Office 101 should explain WNBA rules as WNBA rules rather than assuming an NBA comparison controls the answer. Herstory is also labor history WNBA history is usually organized around championships, MVPs, records and iconic shots. Labor belongs in that archive too. Every rookie who enters on a larger scale, every veteran who receives recognition money, every parent using a negotiated benefit, every retired player accessing preventative-care support and every developmental player working inside a defined contract category is living inside a structure other players negotiated. That makes Ogwumike’s presidency one of the defining off-court careers in league history. It also makes Plum, Collier, Stewart, Clark, Williams, Turner, the team representatives, participating players, union staff and the broader membership part of the same chapter. Some were superstars. Some were classic role players. Some did their most important work in rooms fans never saw. The biggest lesson from the signed CBA is not that the stars won. It is that the union wrote a deal whose value can be found all the way down the roster. Front Office 101 → Back to Herstory → Nneka in Playerpedia → Research receipts Primary source: the signed 2026 WNBA/WNBPA Collective Bargaining Agreement, reviewed in full for the deal terms described in this story. Key provisions used here include Articles V, VII, VIII, X, XII, XX, XXXIII, XXXVI, XXXVIII and XXXIX. items.title: Unrivaled Is Worth $650 Million. The Real Story Is Who Owns the Upside.
items.keywords: Unrivaled is now valued at $650 million. We compare the player-owned 3x3 league with 2026 WNBA franchise values, revenue, expansion fees and media scale to explain why the number matters. Unrivaled Is Worth $650 Million. The Real Story Is Who Owns the Upside. | We Know the W \n FOOD FOR THOUGHT · UNRIVALED BUSINESS · AUGUST 27, 2026 $650 MILLION. NOW WHAT? Unrivaled nearly doubled its valuation in less than a year. The headline is big. The more important story is how quickly investors are pricing women’s basketball — and how much of that upside belongs to the players themselves. By We Know the W Staff 9-minute read Updated October 5, 2026 Home › No Offseason › Unrivaled › Food for Thought $650M 3×3 NEW VALUATION $650M After an oversubscribed Series C round that raised more than $100 million. SEPT. 2025 $340M Unrivaled’s valuation after its Series B round. 2026 REVENUE ~$45M Up from approximately $27 million during the inaugural season. PLAYER EQUITY ~$200M The player ownership pool is now worth nearly 30% of the league valuation. Unrivaled did not simply raise another round of money. It crossed into a valuation tier that makes a two-year-old winter league impossible to dismiss as a side project. The 3 on 3 league founded by Napheesa Collier and Breanna Stewart is now valued at $650 million after an oversubscribed Series C fundraising round led by Ten Pillars Sports Fund and backed by UC Investments. The round brought in more than $100 million and pushed Unrivaled far beyond the $340 million valuation it announced in September 2025. That is an increase of roughly $310 million in less than a year. Put another way, investors have nearly doubled the price they are willing to put on Unrivaled while the league is still preparing for only its third season. THE BOTTOM LINE Unrivaled is no longer being priced like an experiment. Investors are pricing it like a sports property with room to become much larger. OCT. 5 UPDATE Issa Rae joined Unrivaled as an investor through the same oversubscribed Series C round. The $650 million valuation was already set in August; Rae's announcement adds another major entertainment and business name to the ownership group. Unrivaled says this is her first league-wide investment. Read the Snack Shak Byte → The WNBA comparison is startling — but it needs a warning label The easiest way to make the $650 million figure sound enormous is to place it next to WNBA franchise valuations. Forbes estimated in May that the Golden State Valkyries were worth $780 million, the New York Liberty $600 million and the Indiana Fever $580 million. The rest of the 13 established franchises Forbes valued ranged from $430 million for Seattle down to $250 million for Atlanta. If Unrivaled were incorrectly treated like a single WNBA team, its $650 million valuation would slot between Golden State and New York. In other words, the entire Unrivaled league is now valued above 12 of the 13 WNBA franchises included in Forbes’ 2026 ranking. VALUATION SNAPSHOT · FORBES WNBA ESTIMATES Where $650 million sits These are not directly comparable assets: Unrivaled is a whole league, while each WNBA number below represents one franchise. The visual is about scale, not equivalence. Golden State Valkyries $780M Unrivaled · whole league $650M New York Liberty $600M Indiana Fever $580M Seattle Storm $430M Las Vegas Aces $420M Atlanta Dream $250M Forbes valued 13 established WNBA franchises at a combined $5.4 billion in 2026, excluding first-year Portland and Toronto. The warning label matters. A league owns media rights, sponsorship inventory, intellectual property and central operations across every club. A franchise owns one team’s share of a much larger league ecosystem. Comparing the two is like comparing the value of a restaurant chain with the value of one individual location. The broader WNBA still sits on a much larger economic foundation. Forbes put the combined value of those 13 established teams at nearly $5.4 billion, meaning Unrivaled’s $650 million is only about 12 percent of that franchise total. The WNBA also begins a national media-rights package worth roughly $3.1 billion over 11 years. Unrivaled is growing fast, but the WNBA remains the larger league by infrastructure, schedule, franchises and national rights. So why does the comparison matter? Because investors are no longer treating women’s basketball as a market with room for only one valuable professional product. The WNBA can be worth billions collectively while an offseason 3 on 3 league can also be worth hundreds of millions. That is the shift. Women’s basketball is becoming an ecosystem: WNBA franchises, expansion rights, media deals, winter leagues, sponsorship portfolios, athlete-owned ventures and new competition such as Project B can all attract capital at the same time. That changes the old question from “Can women’s basketball support a league?” to “How many valuable basketball properties can this audience support?” The most important $200 million may belong to the players Unrivaled’s most disruptive business feature is not the 3 on 3 format. It is ownership. Players are the league’s largest shareholder group. According to reporting around the Series C round, more than 95 percent of Unrivaled players hold some form of equity, all 36 players from the inaugural season received ownership stakes, and the collective player equity pool is now valued at nearly $200 million — roughly 30 percent of Unrivaled’s total valuation. PLAYER OWNERSHIP Nearly $200 million in equity That number represents paper value, not a cash payout today. But it means the people creating the product can participate directly if the league keeps appreciating. That is a different wealth-building proposition from simply earning a salary for the season. The distinction matters especially in the same year the WNBA adopted a new collective bargaining agreement with dramatically higher salaries and a new revenue-sharing structure. Better wages and revenue sharing improve what players earn from labor. Equity gives players a stake in the asset itself. Those are not the same thing. A player can stop playing and still potentially own part of a company that keeps growing. The revenue is beginning to catch up with the hype Valuation alone can be speculative. Unrivaled has also produced actual business growth. Commissioner Micky Lawler said the league generated approximately $45 million in 2026 revenue, up from about $27 million in its inaugural season. That is roughly 67 percent year-over-year growth. Ticket sales climbed sharply, and the Philadelphia tour stop drew 21,490 fans, a regular-season record for professional women’s basketball. Brooklyn then sold out for the semifinals. Those numbers help explain why Unrivaled is planning a much larger road presence in 2027, with roughly eight tour stops under consideration. The league has also said it has outgrown its approximately 1,000-seat Sephora Arena home near Miami and is considering a move to a larger venue by 2028. But the growth has not been perfectly linear. Unrivaled’s 2026 playoff viewership fell 9 percent from its first season, with the semifinals averaging 213,000 viewers. The championship recovered some of that momentum, becoming the third-most-watched game in league history, but the dip is useful context. VALUATION IS NOT A TROPHY $650 million is an investor judgment, not guaranteed future revenue. Unrivaled still has to grow its audience, convert touring demand into repeatable revenue, justify larger venues and keep elite players choosing its winter calendar. A high valuation raises expectations along with capital. One Unrivaled league is worth more than two new WNBA expansion fees Another useful comparison comes from expansion. Cleveland, Detroit and Philadelphia agreed to pay $250 million each for future WNBA franchises. Unrivaled’s $650 million valuation is about 2.6 times one of those expansion fees. Again, this is not a direct one-for-one asset comparison. A WNBA expansion fee buys entry into the established 5 on 5 league, its long-term media system and its franchise ecosystem. Unrivaled’s valuation prices the entire company. But both numbers tell the same larger story: access to women’s professional basketball has become expensive because investors believe future revenue will be much larger than present revenue. Asset 2026 figure What the number represents Unrivaled $650M Whole-league valuation after Series C financing. Golden State Valkyries $780M Forbes estimate for one WNBA franchise. Average established WNBA team $414M Forbes average across 13 franchises it valued. Future WNBA expansion fee $250M Reported entry price for Cleveland, Detroit and Philadelphia. WNBA national media package ~$3.1B Approximate value across 11 years, showing the larger league’s media scale. Unrivaled does not need to replace the WNBA to change it That may be the most important point. Unrivaled was built as a domestic offseason option, not a summer replacement. Its strongest players are WNBA stars. Its biggest names become more valuable when both leagues grow. Its existence gives players another place to earn, train, build an audience and own part of what they create without spending the winter overseas. The leverage comes from proof. If a young league can pay six-figure salaries, grant equity, sell out NBA arenas on tour, grow revenue and attract capital at a $650 million valuation, then the industry can no longer argue that player-centered economics are incompatible with serious investment. The WNBA’s enormous franchise growth proves women’s basketball has become a premium ownership asset. Unrivaled’s rise asks the next question: how much of that future value can the athletes capture for themselves? The verdict Do not read $650 million as evidence that Unrivaled is already bigger than the WNBA. It is not. Do not read it as guaranteed profit. It is not that either. Read it as evidence that the market for women’s basketball has widened. Two years ago, Unrivaled was an idea built around a winter window. Now it is an eight-club league with growing revenue, touring demand, a third season largely under contract and investors willing to price the company at $650 million. And because the players own roughly 30 percent of it, every future jump in value could mean something women athletes have too rarely received from the sports businesses they helped build: not just a bigger check, but a bigger piece. items.title: Three Cities, Two Games, One Bigger Bet: Unrivaled on Tour
items.keywords: Unrivaled will take Season 3 doubleheaders to Boston, New York and Philadelphia in 2027. We Know the W examines what the tour means for the league, its players and its next stage of growth. Olivia Miles Kahleah Copper DiJonai Carrington Boston New York Philadelphia Three Cities, Two Games, One Bigger Bet: Unrivaled on Tour | We Know the W FOOD FOR THOUGHT · UNRIVALED · SEPTEMBER 11, 2026 THREE CITIES. TWO GAMES. ONE BIGGER BET. Miami remains home, but Unrivaled is taking four clubs and a doubleheader to Boston, New York and Philadelphia. The tour is more than a road trip. It is a live test of how far this league can travel. By We Know the W Staff 6 minute read Updated September 11, 2026 Home › No Offseason › Unrivaled › On Tour 46/48 ABOARD 01 JAN. 8 BOSTON TD Garden → 02 JAN. 22 NEW YORK Barclays Center → 03 FEB. 15 PHILADELPHIA Xfinity Mobile Arena TOUR STOPS 3 Boston, New York and Philadelphia are confirmed. EACH TICKET 2 games Back to back games on one night at every stop. ON THE FLOOR 4 clubs Matchups follow once club assignments are set. ROSTER BOARD 46 of 48 Two Season 3 player seats are still held. Unrivaled is keeping Miami as its home court and making the league portable at the same time. The official Season 3 tour currently has three stops. Boston opens the road schedule at TD Garden on January 8. New York follows at Barclays Center on January 22. Philadelphia gets the final announced date at Xfinity Mobile Arena on February 15. Every stop carries the same promise: one ticket, two games and four Unrivaled clubs playing back to back. The first game tips at 7:30 p.m. Eastern and the second at 9 p.m. The club matchups remain open because Season 3 assignments have not been announced. THE BIG IDEA This is a test of portability. Can the intimacy, star access and speed of Unrivaled still feel like Unrivaled inside three NBA arenas? Miami is still the home. The audience no longer has to come to Miami. Unrivaled’s compact home base has been part of its identity. Players work in one location, broadcasts control the environment, and the crowd sits close enough to make a short court feel loud. The tour does not abandon that model. It asks whether the model can travel for one carefully packaged night at a time. That distinction matters. A full road schedule would add travel, recovery and operating complexity to a league built partly as an alternative to an overseas winter. Three doubleheaders create a national footprint without turning every week into a conventional home and away grind. One ticket, two games is the product. The doubleheader is not just scheduling convenience. It gives fans four clubs and several stars in a single trip. It also lets Unrivaled sell the league, rather than asking a new city to attach itself to one temporary “home” club. FRIDAY · JANUARY 8 TD Garden Game 1 at 7:30 p.m. ET Game 2 at 9 p.m. ET FRIDAY · JANUARY 22 Barclays Center Game 1 at 7:30 p.m. ET Game 2 at 9 p.m. ET MONDAY · FEBRUARY 15 Xfinity Mobile Arena Game 1 at 7:30 p.m. ET Game 2 at 9 p.m. ET Boston, Brooklyn and Philadelphia also give the league three different reads on demand. Each is a major basketball market. Each has a different relationship with women’s professional basketball. Strong crowds would give Unrivaled more than a highlight. They would give the league evidence for sponsors, future venue talks and whatever its next map becomes. The roster makes the tour legible before the clubs do. Unrivaled has revealed 46 of the 48 Season 3 players. Olivia Miles and Flau’jae Johnson sit at the front of a board that also includes returning pillars Breanna Stewart, Napheesa Collier, Chelsea Gray, Kelsey Plum and Paige Bueckers. Gabby Williams, Marine Johannès, Kayla McBride, Kahleah Copper and DiJonai Carrington deepen a field built to sell star matchups. But there is an important blank space. Players are aboard. Clubs are still to be assigned. That is why the tour page cannot yet tell Boston, New York or Philadelphia exactly which four teams they will see. The next reveal turns a city date into an actual basketball matchup. ROSTER STATUS · SEPT. 11 46 confirmed. Two seats held. Club assignments still to come. Open the complete Season 3 roster board → The arena is part of the experiment. Unrivaled’s television product benefits from tight sightlines and a crowd pressed near the floor. TD Garden, Barclays Center and Xfinity Mobile Arena are much larger rooms. Success is not only about the final attendance number. It is also about whether the league can make those buildings look and sound full of its own personality. That means presentation matters: where the court sits, how the lower bowl is sold, how the two games flow together and whether the in arena experience explains the clubs quickly enough for fans who may be seeing them live for the first time. What the tour can prove 01 Stars can travel the brand. If fans buy the doubleheader before club loyalty is fully formed, player recognition is doing real business work. 02 The product can scale. A strong night in an NBA arena shows the short court format can keep its energy beyond the Miami studio. 03 Scarcity can be a feature. One date per city makes the visit feel like an event, while limiting the travel burden on players. 04 The map can grow carefully. Ticket demand, atmosphere and local response can help shape where future tour stops belong. What we still need to know The official board has two player reveals left. Club assignments are pending. Tour matchups are pending. The tour page also does not yet supply a complete broadcast plan for each stop. Those are not small details. They determine which stars each city gets, how the games fit the Season 3 race and how much of the tour reaches fans who are not in the building. For now, Unrivaled has given us the shape of the bet. Miami remains the laboratory. Boston, New York and Philadelphia become the proof points. The verdict The smartest part of this tour may be its restraint. Three cities are enough to test the appetite without remaking the league around travel. Two games are enough to make the ticket feel substantial. Four clubs are enough to let star power cross team lines. If the rooms feel alive, Unrivaled will leave Season 3 with more than three event nights. It will have a repeatable way to turn a Miami league into a national live property, one carefully chosen city at a time. items.title: What Group Play Told Us | 2026 FIBA World Cup
items.keywords: What the 2026 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup group phase revealed about France, USA, Belgium, Spain, the stat leaders and the knockout bracket. We Know the W home What Group Play Told Us graphic with real FIBA player photos, the We Know the W composite ranking, USA leaderboard context and qualification matchups Gabby Williams posing in her France uniform Emma Meesseman and a Belgium teammate during official FIBA coverage Team USA driving against Italy in official FIBA action Spain celebrating after qualifying directly for the quarterfinals Australia player in official FIBA photography What Group Play Told Us | 2026 FIBA World Cup | We Know the W FOOD FOR THOUGHT · FIBA WORLD CUP What Group Play Told Us France has been the tournament’s best team. USA has been its deepest. Belgium has been its most assured. Spain survived the messiest group. Now the format gets cruel. By We Know the W Published September 8, 2026 Data through September 7 8 minute read Home › Snack Shak › Food for Thought › What Group Play Told Us We Know the W graphic. W Score uses completed World Cup games through September 7. Player photography comes from official FIBA coverage. THE OPENING READ Four group winners. Four very different résumés. Group play did more than seed a bracket. It showed us who can dictate a game, who can survive one, and which teams are carrying warning labels into single elimination. France raced through Group B like it had somewhere better to be. USA looked overwhelming twice and deeply human once. Belgium controlled the tournament’s strongest top-two matchup with the patience of a team that knows exactly who it is. Spain lost to Mali, recovered, and still found the direct path to the quarterfinals. Those four teams earned the most valuable prize in a compressed World Cup: a day without an elimination game. Rest matters, but the group phase also showed that a bye is not immunity. The qualification round contains size, shooting, veteran guards and teams with nothing left to save. Every weakness that looked manageable across three games now has forty minutes to become fatal. France owns the cleanest résumé. USA owns the deepest roster. Belgium owns the steadiest identity. The knockout rounds will tell us which advantage travels best. GROUP GAMES 24 The full field played three times before the tournament split. DIRECT QUARTERFINALISTS 4 France, USA, Belgium and Spain skip the qualification round. TOP W SCORE 93.3 France leads the We Know the W composite after group play. USA TOP-THREE STAT SLOTS 1 of 18 Caitlin Clark is third in assists. That is USA’s only top-three entry across six headline categories. WE KNOW THE W COMPOSITE France did not just win. France separated. The W Score blends win rate, point differential, scoring rate and strength of schedule. It is an editorial performance measure, not an official FIBA ranking. Rank Team Record Point Diff. W Score 1 🇫🇷 France 3–0 +127 93.3 2 🇺🇸 USA 3–0 +77 88.7 3 🇧🇪 Belgium 3–0 +38 82.3 4 🇪🇸 Spain 2–1 +41 68.2 5 🇦🇺 Australia 2–1 +20 61.9 45% win rate 30% point differential per game 15% scoring rate 10% strength of schedule Scores recalculate only from completed World Cup games. France scored 305 points and allowed 178, an average margin of 42.3 points. The final group game was not a coast to the finish. France hit a Women’s World Cup record 22 three-pointers against Nigeria, scored 65 points in the first half and finished group play averaging 101.7 points. USA’s 88.7 is still elite, but the route was less linear. The Americans opened with a 33-point win over China, escaped Italy 55–52, then answered with a 105–64 win over Czechia. The composite rewards the ceiling and remembers the wobble. That is exactly what a knockout preview should do. France changed the temperature. Gabby Williams leads the tournament at 18.7 points per game, while France leads the W Score at 93.3. Photo and report: FIBA ↗ Belgium keeps making the right read. Emma Meesseman is tied for the tournament lead in efficiency and Belgium enters the quarterfinals unbeaten. Photo source: FIBA ↗ THE USA PARADOX First in depth. Barely on the leaderboards. USA is not failing to produce stars. It is distributing star-level responsibility so widely that the individual tables barely notice. Italy held USA to 55 points, its lowest Women’s World Cup total since the three-point line was introduced. Photo and report: FIBA ↗ THE NUMBER THAT JUMPS OFF THE BOARD Jackie Young leads USA at 11.3 PPG. That places the team’s leading scorer in a tie for 33rd on FIBA’s group-phase scoring table. Across the six headline leaderboards on the We Know the W FIBA board, efficiency, points, rebounds, assists, steals and blocks, there are eighteen top-three slots. USA occupies one. Caitlin Clark is third in assists at 6.3 per game. No American is top three in the other five categories. Efficiency No USA player in top three Points No USA player in top three Rebounds No USA player in top three Assists Caitlin Clark, third at 6.3 APG Steals No USA player in top three Blocks No USA player in top three That sounds alarming until you look at the rotation. Twelve players share minutes. USA’s group games included two blowouts. Jackie Young, Breanna Stewart and Paige Bueckers are separated by one point per game at the top of the team scoring table. The ball does not need one address. The Italy game is why this still matters. When pace disappeared and every possession became a half-court negotiation, USA missed its first ten three-point attempts. Young was the only American in double figures, with ten. Depth can win a tournament, but a close knockout game eventually asks a specific question: who creates the clean shot when the committee meeting is over? The answer may be Stewart’s versatility, Young’s strength, Bueckers’ touch, Clark’s passing gravity or Chelsea Gray’s control. USA does not need one scorer to climb the leaderboard. It does need the closing hierarchy to be obvious before the final two minutes arrive. WHAT EACH GROUP WINNER PROVED The records match. The evidence does not. Three teams finished 3–0. Spain finished 2–1. Each earned the same direct quarterfinal ticket, but the group phase gave us four different confidence levels. 🇫🇷 GROUP B 93.3 France looks like the standard. Three wins, a plus-127 margin, tournament-record shooting and two perimeter creators in Williams and Marine Johannès who can bend a defense without stopping the ball. France has made the strongest case for favorite status so far. 🇺🇸 GROUP D 88.7 USA showed both ends of its range. The best version overwhelms teams with waves of talent. The vulnerable version can be slowed by disciplined switching, crowded driving lanes and a cold perimeter. The response against Czechia mattered, but the Italy film will travel. 🇧🇪 GROUP C 82.3 Belgium’s identity is already installed. Emma Meesseman remains the organizing force, Julie Allemand keeps the offense on time, and Belgium’s 80–68 win over Australia secured first place without requiring chaos. This is a team built for connected possessions. 🇪🇸 GROUP A 68.2 Spain survived, but the warning remains. Mali’s 82–73 upset exposed Spain’s floor. Wins over Germany and Japan secured first place through the group tiebreak, yet the next opponent will be either the team that nearly beat USA or a perennial medal threat. THE ROAD TO THE QUARTERFINALS Four tickets. No soft entrances. Second and third place teams cross over with the neighboring group. Every qualification game is single elimination, and every winner already knows which group champion is waiting. SEPT. 8 · 17:45 BERLIN QUALIFICATION 🇭🇺 Hungary VS 🇯🇵 Japan Dorka Juhász gives Hungary the tournament’s second-best rebounding average. Japan counters with speed, bench scoring and the kind of three-point volume that can turn one game sideways. WINNER FACES USA SEPT. 8 · 20:45 BERLIN QUALIFICATION 🇩🇪 Germany VS 🇰🇷 Korea Germany brings size, a 47.3 rebound average and a home crowd. Korea brings 43.4 percent three-point shooting and 24 points per game off turnovers. The style collision is the game. WINNER FACES BELGIUM SEPT. 9 · 17:45 BERLIN QUALIFICATION 🇵🇷 Puerto Rico VS 🇨🇳 China Puerto Rico owns the group-phase leaders in rebounding and steals. China has Xu Han, two straight wins and the size to make every miss expensive. France gets the survivor. WINNER FACES FRANCE SEPT. 9 · 20:45 BERLIN QUALIFICATION 🇮🇹 Italy VS 🇦🇺 Australia Italy already proved it can drag an elite offense into the mud. Australia has experience, length and Ezi Magbegor. This feels like a quarterfinal that happens one round early. WINNER FACES SPAIN Spain got the bye. It did not get an easy future. The Group A winner will face Italy or Australia. Photo and report: FIBA ↗ Australia is the fifth-ranked W Score team. The Opals must survive Italy before they can test Spain. Photo source: FIBA ↗ 01 Shooting variance gets louder. France made 22 threes in one game. Italy held USA to one make through its first eleven attempts. In a series, percentages can normalize. Here, the horn sounds first. 02 Rebounding travels. Juhász, McGee-Stafford, Xu Han and Magbegor can create extra possessions without a play call. That is the most portable advantage in the qualification field. 03 Late-game clarity becomes currency. Blowout depth is a luxury. Close-game organization is survival. The teams that already know their final-five roles have an edge when the score gets tight. SHAK’S KNOCKOUT READ France is 1A. USA is 1B. Belgium is not far behind. France leaves group play with the best full résumé, the highest W Score and the hottest offense. USA remains the deepest team and the defending champion, but Italy supplied a blueprint for making that depth uncomfortable. Belgium has the clearest identity of the next tier. Spain owns the direct ticket, while the Italy versus Australia survivor may arrive with the sharper edge. The gap is real, but this bracket is not ceremonial. Player to watch Emma Meesseman is tied for first in efficiency, second in scoring and tied for second in blocks. In a tournament full of stars, nobody has influenced more categories at once. The most important USA statistic may be the absence of one. No runaway scorer means opponents cannot simply remove one option. It also means the Americans must identify the right option faster when a game slows down. If that decision becomes clean, USA’s low individual rankings will look like proof of abundance. If it stays uncertain, France and Belgium have enough continuity to turn a balanced roster into a complicated problem. Group play told us who earned rest. The next five days will tell us who earned trust. THE RECEIPTS Scores, leaders, bracket and photo sources. The FIBA dashboard remains the live layer. This article freezes the group-phase picture at the end of September 7 so the analysis does not move underneath the reader. items.keywords: Shak builds an all time WNBA Starting Five, Bench Mob and Honorable Mentions, with a transparent We Know the W rating for every player. We Know the W graphic showing Shak's all time WNBA Starting Five We Know the W graphic showing Shak's all time WNBA Bench Mob We Know the W graphic showing Shak's all time WNBA Honorable Mentions Sixteen Seats, Thirty Seasons | WNBA All Time Roster Food for Thought · All Time Edition Sixteen Seats. Thirty Seasons. Shak builds an all time WNBA Starting Five, Bench Mob and Honorable Mentions. This is not simply a list of the best résumés. It is a roster built to play, defend, adjust and win. SEPTEMBER 15, 2026 16 PLAYERS 4 ERAS 1 ARGUMENT STARTER THE RATING How the W Score works The W Score is a We Know the W editorial rating, not an official league statistic. Peak matters, but it does not erase longevity. Rings matter, but context matters too. Defense is not a footnote, and neither is the ability to thrive beside other stars. 25 Peak dominance 20 Winning and playoff translation 20 Two way impact 15 Longevity 10 Role portability 10 League imprint Why no perfect 100? The league is still writing its history. The top of the scale should leave room for the next chapter. THE FIRST UNIT Shak’s All Time Starting Five Bird organizes. Taurasi bends the floor. Moore connects everything. Wilson attacks the present. Leslie protects the paint and represents the foundation. 97.8 Sue Bird PG · Bridge Era · Seattle Storm Every superteam needs someone who sees the next advantage before it appears. Bird owns the league career assists record, won four championships and could control pace without hijacking possessions. 99.2 Diana Taurasi SG · Bridge to Modern · Phoenix Mercury The all time scoring leader supplies range, audacity and late game nerve. This lineup does not need her to create every shot. That makes her even more dangerous. 98.1 Maya Moore SF · Dynasty Era · Minnesota Lynx Moore is the connector who can also become the best player on the floor. She scores from every level, defends across the perimeter and understands how to win inside a loaded lineup. 99.5 A’ja Wilson PF · Modern Era · Las Vegas Aces Wilson is the frontcourt answer to almost every question. She can erase mistakes at the rim, switch onto smaller players and carry a postseason offense. In 2026, she became the first five-time MVP and the first to win three straight. 98.4 Lisa Leslie C · Foundation Era · Los Angeles Sparks Leslie gives the group size, touch, rim protection and foundational greatness. She won three MVP awards and two championships, and delivered the first dunk in WNBA history. THE PRESSURE WAVE The Bench Mob This is not the second team. It is the group that changes the temperature of a game. Player Position Era W Score Why she changes the game Cynthia Cooper G Foundation 99.0 The first great Finals closer, with four straight championships and four straight Finals MVP awards. Sheryl Swoopes G/F Foundation 98.6 Elite creation, elite defense and the versatility to guard the opposing star. Tamika Catchings F Bridge 98.3 A possession winner who turns deflections, rebounds and effort into championship basketball. Candace Parker F/C Dynasty 97.9 A point forward who can initiate, post, rebound and solve matchup problems at either big position. Lauren Jackson F/C Bridge 98.2 A three time MVP with interior force, shooting touch and the skill to punish traditional centers. Sylvia Fowles C Dynasty 96.9 Historic rebounding, efficient finishing and paint defense that travels to any era. Wait, Cooper scored 99.0 and comes off the bench? Correct. Tier placement is about construction, not disrespect. Bird organizes the first unit. Cooper is the first call when the game needs ruthless downhill scoring and closing. THE DEPTH TEST Honorable Mentions Leaving these five outside the first eleven shows how unforgiving an all time WNBA exercise becomes. 97.4 Breanna Stewart F · Modern Era MVP level scoring, weak side defense and a postseason ceiling built for any lineup. 95.8 Tina Charles C · Dynasty Era The league’s career rebounding leader and one of its most durable interior scorers. 95.5 Nneka Ogwumike F · Dynasty to Modern Efficiency, movement, leadership and championship impact across a remarkably long prime. 95.2 Elena Delle Donne F · Dynasty Era A singular scoring profile, historic efficiency and the centerpiece of a championship offense. 94.8 Seimone Augustus G/F · Dynasty Era Midrange mastery, playoff shot making and essential scoring on four Minnesota titles. FOOD FOR THOUGHT Recency bias does not get to run the fast break, but nostalgia does not get an automatic starting spot either. The hardest part is not naming greatness. It is deciding what kind of greatness a team needs. The W Score gives us a common language. The roster gives us an argument. Thirty seasons of WNBA history give us more than enough greatness for both. Research: WNBA all time milestones · The W25 · Houston Comets defining era · A’ja Wilson’s 2025 MVP

Depth rewards multiple long-term starters and All-Star-level players. Winning measures championship roles, not just roster membership. Longevity rewards careers that survived multiple eras. items.title: What's in a Name? The W Has Stories to Tell | Food for Thought
items.keywords: From the Dream's civil rights roots to the Wings' Pegasus, explore the stories behind WNBA team names and visit every team hub. Houston Comets historical logo Cleveland Sirens logo Atlanta Dream logo Chicago Sky logo Connecticut Sun logo Dallas Wings logo Golden State Valkyries logo Indiana Fever logo Las Vegas Aces logo Los Angeles Sparks logo Minnesota Lynx logo New York Liberty logo Phoenix Mercury logo Portland Fire logo Seattle Storm logo Toronto Tempo logo Washington Mystics logo What's in a Name? The W Has Stories to Tell | Food for Thought FOOD FOR THOUGHT · IDENTITY & HISTORY WHAT’S IN A NAME? The W has stories to tell. Civil rights, winged horses, neighborhood pride and a little Las Vegas swagger all made the roster. By Shakeema Funchess · October 17, 2026 Find your team’s story ↓ THE NAME BEFORE THE NUMBERS A jersey introduces the team before the scoreboard does. Say “Dream” and you might picture a championship parade. Atlanta’s name asks you to look further back, to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and a promise much larger than basketball. Say “Wings” and dinner might cross your mind. Dallas is thinking Pegasus. The menu can wait. A team name is a tiny piece of public storytelling. It has to fit across a jersey, survive a chant and give people something to claim. In the W, those few letters can carry a city’s landmarks, its history or the future a franchise wants to build. Some names belong to the place. Others ask the place to dream. Liberty makes New York recognizable without a map. Chicago’s Sky lifts your eyes toward its skyline. Minnesota’s Lynx draws from the natural world, while Seattle’s Storm turns regional weather into competitive personality. These names give a team local roots before it has a signature player. Atlanta adds another layer: civic memory. A name rooted in civil rights invites a question that a win-loss record cannot settle. How does a franchise honor the promise it wears? That is an editorial question, not a claim that a name alone guarantees community impact. The mythology has range. Golden State’s warrior women and Dallas’ winged horse make imagination part of the uniform. Washington’s magical name also has a practical family connection to the Wizards. Cleveland’s future Sirens look toward Lake Erie. Myth can give a franchise an instant visual language, but the local connection is what helps it stick. There is a difference between a name’s documented origin and what fans hear in it now. Sparks sounds electric. That does not establish who first proposed it or why it won. A good origin story needs receipts, even when the imagined version sounds better. A move changes the name. It does not erase the miles. The Wings’ trail runs through Detroit and Tulsa. The Aces’ franchise passed through Utah and San Antonio. Connecticut’s Sun followed the Orlando Miracle. A new identity can welcome a new city while leaving longtime fans with an older name stitched into their memories. Portland requires a different distinction. The Fire name returned for 2026, but the expansion franchise is separate from the original 2000–2002 team. Cleveland’s Sirens are likewise a new franchise, rather than a renamed continuation of the Rockers. Shared cities and revived names do not automatically create shared record books. Houston’s return carries two histories. The Comets are essential to this conversation. Their space-themed name paired naturally with the Rockets, but Cynthia Cooper, Sheryl Swoopes and Tina Thompson helped make it mean something bigger than an NBA connection. Four straight titles gave Houston the W’s first dynasty. The original team folded after 2008. The Comets’ approved return in 2027 brings the name back through the Sun’s relocation. That is a revival of a beloved identity and the next chapter of the Orlando–Connecticut franchise, rather than a new expansion slot. Houston fans get their name back without either history needing to disappear. Follow the Comets home → · Official relocation announcement ↗ The best name still needs people. Tempo offers a useful closing thought: an identity can be built around movement, sound and belonging. The name was designed to work in French and English. That choice helps a Canadian franchise speak to more than one audience from the start. Our take? The strongest names give fans something to discover after they learn the chant. Players supply the highlights. Communities supply the meaning. A logo opens the door; the people decide whether it becomes home. THE NAME GAME Find the story. Follow it home. The name fits Space City, but Houston’s women built a legacy all their own: the original Comets won the first four WNBA championships, from 1997 through 2000. The approved 2027 return comes through the Connecticut Sun’s relocation. It revives the Houston name, while the original Comets’ four titles remain part of a separate franchise’s history. items.title: Skylar Diggins Is Back in South Bend. This Time, Her Game Is Guidance.
items.type: Story · FOOD FOR THOUGHT · LEADERSHIP & LEGACY
items.keywords: Skylar Diggins Is Back in South Bend. This Time, Her Game Is Guidance. Notre Dame's former All-American joins Niele Ivey as an outside special advisor, with leadership, personal development and brand-building at the center. Why this is bigger than a coaching headline. Notre Dame women's basketball · October 26, 2026 FOOD FOR THOUGHT · LEADERSHIP & LEGACY feature FOOD FOR THOUGHT · LEADERSHIP & LEGACY Skylar Diggins Is Back in South Bend. This Time, Her Game Is Guidance. Notre Dame women's basketball · October 26, 2026 Notre Dame's former All-American joins Niele Ivey as an outside special advisor, with leadership, personal development and brand-building at the center. Why this is bigger than a coaching headline. Skylar Diggins Chicago Sky contain Skylar Diggins, official WNBA player headshot Skylar Diggins. Official WNBA player portrait. South Bend is home for Skylar Diggins, and now the relationship has an official title. Notre Dame announced October 26 that its former All-American will work as an outside consultant and Special Advisor to head coach Niele Ivey. This is not an appointment as an assistant coach. The scope is unusually telling: advise the staff, mentor student-athletes away from the floor and help young women navigate leadership, personal development and brand building. In an era when the athlete's public identity can move faster than her college career, a player who has lived those decisions brings a different kind of scouting report. A legend returns with more than a playbook Diggins starred at Notre Dame from 2009 to 2013, led the Irish to three consecutive Final Fours, scored 2,357 collegiate points and handed out 745 assists. She was a two-time consensus first-team All-American and twice won the Nancy Lieberman Award. These are accomplishments, but they are also lived evidence of what it takes to build a college program's culture. Niele Ivey called her arrival a legendary addition. Notre Dame says the arrangement will run until Diggins joins her club for the 2027 Unrivaled season. She is expected to advise the coaching staff and serve as an off-the-floor mentor, not take over formal on-court instruction. The NIL era needs mentors, not just marketers Brand building is in the job description for a reason. Modern college athletes are asked to perform, study, negotiate visibility, develop audiences and plan careers simultaneously. An experienced professional can help players ask who they want to be long before someone offers to monetize it. The crucial measure of this appointment is not whether it generates an exciting recruiting photo. It is whether athletes leave better prepared to advocate for themselves, navigate attention, and make decisions after basketball. That work rarely registers in a box score. Why the title matters It is tempting to call Diggins a new Notre Dame coach. The university identifies her instead as a special advisor and outside consultant. That distinction protects the story's accuracy and explains why her expertise will focus on guidance and staff support. This can be a meaningful model for the alumni-to-athlete pipeline: accomplished professionals sharing the business, culture and personal realities of the sport without treating everyone as an assistant coach in waiting. My ballot changes two names. The official First Team is A’ja Wilson, Olivia Miles, Kelsey Mitchell, Caitlin Clark and Breanna Stewart. It matches the five highest finishers in MVP voting. Wilson’s fifth MVP, Miles’ unanimous Rookie of the Year season, Mitchell’s record scoring, Clark’s creation and Stewart’s all-around production all make strong cases. My ballot keeps Wilson, Miles and Mitchell. I give the other two First Team places to Angel Reese and Gabby Williams. Clark and Stewart remain All-WNBA players on my Second Team. The question is how to value a full season, not whether the official five had great years. Angel was selected. The question is where. Reese averaged 16.4 points, 12.1 rebounds, 2.8 assists and 1.8 steals. She led the league in rebounding, set the WNBA single-season double-double record with 32, passed 500 rebounds, and became the first player in Atlanta Dream history to win Defensive Player of the Year. That is more than a specialist’s résumé. Reese carried a large share of Atlanta’s scoring, ended possessions on the glass and earned the league’s top defensive honor. The Second Team nod is deserved. Her First Team case is real. My two First Team moves: Reese and Williams up The Reese-Stewart decision is close. Stewart averaged 20.8 points, 8.3 rebounds and 3.3 assists, finished fifth in win shares, and ranked in the top ten in scoring, rebounding and blocks. She was one of the league’s best players. I still move Reese ahead because her record rebounding, 32 double-doubles and Defensive Player of the Year season changed the game on both ends. The Clark-Williams call is about how I weigh offense and defense. Clark averaged 22.3 points and 8.3 assists, finished in the top three in both categories and created 41.2 points per game. That is a First Team season. On my ballot, she slides to Second because Williams paired 14.4 points per game with All-Defensive First Team defense, a runner-up finish for Defensive Player of the Year and a leading role on Golden State’s 32-win team. Williams is not getting a First Team place because Caitlin Clark had a bad year. She did not. I’m rewarding Williams’ two-way responsibility and the way she carried it over a full regular season. Clark stays in my top ten. A’ja, Olivia and Kelsey keep their seats Wilson led the league with 26.2 points per game and 9.43 win shares. Mitchell scored 24.7 per game and set the single-season points record. Miles averaged 19.8 points and 6.0 assists, won Rookie of the Year unanimously, finished second in MVP voting and helped lead Minnesota to the league’s best record. Those are First Team seasons too. I can make the Reese and Williams case without pretending the other three were ordinary. They weren’t. Second Team still means All-WNBA Paige Bueckers paired 20.9 points with 5.9 assists and shot 51.2 percent from the field, 41 percent from three and 87.1 percent at the line. Jackie Young posted 18.9 points and 6.8 assists while shooting nearly 49 percent. Rhyne Howard averaged 17.7 points, led the league in steals and finished second in three-pointers. Stewart and Clark join those three on my Second Team. Shakira Austin’s 17 points, 9.5 rebounds and 20 double-doubles make her a serious candidate. With Reese and Williams moving up, Austin is the tough cut from my alternate ten. The official Second Team selection is well deserved. Golden State had two All-WNBA cases The Valkyries went 32–12, finished second in the standings and reached the Finals without an All-WNBA selection. The Finals run cannot rewrite a regular-season award. Williams’ regular-season case stands on its own. Williams averaged 14.4 points and 1.6 steals, led Golden State in scoring, made the All-Defensive First Team and finished runner-up for Defensive Player of the Year. I’d put her on the First Team. She is the Valkyries’ clearest omission. Veronica Burton also deserves a mention. She averaged 12.2 points and 5.7 assists, made All-Defensive Second Team, and finished with 7.55 win shares, second in the league only to Wilson. Her scoring was lower than the other honorees, but her two-way value and effect on winning were hard to miss. Reese was not left off the list. My snub call is about her placement. Golden State’s blank All-WNBA row is the other story, and Williams is the name I would put on the First Team. Would you put Angel Reese and Gabby Williams on the First Team over Breanna Stewart and Caitlin Clark? Should Caitlin Clark stay on First Team, or does Gabby Williams’ two-way season earn the seat? Which Valkyries player had the stronger All-WNBA case: Gabby Williams or Veronica Burton? My First Team, two names changed My First Team is Wilson, Miles, Mitchell, Angel Reese and Gabby Williams. Clark and Stewie slide to Second. I’m not saying Caitlin Clark had a small season. I’m saying Gabby’s defense and offense together earn my fifth spot. Veronica Burton is right there, and Shakira Austin just missed my ten. Where does your ballot break? items.title: The $700 Million Sparks Question: What Is the Team Actually Worth?
items.type: Story · SNACK SHAK BYTE · BUSINESS OF THE W
items.keywords: The $700 Million Sparks Question: What Is the Team Actually Worth? A report says Mark Walter is seeking more than $700 million for the Sparks and their planned practice facility. That is an asking price for a package, not a confirmed valuation of the team alone. SNACK SHAK BYTE · BUSINESS OF THE W byte SNACK SHAK BYTE · BUSINESS OF THE W The $700 Million Sparks Question: What Is the Team Actually Worth? A report says Mark Walter is seeking more than $700 million for the Sparks and their planned practice facility. That is an asking price for a package, not a confirmed valuation of the team alone. Los Angeles Sparks More than $700 million is the number attached to the Los Angeles Sparks this week. Bloomberg reporting, carried by the Los Angeles Times, says controlling owner Mark Walter is seeking that amount for the franchise and its related practice facility. That figure is not a completed sale, a confirmed offer, or a stand-alone price for the team. The package includes a major facility project, so the headline number needs a label before anyone calls it the Sparks’ valuation. THE REPORTED SPARKS PACKAGE · OCTOBER 23, 2026 Three numbers. Three different measures. An asking price, a third-party estimate and a completed transaction are not interchangeable. >$700M reported ask for the Sparks + practice facility The report describes a sale effort, not a completed deal. >$700M Reported package asking price Sparks franchise plus its related El Segundo practice facility, according to Bloomberg reporting. $400M Sportico franchise estimate A team-only estimate cited by the Los Angeles Times; published in April 2026. $300M Reported Sun transaction The Connecticut Sun sale price, cited as the previous WNBA record. Different scope and timing: the reported $700M+ ask bundles the team and facility; $400M is an estimate of the franchise; $300M is a reported sale price. They are context, not direct comparables. What the report actually says Bloomberg’s report says Walter is seeking more than $700 million for the Sparks and a related practice facility. The Los Angeles Times, which published the report, says the package would be the largest WNBA franchise sale to date if a deal reached that level. No buyer or completed agreement is named in the report. A seller’s asking price can start a conversation; it does not tell us what a buyer will pay or what the league will approve. The facility is a real part of the package The Sparks announced a $150 million headquarters and practice facility in El Segundo, with an opening planned before the 2027 season. The project adds dedicated training and performance space to the assets being discussed. Construction cost is not the same as market value. The published report does not break out how much of the asking price is attributed to the team, the facility, or other deal terms. The comparison needs a warning label The Los Angeles Times cites Sportico’s April 2026 estimate of $400 million for the Sparks franchise. It also cites the $300 million reported price for the Connecticut Sun as the previous WNBA sale record. Those figures help explain why the report is striking, but they measure different things. The $700 million-plus figure includes the facility; the $400 million estimate is for the team; and the Sun number reflects a separate transaction. We should not present them as a clean three-team valuation chart. Why this matters beyond Los Angeles The Sparks are an original WNBA franchise in one of the country’s largest sports markets, and their new facility represents a substantial long-term investment. At the same time, the team has missed the playoffs for six straight seasons. A buyer would be weighing the brand and market against the work still needed on the court. The league reported more than 90 million unique viewers across national networks during the 2026 regular season. That is meaningful growth context, but it is a league-wide audience figure, not proof of what the Sparks are worth. What would make the number real? The next receipts would be a named buyer, a reported or approved transaction price, and clarity about what the deal includes: the team, the facility, any retained ownership interests, and related obligations. Until then, $700 million-plus is a reported asking price for a package—not a confirmed sale price. We will update the board if the Sparks, Walter, a buyer, or the WNBA confirms new terms. A headline has a number. A sale has terms. The $700M question is worth watching. The answer depends on what changes hands, who buys it, and what the league approves. items.title: The Fever’s Front-Office Reset: What Comes Next for Cox, White and Kelsey?
items.type: Story · FOOD FOR THOUGHT · FEVER FRONT OFFICE
items.keywords: The Fever’s Front-Office Reset: What Comes Next for Cox, White and Kelsey? Kelly Krauskopf’s step-down is official. The Athletic reports the Fever will part ways with COO and GM Amber Cox, though the team has not confirmed that report. With no successors named, Stephanie White’s future and Kelsey Mitchell’s free agency now sit inside a larger leadership reset. FOOD FOR THOUGHT · FEVER FRONT OFFICE feature FOOD FOR THOUGHT · FEVER FRONT OFFICE The Fever’s Front-Office Reset: What Comes Next for Cox, White and Kelsey? Kelly Krauskopf’s step-down is official. The Athletic reports the Fever will part ways with COO and GM Amber Cox, though the team has not confirmed that report. With no successors named, Stephanie White’s future and Kelsey Mitchell’s free agency now sit inside a larger leadership reset. Kelly Krauskopf speaks at a press conference after returning to the Indiana Fever as president. Kelly Krauskopf at her 2024 return press conference. Photo: Indiana Fever / WNBA. Indiana Fever Kelly Krauskopf Amber Cox Stephanie White Kelsey Mitchell Caitlin Clark Aliyah Boston The Indiana Fever announced on October 23 that Kelly Krauskopf will step down as team president. The official statement did not name a successor or say where Krauskopf will go next. Separately, The Athletic reported that Indiana plans to fire COO and general manager Amber Cox. The Fever’s announcement addressed Krauskopf’s departure; it did not confirm Cox’s reported exit. The Athletic also reported Krauskopf had made her decision before the 2026 regular season ended, so the two developments should not be treated as one cause-and-effect move. No replacement has been announced. Our early forecast: ownership needs to define who leads basketball operations before the next free-agency window. That decision now shapes the coaching review and the pitch to unrestricted free agent Kelsey Mitchell. THE NEXT CHAPTER · OUR READ Four questions, four calls One departure is confirmed; one is reported. Forecasts are labeled and kept separate from team announcements. UPDATED OCTOBER 23, 2026 PRESIDENT + GENERAL MANAGER Successors not named One vacancy confirmed; one reported Our low-confidence call is that ownership names a president with clear basketball authority, then lets that leader shape the GM hire. That gives the next roster decision-maker a defined mandate. No credible front-runner has been reported, so we are not putting a name on the board. LOW AMBER COX · NEXT CHAPTER No next role reported The Athletic reports Indiana will part ways Cox’s career spans WNBA team operations and senior roles across professional sports. A return to a team or league operations post is plausible, but no destination or hiring interest has been reported. A specific team guess would be speculation without evidence. LOW HEAD COACH Stephanie White One more season remains our lean White said she wants to return, and Indiana won 28 regular-season games before losing its first-round series 1–2. We lean toward keeping her for 2027, but the new president and basketball lead may want to choose their own coach. The leadership change lowers our confidence. LOW–MEDIUM 2027 UNRESTRICTED FREE AGENT Kelsey Mitchell Slight lean toward a move A fresh leadership group could reset the relationship, but Mitchell needs a clear role and a credible plan to build a playoff defense. She has said she will put her own needs first. Indiana can make a competitive offer; it cannot count on core designation to control her decision. LOW Forecasts are editorial judgment, not reporting about private negotiations. The Fever have not announced a new president, general manager, coach decision, or contract offer to Mitchell. Two developments, two different levels of confirmation The Fever’s October 23 statement confirms that Kelly Krauskopf will step down as team president after nearly three decades with Pacers Sports & Entertainment. It does not identify a successor or explain the decision. The Athletic separately reports that Indiana will fire Amber Cox, who held the combined COO and general-manager roles. That report is based on multiple sources; the Fever had not confirmed it in the statement about Krauskopf when this update was prepared. The Athletic also says Krauskopf’s decision came before the end of the regular season. The timing puts both leadership questions in front of the franchise at once, but it does not establish that the decisions were connected. Who leads basketball operations next? There is no public candidate list. Our forecast is structural rather than a name prediction: ownership hires or designates the person who will lead the Fever as a whole, then clearly assigns that leader responsibility for the general-manager search and roster decisions. An internal promotion is possible, but we do not have a verified report identifying a front-runner. We lean toward a broader search because the president and GM roles now need clear lines of accountability, and the franchise cannot let the coaching decision and Mitchell’s free agency drift without an owner. Our early call: the Fever bring in a president with basketball authority and have that executive select or formally empower a GM. Confidence is low. The next announcement, not fan speculation, will tell us whether Indiana chooses continuity or a full reset. What could be next for Amber Cox? No next job has been reported. Cox has worked in senior team and league-facing roles across women’s basketball and professional sports, including the Phoenix Mercury, Connecticut Sun, Dallas Wings and Indiana Fever. That experience makes another team or league operations role plausible. A return to a broader COO or president’s post is one possible lane; taking time before choosing the next role is another. There is no evidence tying her to a particular franchise, so we will not turn a résumé-based possibility into a destination rumor. Could Steph get one more year? White has a case to return. Indiana finished 28–16, and White was named WNBA Coach of the Month for July. The Fever then lost their first-round series to Las Vegas 1–2, making playoff defense and late-game execution the next tests. White said after the season that she felt supported and hoped to continue, while acknowledging the decision belongs to the organization. Our lean is still to bring her back for 2027. A coach who delivered 28 wins deserves a serious review, and continuity could help a new front office settle the roster. That is now a lower-confidence call. A new president or GM may want to hire a coach they selected, and the defensive problems will be part of that discussion. White’s job has not been announced as safe or in jeopardy. Will the reset be enough to keep Kelsey Mitchell? Mitchell’s 2026 season made the question impossible to postpone. She averaged 24.7 points per game and set Indiana’s single-season scoring record with 1,086 points. After nine seasons with the Fever, she is entering unrestricted free agency in 2027. Mitchell has said she intends to be selfish about what she needs from her next decision. The reported leadership change gives Indiana a chance to make a new pitch, but it also means the people selling that pitch may not yet be in place. A familiar jersey and a strong offer are not the same thing as a convincing basketball plan. The Fever’s 2026 supermax agreement does not automatically settle her next contract. Indiana cannot rely on another core designation to keep her from choosing among teams. The new basketball lead will need to show Mitchell her role beside Caitlin Clark and Aliyah Boston, how the roster will improve its playoff defense, and who is accountable for that plan. Our current read remains a slight lean toward Mitchell exploring a move. A new leadership team could change that answer if it arrives quickly with a clear role, a credible roster plan, and the freedom to make a competitive offer. The reset alone will not keep her; what the reset builds might. The decision that reaches beyond one contract The question is larger than whether Indiana keeps one star or one coach. The Fever have to decide who owns the basketball plan, who makes the case to Mitchell, and what kind of team they are building around Clark and Boston. Our best forecast today: Krauskopf’s next destination remains unknown, Cox may return to team or league operations after a pause, Indiana is more likely than not to keep White for another season, and Mitchell is the swing decision. Each call is low confidence until the Fever name their leadership and put a real 2027 plan on the table. What would convince Kelsey Mitchell to stay? Would a new front office be enough, or does Indiana need to show Kelsey Mitchell a specific plan for the roster, defense and her role beside Caitlin Clark and Aliyah Boston?
