items.type: Story · SNACK SHAK BYTE · WNBA PAY HISTORY
items.keywords: From $15K to $270K: WNBA Minimum Pay Through the Years The lowest standard full-season minimum was $15,000. Trace the pay milestones, the 2026 CBA jump and the league growth behind the new numbers. SNACK SHAK BYTE · WNBA PAY HISTORY byte SNACK SHAK BYTE · WNBA PAY HISTORY From $15K to $270K: WNBA Minimum Pay Through the Years The lowest standard full-season minimum was $15,000. Trace the pay milestones, the 2026 CBA jump and the league growth behind the new numbers. The WNBA’s lowest standard full-season minimum base salary was $15,000 in its early seasons. For 2026, the new collective bargaining agreement sets the minimum between $270,000 and $300,000, depending on service time. That is an 18-fold rise at the low end, in dollars of the day. The climb came in labor-deal steps, not one smooth annual curve. The timeline tracks the lowest salary tier and keeps base pay separate from the Finals bonuses shown below. WNBA MINIMUM BASE SALARY · NOMINAL DOLLARS A $15,000 floor became $270,000 Select a milestone to see what changed. Bars share a $0–$300,000 scale and track the lowest standard salary tier. 18× the early WNBA floor by 2026 Nominal dollars; no inflation adjustment. 1997–98 $15,000 Early WNBA floor The starting point Contemporary reporting on the league’s first player labor deal identifies $15,000 as the previous minimum for both rookies and veterans. 1999 $25,000 Rookie minimum The first player CBA The 1999 agreement raised the rookie minimum to $25,000 and the veteran minimum to $30,000. 2008 $34,500 Rookie minimum A new six-year scale The 2008 agreement set the rookie minimum at $34,500 in its first season. 2013 $37,950 Rookie minimum End of the 2008 scale The rookie minimum climbed to $37,950 by the sixth and final year of the 2008 agreement. 2019 $41,965 0–2 years of service The last year before the 2020 deal Under the old scale, the minimum was $41,965 for players with up to two years of service and $56,375 for more experienced players. 2020 $57,000 0–2 years of service The 2020 CBA takes effect The new scale started at $57,000 for players with fewer than three years of service and $68,000 for experienced players. 2025 $66,079 0–2 years of service The final season of the old scale The 2025 minimum was $66,079 for players with zero to two years of service and $78,831 for players with three or more. 2026 $270K–$300K By years of service The new CBA reset The 2026 minimum ranges from $270,000 to $300,000, based on years of service. The higher figure is a service-time tier, not the floor. 3.8M fans in 2026 Record attendance across 330 regular-season games. 11,474 fans per game Average attendance, 21% above the previous record set in 2025. 90M+ unique viewers A WNBA regular-season record in 2026. 4B social views Record WNBA social views, up 28% from 2025. Champions · each player Runner-up · each player Finals MVP Standard full-season base-salary minimums, shown in nominal dollars. The lowest tier depends on years of service; where the salary schedule had multiple tiers, notes show the relevant higher minimum. Bonuses, endorsements, offseason pay and prorated partial-season contracts are separate. The least was $15,000 That is the league’s early standard minimum base salary. It is not an estimate of what every player earned. The first player labor agreement raised the minimum in 1999 to $25,000 for rookies and $30,000 for veterans. Years of service have shaped the minimum ever since. The timeline shows selected salary floors, not every season. It also uses nominal dollars: $15,000 in 1997 did not buy what $15,000 buys today. The steepest jump arrived with a new labor deal The 2020 agreement moved the inexperienced-player minimum to $57,000 and the experienced-player minimum to $68,000. By 2025, the lower tier had reached $66,079, with the veteran tier at $78,831. Then the 2026 agreement reset the scale. Its $270,000 low-end minimum is about 4.1 times the 2025 low end, a roughly 309% increase in one season. The $300,000 figure applies to higher service tiers. The league is growing around the pay scale The 2026 season drew a record 3.8 million fans across 330 regular-season games. Average attendance was 11,474 per game, 21% above the previous record; the league also reported more than 90 million unique viewers and 4 billion social views, up 28% from 2025. The new CBA lifted the team salary cap from $1.5 million in 2025 to $7 million in 2026 and added a comprehensive revenue-sharing model. The league says future caps will adjust with team and league revenue growth. That is a negotiated way for player compensation to move with the business. That does not mean every new fan automatically increases a player’s paycheck. Finals bonuses are a separate win Finals bonuses climbed sharply too: a player on the 2025 championship team received $22,908, compared with $60,000 under the 2026 schedule. The Finals MVP bonus rose from $5,000 to $30,000, while the runner-up bonus moved from $8,521 to $20,000. These are per-player postseason bonuses, on top of base salary. They should not be read as annual pay. The floor changed; the fight built the ladder From $15K at the start to a $270K minimum in 2026: a dramatic 18× jump in nominal dollars, with the next chapter tied to how the league’s revenue grows. This does not rank championships, Finals MVPs or overall careers. The tie changes the fifth slot The WNBA’s official season-by-season list confirms five for Wilson; three apiece for Swoopes, Leslie and Jackson; and two each for Cooper, Parker, Delle Donne and Stewart. That creates a four-player tie for fifth by award count. A fifth portrait can start the next row, but a complete history needs all four. Parker’s résumé makes her an especially fitting addition. She earned MVP and Rookie of the Year in 2008, then added her second MVP in 2013. Cooper’s two came in consecutive seasons at the league’s start; Delle Donne won with Chicago and Washington; Stewart’s came with Seattle and New York. MVP count is one lens, not a GOAT ballot This board counts regular-season MVP awards. It does not add Finals MVPs, titles, All-WNBA selections or career totals. Those are different questions, and combining them would turn a clean record into a subjective score. The useful takeaway is the shape of the record: Wilson has separated at five, the three-time tier remains a shared piece of league history, and the two-time tier is four-deep. One class, six different jobs The AP’s sixth selection is not a second-tier footnote. A tie for fifth expands a five-place honor to six. It also shows the voting problem: rookies do not enter identical situations. A guard asked to create every night has a different statistical profile from a shooter, a reserve organizer or a wing learning a veteran team’s system. Miles’ 19.8 points and 6.0 assists make the highest-volume case. Fudd’s 39.7% from three is the cleanest spacing signal in this group. Johnson pairs 14.9 points with 4.8 rebounds. Rice’s 12.9 points, 3.5 rebounds and 3.5 assists show why a short season can still leave a mark. Those numbers do not settle who has the best career ahead. They describe the work each player did in this season, in this role. A useful rookie award can honor that without pretending to be a draft redo. The 2018 class owns the highest peak because of Wilson. The 2006 five rises when the question is depth; its three headliners carried long, decorated careers. Press “Peak star” or “Class depth” and those trade-offs become visible instead of hiding inside one number. 2019 and 2014 rank well because their strength is spread across several proven careers. 2013 is a top-three peak class. 2016 is more complicated: Stewart makes the official five exceptional, but the absent Jonquel Jones and Kahleah Copper eventually won league MVP and Finals MVP awards. The snub file puts that counterfactual in view without quietly changing the official team. This is an editorial ranking with a defined window, not a claim that older players are better. Classes from 2020 onward get a watchlist treatment because their career records are still being written. Time is part of the comparison. The Food for Thought question If you could replay the rookie ballot with only that season’s evidence, which borderline choice would you change? Now ask the harder version: if you knew the whole career, would your answer change? The first question is about judging a season fairly. The second is about how poorly one early label can measure the distance a player still has to travel. Jonquel Jones and Kahleah Copper make the 2016 question almost unfair in hindsight. Their rookie years were quiet; their later peaks were not. All-Rookie is a strong note on the opening chapter. It is not the ending. One vote is a snapshot The 2026 rookie class gave us six honest cases for five spots. Career hindsight gives us another lesson: a rookie list can tell you who stood out first. It cannot tell you how far the player will go. items.title: Preseason Hype Has Homework: Who Really Looks Ready for 2026–27?
items.type: Story · FOOD FOR THOUGHT · COLLEGE BASKETBALL
items.keywords: Preseason Hype Has Homework: Who Really Looks Ready for 2026–27? South Carolina leads ESPN’s Top 25, JuJu returns to USC, and UCLA starts at No. 13. The real debate is what each contender still has to prove. FOOD FOR THOUGHT · COLLEGE BASKETBALL feature FOOD FOR THOUGHT · COLLEGE BASKETBALL Preseason Hype Has Homework: Who Really Looks Ready for 2026–27? South Carolina leads ESPN’s Top 25, JuJu returns to USC, and UCLA starts at No. 13. The real debate is what each contender still has to prove. Joyce Edwards drives against Sarah Strong contain JuJu Watkins Sarah Strong Jazzy Davidson Joyce Edwards South Carolina UConn USC Duke Michigan Louisville Iowa LSU Texas North Carolina Vanderbilt Washington UCLA Notre Dame Kentucky Minnesota Ohio State Maryland TCU Illinois Oklahoma State Arizona State Oklahoma Ole Miss West Virginia October crowns do not come with nets Preseason rankings are basketball’s seating chart. They tell us who gets the good table before anybody has served the food. ESPN’s October 13 list puts South Carolina, UConn and USC in the first three seats. That is a useful starting point. It is also an invitation to ask what would make those choices look smart in March. Our question is simple: are we ranking a program’s reputation, a roster’s ceiling, or the team we expect to trust when a close game turns ugly? Those can be three different answers. A roster can win the introduction and still need months to learn how to win the possession. The ranks below belong to ESPN, not an AP poll and not a We Know the W score. The watch questions and verdicts are our editorial analysis. Nobody has earned a 2026–27 regular-season résumé yet. South Carolina: being the favorite means showing your work South Carolina at No. 1 is defensible. It should also invite the toughest examination. Our test for Dawn Staley’s team is the quality of its half-court possessions: who organizes the offense, who gets the ball to the right spot, and who creates a good shot after the first option disappears? A favorite does not need to look flawless in November. It needs workable answers. Watch late-clock decisions, spacing around the paint, and whether the same action can produce multiple reads instead of one predictable finish. Defensive pressure can create easy points; a championship opponent will try to take those away. The W verdict: keep South Carolina in the first tier. Make it earn separation through possession quality. The logo is an introduction; the execution is the argument. UConn: Sarah Strong is the foundation, not the entire building UConn enters with Sarah Strong, the reigning national player of the year and unanimous BIG EAST preseason player of the year. KK Arnold and Blanca Quiñonez also earned unanimous preseason all-conference selections. Those are real reasons to expect a contender, confirmed by the program’s October 1 announcement. Our film question is what happens when opponents load up on Strong. Can the next receiver attack the advantage before the defense resets? Can a second creator rescue a possession without turning it into a difficult solo shot? The supporting cast matters most when an opponent has spent a week designing a plan for the star. For WNBA scouting, Strong’s value is not confined to scoring. Track the speed of her reads, defensive coverage changes, and decisions against help. A prospect who makes the right play when the easiest play is unavailable is telling us something useful. USC: JuJu is back. The chemistry still has to arrive USC confirms JuJu Watkins is returning after missing 2025–26 through injury. Both conference coaches and media named her Big Ten preseason player of the year. Jazzy Davidson joins her on the preseason all-conference teams after leading USC in points, rebounds, assists, steals and blocks last season. That makes No. 3 understandable. It does not make cohesion automatic. A returning star and an established young creator need shared timing: when to initiate, when to cut, when to clear a side, and when to turn a touch into an advantage for somebody else. We should judge Watkins’ return through basketball evidence rather than demanding a highlight reel immediately. Watch how the offense functions across multiple games, how responsibilities are distributed, and how the group responds to physical defense. A preseason honor is recognition, not a medical clearance or a guarantee about workload. The W verdict: USC has an exciting ceiling. The first useful question is whether its talented players can make one another easier to guard less often. Talent gathers attention. Connected talent gathers wins. UCLA at 13: disrespect, or a different roster? The defending champion starting at No. 13 is the obvious debate starter. UCLA’s own draft announcement supplies important context: six Bruins were selected in April, including five in the first round. That is a record-setting professional pipeline and a substantial amount of college production walking out the door. Our read: the championship deserves full credit, while the new team deserves its own evaluation. It is reasonable to forecast uncertainty after that kind of departure. It is also reasonable to expect the coaching staff’s habits to carry over. Neither point settles what the next roster can accomplish. Watch rebounding responsibilities, communication in transition, and which combinations remain functional when starters sit. Those details will tell us whether the Bruins are rebuilding continuity quickly. Calling every lower ranking disrespect skips the roster question; treating the title as irrelevant skips the coaching question. The rest of the table can change the conversation Duke and Michigan complete ESPN’s top five. Louisville and Iowa sit sixth and seventh, ahead of LSU and Texas. North Carolina closes the top ten. Our challenge to that group is the same: identify the lineup you trust against a quality opponent, then show why it works. The lower half deserves more than a drive-by. A team ranked in the teens can become a serious threat if its complementary pieces fit faster than expected. Conversely, a top-ten roster can spend the winter working through a problem everyone politely ignored in October. For fans, the most useful early result is not always the biggest win. Watch what happens after a team’s preferred style gets disrupted. Can it defend without fouling, survive a cold shooting stretch, and finish a possession with a rebound? That is where preseason optimism starts becoming evidence. Who Got Next? Scout the job, not just the name This season is also a new chapter in the WNBA pipeline. Watkins and Strong deserve attention, but scouting should not become a contest to see who can repeat the most famous names. Every prospect has to show skills that fit a professional role. For a lead guard, watch decisions against pressure and the ability to manipulate help. For a wing, watch shooting preparation, closeout attacks and defensive assignments. For a big, watch screening angles, defensive positioning, finishing windows and passing when the paint is crowded. College ranking, individual awards and draft position answer different questions. A freshman can reshape a contender without being part of the next draft. A veteran can be a compelling prospect on a team outside the top ten. Draft eligibility and declarations should be verified separately; being on our radar is not a declaration. The Food for Thought takeaway: keep the rankings, keep the debate, and ask for the film. October gives us the hypothesis. The season gets to grade the homework. Atlanta’s Finals berth puts Renee Montgomery back on the championship stage as a co-owner and vice president. Two titles, a new seat Montgomery won WNBA titles with Minnesota in 2015 and 2017. She finished her 11-season playing career with Atlanta, sat out 2020 to focus on social reform, and joined the Dream’s ownership group in 2021. The team lists her as partner and vice president. A first with Atlanta Atlanta clinched its first Finals berth since 2013 with an 85–83 win over New York on October 9. Lining up Montgomery’s Finals appearances with her ownership timeline makes her the first person in WNBA history to reach the series in both capacities: first with Minnesota as a player, now with Atlanta as a team owner. The WNBA already marks her as the first former player to hold both team equity and an executive role. The 2026 berth adds a Finals milestone to that path. Why this belongs in the Finals story The Dream’s players will decide the series on the floor; Montgomery is not suiting up. Her place in the story is different: a former player helps lead the franchise as it competes for its first championship. That path from the court to ownership shows how a WNBA career can keep shaping the league after the final season ends. The reporting identifies the Valkyries as the first women’s professional sports team to reach that mark. That is revenue: money coming into the business before expenses. It does not establish $100 million in profit. A franchise valuation is a separate estimate of what the team is worth. Full buildings, then a Finals berth Golden State sold out all 22 regular-season home games and finished 32–12. The second-year franchise then swept Las Vegas, clinching its first Finals appearance with an 87–77 overtime win on October 9. Sportico also projected that a Finals run could lift gross revenue above $130 million. Golden State has now reached the series; that projection remains a projection, not a confirmed final total. Shak’s take Ballhalla brought the noise. The balance sheet brought receipts. A packed arena and a winning roster make a strong business story, but one exceptional franchise is not a financial statement for the entire league. The useful question now: how does that demand translate into lasting investment in players, staff and the fan experience? Golden State has shown what a market can support. The next chapter is what the organization does with it. The Valkyries are the first expansion franchise to reach the championship series that quickly. Atlanta is the closest comparison. Three championships, two Finals MVPs, three Defensive Player of the Year awards, a national title and international gold make the case broader than one vote. Las Vegas Aces contain A fifth award changes the WNBA record book A’ja Wilson has won the 2026 Kia WNBA Most Valuable Player award, her fifth. Her first came in 2020, followed by 2022 and then three in a row from 2024 through 2026. That last stretch is a league first: no WNBA player had won three consecutive MVPs. The award follows another historic regular season. Wilson averaged 26.2 points, 9.4 rebounds, 3.2 assists, 1.4 steals and 1.9 blocks in 41 games. She led the league in scoring, blocks and win shares. Her 26.2 points per game is the second-highest scoring average in WNBA history; only Wilson’s own 26.9 in 2024 is higher. The numbers show why the season resisted a one-skill description. She carried an elite scoring load, controlled the glass and remained one of the league’s most disruptive rim protectors. The wider basketball comparison—and its limits Five regular-season MVPs puts Wilson in rare company across professional basketball. It matches Michael Jordan’s five NBA MVPs and leaves her one behind Kareem Abdul-Jabbar’s NBA-record six. That is a useful measure of how scarce the honor is, not proof that awards from different leagues or eras are interchangeable. The NBA and WNBA have distinct histories, schedules and voting contexts. The fair point is narrower: Wilson’s count now belongs beside the best-known MVP totals in the sport, while standing alone at the top of the WNBA. The full résumé reaches beyond the regular season Wilson is also a three-time WNBA champion, a two-time Finals MVP and a three-time Defensive Player of the Year. She entered the league as its 2018 Rookie of the Year. The spread matters: her record includes sustained regular-season dominance, postseason performance, defense and team success. Her international record adds another layer. USA Basketball lists Wilson as a two-time Olympic gold medalist, a two-time FIBA Women’s World Cup champion, the MVP of the 2022 World Cup and the MVP of the 2024 Paris Olympics. At South Carolina, she helped win the 2017 NCAA title and was named Final Four Most Outstanding Player. The record is settled; the season is still live On October 7, Wilson scored a game-high 24 points and collected seven rebounds, but Las Vegas lost Game 2 of its semifinal series to Golden State, 83–81. The Aces now trail 0–2 in the best-of-five series and need a win at home to extend their title defense. That tension is useful context for a legacy story. Individual awards recognize what a player did over a regular season; they do not decide what comes next. Wilson’s fifth MVP is already a record. The 2026 playoff chapter is still being written. Shak’s take The fifth MVP is the headline, but the case for Wilson’s place among basketball’s most decorated players comes from the combination: a WNBA record, three straight MVPs, titles, Finals MVPs, defensive awards, Olympic and World Cup gold, and a college championship. Wilson now owns more regular-season MVP awards than anyone in WNBA history. Her combination of individual honors and team success puts her among basketball’s most accomplished players. Which part of Wilson’s résumé stands out most: the fifth MVP, the three-year streak, the defensive honors or the international record? How much should cross-league MVP comparisons shape an all-time basketball conversation? items.title: Down 0–2: Somebody Has to Be First
items.type: Story · SNACK SHAK BYTE · PLAYOFF HISTORY
items.keywords: Down 0–2: Somebody Has to Be First Has a WNBA team ever won a playoff series after falling behind 0–2? As of October 8, 2026, no. Phoenix got closest in 2018. Then Masked Sue Bird happened. Playoff history · Oct. 8, 2026 SNACK SHAK BYTE · PLAYOFF HISTORY byte wnba-playoffs SNACK SHAK BYTE · PLAYOFF HISTORY Down 0–2: Somebody Has to Be First Playoff history · Oct. 8, 2026 cover 50% 35% Sue Bird drives past Yvonne Turner in Seattle against Phoenix during Game 5 on September 4, 2018 Sue Bird drives past Phoenix’s Yvonne Turner during Game 5 in Seattle, September 4, 2018. Photo: Elaine Thompson/AP, via The Spokesman-Review. Phoenix Mercury Seattle Storm New York Liberty Las Vegas Aces Atlanta Dream Golden State Valkyries Sue Bird Diana Taurasi Brittney Griner DeWanna Bonner Has a WNBA team ever won a playoff series after falling behind 0–2? As of October 8, 2026, no. Phoenix got closest in 2018. Then Masked Sue Bird happened. The short answer: not yet No WNBA team has won a playoff series after losing its first two games, as of October 8, 2026. Coming back to tie a series is a different accomplishment from finishing the comeback. The 2018 Phoenix Mercury managed the first. Nobody has managed the second. New York and Las Vegas now trail Atlanta and Golden State 0–2 in their best-of-five semifinals. Each needs three consecutive wins to advance. One win buys another game; it does not erase the deficit. Phoenix knocked. Bird changed the locks. In 2018, Phoenix lost the first two semifinal games in Seattle, then won both games at home to force Game 5. The Mercury became the first WNBA team to push a series to a deciding fifth game after an 0–2 start. Game 4 was its own escape act. Phoenix erased a 17-point deficit and won 86–84 on September 2. Brittney Griner scored the go-ahead basket with 14.1 seconds left, then helped deny Seattle’s final attempt. Two nights later, Sue Bird shut the door. Wearing a protective mask after breaking her nose in Game 4, she scored 14 of her 22 points in the fourth quarter as Seattle won Game 5, 94–84. Phoenix reached the doorstep. Seattle kept the keys. Shak’s take An 0–2 deficit is a history assignment with no completed answer key. The Liberty and Aces do not need to win three games on Friday. They need to win one, make the leaders pack for another, and repeat. Impossible? The format allows it. Unprecedented? Absolutely. Somebody has to be first. Until then, Phoenix owns the closest call and Masked Sue owns the ending. items.keywords: Issa Rae Is Unrivaled: Another Big Name Buys Into the $650M Bet Issa Rae went from courtside to the cap table. Her investment came through the same oversubscribed Series C that valued Unrivaled at $650 million, giving the league another culture-shaping name as Season 3 approaches. Unrivaled business · Oct. 5, 2026 SNACK SHAK BYTE · UNRIVALED BUSINESS byte SNACK SHAK BYTE · UNRIVALED BUSINESS Issa Rae Is Unrivaled: Another Big Name Buys Into the $650M Bet Unrivaled business · Oct. 5, 2026 cover 50% 34% Issa Rae in Unrivaled's official investor announcement Issa Rae joins Unrivaled as an investor. Official image via Unrivaled. Issa Rae went from courtside to the cap table. Her investment came through the same oversubscribed Series C that valued Unrivaled at $650 million, giving the league another culture-shaping name as Season 3 approaches. From courtside to the cap table Unrivaled announced on October 5 that actor, producer and entrepreneur Issa Rae has joined the league as an investor. The investment was made through the oversubscribed Series C round the league announced in August. Rae said seeing Unrivaled firsthand last season convinced her that the league was building something special. Unrivaled also described this as her first league-wide investment, adding another entertainment and business name to an investor group already packed with athletes, coaches and cultural heavyweights. The number did not change. The signal did. The $650 million valuation is not a fresh re-price caused by Rae's investment. That figure was set when Unrivaled announced the Series C on August 26. The round, led by Ten Pillars Sports Fund, surpassed its original $100 million target and was oversubscribed. What changed today is the cap table. Rae joins an investor list that already includes Stephen Curry, Giannis Antetokounmpo, Coco Gauff, Billie Jean King, Alex Morgan, Dawn Staley, JuJu Watkins and others. Players remain the league's largest equity group, with Unrivaled valuing the player equity pool at nearly $200 million when the round was announced. Shak's bite Celebrity money by itself is not a business model. But the kind of people choosing to buy in tells you what they think the business can become. Issa Rae brings something different from another athlete investor: entertainment reach, brand-building experience and a track record of creating culture instead of simply attaching her name to it. Unrivaled has spent two seasons proving it can make basketball feel like an event. Now it is adding investors who know how to turn an event into a larger ecosystem. Does Issa Rae's involvement make Unrivaled more interesting as a media and culture brand, not just a basketball league? Which matters more for the league's long-term ceiling: celebrity investors, touring growth or player equity? Unrivaled · Issa Rae announced as investor Unrivaled · Series C at $650 million valuation

They matter because the AP has kept the same core award slate since 2016 and its voters offer a clean, independent snapshot of the season. They are not the WNBA's official league awards, which are announced separately. That distinction belongs in the first paragraph, not in fine print after the confetti. The 2026 ballot is unusually good at showing both kinds of greatness an award list can capture. Wilson added another layer to a career that already owns plenty of hardware. Reese, Miles, Clark, Shepard and Salaün each won their category for the first time. Reeve did both at once: another trophy, but a new kind of season to explain it. A'ja did not just win. She moved the record Wilson received 15 of the 17 first-place votes, and the number that matters most is four. Her AP Player of the Year wins now span 2020, 2024, 2025 and 2026. Breanna Stewart had been the only three-time winner. Wilson did not join her; she stepped past her. The vote reads like a reward for total control. Wilson led the league in scoring at 26.2 points per game, made nearly 53 percent of her shots, pulled down 9.4 rebounds and blocked 1.9 shots. The 3.2 assists were a career best. That last number is the quiet one: the best scorer on the floor kept improving the decisions that happen after the second defender arrives. Reese won the argument at the end of possessions The defensive award had belonged to Wilson in three of the previous four AP seasons. Reese broke that grip with a case built on volume, activity and possession control. She led the league in rebounding for the third straight year, finished the regular season with 521 boards and placed third in steals. Rebounding is not every part of defense, but ending the possession is not a decorative skill. Reese's best argument was how often Atlanta got to stop playing defense once she entered the play. Her hands created turnovers, her range let the Dream move her through coverages, and her work on the glass kept opponents from turning one good action into two shots. Miles and Clark tell two different return stories Miles was the unanimous rookie choice because she never looked like she was waiting for the game to slow down. She averaged 19.8 points and 6.0 assists, set the league's rookie scoring record and operated the offense for the No. 1 seed. The history tab makes the larger point: AP Rookie of the Year has produced a different winner in all 11 seasons, and Miles belongs to a line that runs from Breanna Stewart to Caitlin Clark to Paige Bueckers. Clark's Comeback Player award is about availability as much as stardom. After injuries limited her in 2025, she played 40 games, averaged 22.3 points and 8.3 assists, and restored Indiana's ability to stretch a defense until it snapped. The comeback category has never repeated a winner. That is fitting: its value is in the specific road back, not a permanent tier of player. Shepard and Salaün stretched their job descriptions Most Improved is sometimes treated like a scoring-jump prize. Shepard made a more interesting case. She averaged 14.5 points, 11.1 rebounds and 5.3 assists and recorded six triple-doubles. Dallas gave her more minutes, but the real leap was the number of possessions she could organize from the frontcourt. Salaün's sixth-woman case was cleaner and louder. She came off Golden State's bench in all 40 games and led every reserve with 509 points. Her 93 made threes were a reserve record, and she shot 39.2 percent from deep. A bench label usually describes when someone checks in. Salaün made it describe how quickly the geometry changed. Reeve's third trophy was a systems award Minnesota reached the top seed even though Napheesa Collier missed the first half of the season. Reeve had to build one version of the Lynx without the franchise star, then make room for Collier without asking everyone else to forget what had worked. That is not simply surviving an absence. It is designing a team that can absorb a superstar and remain itself. The win gives Reeve three AP Coach of the Year awards, one more than Curt Miller. Her 2020, 2024 and 2026 trophies also describe three different coaching problems, which is the strongest part of the record. The history dashboard tells on the ballot Some awards build dynasties. Wilson and Stewart have won seven of the 11 Player of the Year votes. Wilson and Sylvia Fowles account for six of the 11 defensive trophies. Reeve and Miller own five Coach of the Year wins between them. Other categories resist a repeat. Rookie and Most Improved are 11-for-11 on unique winners. Comeback has 12 recipients because Collier and Brittney Griner shared the 2023 honor, and none has repeated. Sixth Woman sits between those worlds: Dearica Hamby is the only two-time winner. The interactive history is useful because it makes those category personalities visible without pretending every award measures greatness the same way. The AP teams are an honor roll, not a lineup card Wilson, Clark, Miles, Kelsey Mitchell and Stewart made the first team. Reese, Rhyne Howard, Paige Bueckers, Jackie Young and Gabby Williams made the second. The selections reward the season's best work; they are not a promise that the five names fit neatly into traditional positions. The six-player All-Rookie team came from a ballot tie: Miles, Azzi Fudd, Sydney Taylor, Flau'jae Johnson, Pauline Astier and Kiki Rice. It is a good problem for an awards list to have. The 2026 class did not need the ballot to shrink so its impact would look tidy. The WNBA’s All-Defensive First Team is a separate honor Update · Oct. 15, 2026: The WNBA’s official All-Defensive First Team is Shakira Austin of the Washington Mystics, Rhyne Howard and Angel Reese of the Atlanta Dream, Gabby Williams of the Golden State Valkyries, and A’ja Wilson of the Las Vegas Aces. This is the league’s team selection; the awards and All-AP teams above are Associated Press honors. Reese’s first Kia Defensive Player of the Year award adds context to her First Team selection. She received 46 votes from the 74-member national panel, ahead of Williams (20) and Wilson (4). Reese also led the league with 12.1 rebounds per game and set single-season records with 521 total rebounds and 206 offensive rebounds. Atlanta finished third in defensive rating at 103.5. The overlap is striking: all four leading finishers in the league’s Defensive Player of the Year vote—Reese, Williams, Wilson and Austin—made this First Team, and Howard joined them. Atlanta is the only team with two selections. The official league team and the AP ballot remain distinct honors. How much weight should a defensive ballot give to ending possessions on the glass? Which is harder to repeat: Most Improved, Comeback Player or Rookie-level impact in year two? Read the list twice The first read is for the winners. The second is for the shape of the league: Wilson's sustained peak, Reese's possession-ending defense, Miles running a contender immediately, Clark getting a healthy season back, and role players whose roles stopped fitting in one sentence. That second read is where an award list becomes a season story. Ian Maule/AP contain finals-in-motion #finals-game-dashboard Open the Finals game dashboard ↓ Game 6: Atlanta keeps its season alive Atlanta beat Golden State 80–69 at State Farm Arena on October 29, tying the best-of-seven Finals 3–3 and forcing Game 7. The Dream opened on a 13–0 run and made six of its first eight three-pointers. Allisha Gray led Atlanta with 23 points, Rhyne Howard added 21, and Gabby Williams led the Valkyries with 26. The result sends the Finals to the first Game 7 in WNBA Finals history. Golden State will host the deciding game Saturday at Chase Center. Game 6: the opening run changed the math Atlanta led 32–15 after the first quarter and 46–26 at halftime. Golden State won the third quarter 21–17, but still trailed by 16 entering the fourth. The Valkyries made a late push, but Atlanta kept its lead. Allisha Gray’s fifth three-pointer came with just over a minute left, restoring breathing room for the Dream. Game 5: one win away, every possession earned Golden State won 64–55 at Chase Center on October 26 and leads the best-of-seven Finals 3–2. Kiah Stokes supplied 13 points, eight rebounds, three blocks and three made threes. Veronica Burton matched her 13 points and eight rebounds while adding four blocks. Tiffany Hayes and Cecilia Zandalasini scored 12 apiece. This was a win built to survive a quiet Gabby Williams scoring night: nine points on 3-for-14 shooting. Golden State’s defense held Atlanta to 29.2 percent from the field and 55 points. Rhyne Howard scored 20; Angel Reese finished with seven points, 15 rebounds and five assists. Game 5: the turnover bill came due Atlanta committed 17 total turnovers to Golden State’s nine. The Valkyries converted those mistakes into a 21–6 advantage in points off turnovers, a 15-point swing in a nine-point game. Atlanta’s 19–6 edge in second-chance points kept it alive, but extra chances could not erase the cost of lost possessions. Stokes has recorded at least three blocks in six consecutive playoff games, matching Lisa Leslie’s 2003 single-postseason streak. Burton’s four blocks tied Diana Taurasi’s Finals record for a guard. Those are historical receipts with tactical meaning: Atlanta’s guards encountered resistance before and at the rim. Golden State does not need its leading scorer to rescue every possession when Stokes spaces the floor and Burton changes shots. Atlanta’s next counter has to create cleaner finishing angles and protect the ball, not simply ask Reese to rebound more. Game 4: Golden State answers in Atlanta Golden State beat Atlanta 67–62 at State Farm Arena on October 24, leveling the best-of-seven Finals at 2–2. Gabby Williams scored 17, Rhyne Howard led Atlanta with 19, and the Dream was held to 33.3 percent shooting. Atlanta made the ending tense: Howard’s three-point play with 28 seconds left cut the margin to four. Golden State answered at the line, then Atlanta missed its final two three-point attempts. Tiffany Hayes scored all 13 of her points after halftime; Kiah Stokes pulled down 16 rebounds, including eight on the offensive glass. The turnover swing changed the possession math Atlanta won the rebound count 51–42, but Golden State won the turnover battle 9–18 and scored 16 points off those mistakes to Atlanta’s eight. That eight-point edge in turnover scoring was larger than the five-point final margin. The takeaway: Atlanta created more total possessions; Golden State got more immediate value from the giveaways. There was a second lever. Golden State grabbed 13 offensive rebounds to Atlanta’s 12, with Stokes collecting eight of them. Atlanta still edged second-chance points 8–5, so the extra boards did not become a scoring advantage by themselves. They kept the Valkyries’ offense alive while its shots were not falling: Golden State made 36.1 percent from the field and 16 percent from three. Game 3: dreams to nightmares in Atlanta Atlanta beat Golden State 97–71 at State Farm Arena on October 21. The Dream led 23–15 after one quarter and 46–40 at halftime, then answered Golden State’s third-quarter push with an 8–0 run over the final 2:11. Atlanta closed with a 26–14 fourth quarter, turning a competitive middle stretch into the largest win of the series. Angel Reese finished with 21 points, 12 rebounds, three assists and two steals, recording a double-double in each of her first three Finals games. Rhyne Howard added 16 points, five steals and four assists; Naz Hillmon scored 15. The final official box score lists Howard at 16, resolving an early live-blog line that reported 18. Golden State got 15 points from Gabby Williams, 14 from Tiffany Hayes and 13 apiece from Cecilia Zandalasini and Janelle Salaün. Kiah Stokes blocked four shots. The Valkyries’ bench won 38–27, but Atlanta’s starting group supplied 70 points and controlled the decisive stretches. The possession math behind the 26-point gap Atlanta shot 34-for-69 from the floor (49.3 percent) and 9-for-22 from three (40.9 percent). Golden State finished 24-for-69 (34.8 percent) and 12-for-30 from three (40.0 percent). The Valkyries matched Atlanta’s perimeter accuracy, but Atlanta made 22 two-point baskets to Golden State’s 12 and won the paint 44–20. The free-throw margin mattered without carrying the whole result: Atlanta went 20-for-29, Golden State 11-for-17. Ball security created the sharper divide. The Dream committed 10 total turnovers and scored 22 points off Golden State’s 17; the Valkyries scored seven points off Atlanta’s miscues. Atlanta also assisted on 26 of 34 field goals. Golden State owned the offensive glass 9–6, second-chance scoring 10–4 and bench scoring 38–27. Atlanta still won total rebounds 51–44 because it finished possessions with 31 defensive rebounds and kept converting stops into organized offense. Those counters explain why the visitors’ useful advantages never became scoreboard pressure. Game 2: Atlanta answers at Chase Center Atlanta won 79–65 on October 19, earning its first Finals victory and evening the series. The third quarter delivered the decisive separation: Atlanta 21, Golden State 9. A two-point halftime gap became 14 entering the fourth, and the teams traded 19 points apiece from there. Angel Reese finished with 30 points, 16 rebounds and three assists. Allisha Gray supplied 18 points; Jordin Canada paired 13 points with 10 assists and seven rebounds. Rhyne Howard scored only five, but her six steals show why scoring alone misses Atlanta’s most disruptive work. Golden State had 14 points from Gabby Williams, 11 rebounds and four blocks from Kiah Stokes, and three made threes from Kaila Charles. The bench outscored Atlanta 33–11. Veronica Burton added 11 points. That depth kept producing, but the starters combined for only 32 points. Game 1: Williams finishes the job Golden State won 68–64 on October 17. Atlanta led 22–14 after one quarter; Golden State answered 28–17 in the second. Atlanta regained a 56–51 edge entering the fourth before the Valkyries won that period 17–8. Gabby Williams supplied 26 points, including 16 in the second quarter, a total the official team recap places tied third in Finals quarter history. Golden State scored the final seven points, with Williams making six free throws. Kiah Stokes added nine points, seven rebounds and four blocks. The support came through possession work: Kaila Charles had 10 rebounds, Tiffany Hayes six rebounds and four assists, and Laeticia Amihere five points and five rebounds. Golden State won player rebounds 41–35 and bench scoring 20–6. Its 17 points off turnovers more than doubled Atlanta’s eight. Allisha Gray scored 19, Angel Reese 14 with 12 rebounds, and Rhyne Howard 12. Gray and Howard combined to shoot 8-for-33. Golden State survived limited scoring breadth by extending possessions, protecting the rim and closing with Williams. Atlanta’s response came two days later. Game 2: the arithmetic behind Atlanta’s answer Both teams made 21 field goals and seven three-pointers. Those totals describe the difference in the box score; they do not establish whether any particular whistle was correct. Atlanta also won the possession exchanges. Golden State committed 19 turnovers to Atlanta’s 14, while the Dream scored 24 points off turnovers against 13 for the Valkyries. Atlanta’s 17–7 edge in second-chance points added another route to scoring without needing a better shooting percentage. Analysis: a nearly identical field-goal output can disguise very different offensive nights. Atlanta generated enough trips to the line and extra-possession scoring to win comfortably despite shooting 33.9 percent from the floor. Golden State’s 34.4 percent was scarcely better; the ball security and foul-line gaps made that shared struggle much more expensive for the home side. Atlanta gets the last possession right The Dream beat New York 85–83 on October 9 and swept the semifinals 3–0. DeWanna Bonner secured the late rebound and made both free throws; Breanna Stewart’s final putback could only trim the margin. Angel Reese supplied 22 points and nine rebounds, Rhyne Howard scored 21 and Jordin Canada paired 19 with 11 assists. Bonner added 13 points and 13 boards; Isobel Borlase scored 10 off the bench. Atlanta returns to the Finals for the first time since 2013. Its next test is Golden State’s defensive pressure and depth. The Valkyries turn five extra minutes into a ticket Golden State finished Las Vegas 87–77 in overtime, completing a 3–0 sweep. A 17–0 third-quarter run changed the game; an 8–0 fourth-quarter burst helped force the extra period. The Valkyries won overtime 16–6. Kayla Thornton scored 18, Gabby Williams 16, and Tiffany Hayes and Kiah Stokes 11 each. Stokes went 5-for-5 and recorded a double-double. Hayes passed 500 career playoff points. Golden State reaches its first Finals in its second season, with home court against Atlanta. Two exits change the talent audit New York and Las Vegas are eliminated. Their draft pedigrees remain part of the semifinal story, but no longer count toward the players still chasing this title. The two finalists have 11 top-10 picks between them: seven for Atlanta and four for Golden State. Rhyne Howard is the lone No. 1 pick among those two rosters. Analysis: premium picks can supply options, but depth, defensive coordination and late-possession execution decide whether those options survive a series. A first title is guaranteed Atlanta and Golden State are each chasing the first WNBA championship in franchise history. The No. 2 seed Valkyries and No. 4 seed Dream have reached a best-of-seven Finals after taking different routes through the postseason. Renee Montgomery’s story has two Finals seats Dream partner and vice president Renee Montgomery won WNBA championships with Minnesota in 2015 and 2017. She joined Atlanta’s ownership group in 2021; when the Dream clinched a 2026 Finals berth, she became the first person in WNBA history to reach the Finals as both a player and team owner. The WNBA describes Montgomery as the first former player to hold both team equity and an executive title. Her Finals story now spans two franchises and two roles: champion on the floor, then a Finals-bound owner in Atlanta. Game 7 is Saturday in San Francisco Game 6 final: Atlanta 80, Golden State 69. items.title: One Last Sunrise: Farewell to the Connecticut Sun
items.type: Story · FOOD FOR THOUGHT · CONNECTICUT SUN FAREWELL
items.keywords: One Last Sunrise: Farewell to the Connecticut Sun The final record was 11–33. The final result was a win. Between those two facts sits 24 seasons of Connecticut basketball that deserve to be remembered. The final season · 2003–2026 FOOD FOR THOUGHT · CONNECTICUT SUN FAREWELL feature wnba-playoffs FOOD FOR THOUGHT · CONNECTICUT SUN FAREWELL One Last Sunrise: Farewell to the Connecticut Sun The final season · 2003–2026 Connecticut Sun fans celebrate the franchise at its final home game in Mohegan Sun Arena The final record was 11–33. The final result was a win. Between those two facts sits 24 seasons of Connecticut basketball that deserve to be remembered. A final night worth keeping Connecticut beat Toronto 95–81 at Mohegan Sun Arena on Sept. 24, 2026. The Sun ended their last season 11–33, with a one-game winning streak. A hard year did not get the last word: the players and crowd got one more win together. The team is moving to Houston and will be renamed the Comets in 2027. Connecticut fans have every right to hold on to what was built in Uncasville. 2003: a home by the river After the Orlando Miracle relocated, the Mohegan Tribe brought the franchise to Connecticut in 2003. Playing at Mohegan Sun Arena made the Sun a place people traveled to, returned to and claimed as their own. The Tribe’s ownership was a defining part of the identity. 2004 and 2005: the first close calls Mike Thibault’s early Sun reached back-to-back WNBA Finals. Seattle won in 2004; Sacramento won in 2005. Lindsay Whalen, Nykesha Sales and Asjha Jones helped set a standard: Connecticut could meet the league’s best on the biggest stage. 2019 and 2022: the door stayed open The 2019 Sun took Washington to a deciding fifth game in the Finals. In 2022, behind a bruising frontcourt featuring Alyssa Thomas, DeWanna Bonner, Brionna Jones and Jonquel Jones, Connecticut made its fourth Finals appearance. Different faces, familiar promise: the Sun were never easy to put away. The people who gave the jersey its weight Jonquel Jones won the 2021 MVP award as a Sun and had her No. 35 honored at the arena in 2026. Alyssa Thomas turned versatility and toughness into a team language. Across eras, players, coaches, staff and supporters made Connecticut a fixture in the postseason conversation. No championship banner arrived. Four Finals trips did, and so did the habit of believing the next one could be different. That is a legacy bigger than one difficult final standings line. One game, one streak, decades of light The final box score reads Sun 95, Tempo 81. It cannot show every seat filled across 24 seasons, or every player who grew into herself in this building. The name leaves the schedule. The memories, and the people who made them, stay in Connecticut. items.title: The Fever Got the Bench. What Did Minnesota Actually Give Away?
items.type: Story · FOOD FOR THOUGHT · PLAYOFF BENCH TEST
items.keywords: The Fever Got the Bench. What Did Minnesota Actually Give Away? Indiana needed the win. Minnesota needed to get healthy. By halftime, those priorities were obvious. The Fever took the 96-77 win, but the second half became something else: a live playoff-depth test. Final week · bench check FOOD FOR THOUGHT · PLAYOFF BENCH TEST 50% 38% cover feature wnba-playoffs FOOD FOR THOUGHT · PLAYOFF BENCH TEST The Fever Got the Bench. What Did Minnesota Actually Give Away? Final week · bench check Minnesota Lynx players gather during a game Minnesota Lynx game photography, via the official September 22 game preview. Minnesota Lynx Indiana Fever Golden State Valkyries New York Liberty Dallas Wings Las Vegas Aces Washington Mystics Atlanta Dream Caitlin Clark Kelsey Mitchell Olivia Miles Chloe Bibby Liatu King Janelle Salaun Marine Johannes Sophie Cunningham Jewell Loyd Indiana needed the win. Minnesota needed to get healthy. By halftime, those priorities were obvious. The Fever took the 96-77 win, but the second half became something else: a live playoff-depth test. Golden State Valkyries 36.1 bench PPG The deepest playoff bench by a mile. Janelle Salaun is a Sixth Player favorite, Tiffany Hayes brings another veteran creator, and Golden State can change lineups without changing its identity. New York Liberty 23.0 bench PPG Marine Johannes gives New York instant offense and movement. The Liberty second unit is efficient enough to survive short starter rests without asking one player to do everything. Dallas Wings 21.6 bench PPG Dallas gets useful scoring and activity from its reserves. The question is how much of that survives when playoff rotations shrink. Las Vegas Aces 21.4 bench PPG Jewell Loyd gives Vegas something most benches do not have: a former All-Star who can still take over possessions. The Aces do not need huge bench minutes, just dependable ones. Indiana Fever 21.1 bench PPG Sophie Cunningham keeps pace and spacing around the stars. Indiana's bench is not the headline, but it can keep the offense from falling off a cliff. Washington Mystics 20.3 bench PPG Young, physical and willing to defend. Washington's depth matters because the Mystics can keep size on the floor when the starters sit. Atlanta Dream 17.9 bench PPG Atlanta leans harder on its starting group. The bench has been efficient, but the playoff question is whether it can buy enough clean minutes for the stars. Minnesota Lynx 14.3 bench PPG Lowest regular-season bench scoring among the playoff field, but Tuesday showed why raw bench PPG can lie. Minnesota's reserves cut a 29-point hole to eight before Indiana's starters closed it out. Sixth woman Team Bench case Playoff job Janelle Salaun Golden State 12.9 PPG, 39.7% from three, league-leading 492 bench points Primary second-unit scorer and a real late-game option Marine Johannes New York 8.7 PPG with playmaking and movement shooting Change the geometry of the floor when New York gets sticky Sophie Cunningham Indiana 8.3 PPG in bench games, 43%+ from three Keep pace, spacing and edge around Clark and Mitchell Jewell Loyd Las Vegas Veteran shot creation from the second unit Give Vegas a scorer who does not need the starters to create her look Did Minnesota prioritize rest? Not from the opening tip. Olivia Miles was already out with a calf injury, but Minnesota started Napheesa Collier, Kayla McBride, Courtney Williams and the rest of its available first unit. Indiana then punched them in the mouth. The Fever led 31-16 after one quarter and pushed the margin to 29 in the first half. That is when Cheryl Reeve changed the assignment. She sat her starters for most of the final two and a half quarters because she did not want to risk another injury. So yes, rest and health became the priority, but only after Indiana had already taken control. Calling the entire win gift wrapped lets Minnesota's starters off too easily. Still, Indiana got a very nice gift Indiana needed this one to keep its home-court hopes alive. Instead of spending 40 minutes dealing with Minnesota's best five, the Fever spent most of the second half playing the Lynx reserves. The funny part is that the bench made Indiana work. Chloe Bibby hit five threes and scored 15. Liatu King had 12 points, four rebounds and three steals. Aari McDonald added 10 points and five assists. Minnesota cut a 29-point deficit to eight before Caitlin Clark, Kelsey Mitchell and Aliyah Boston finally shut the door. That is the part Minnesota should keep The loss matters because the No. 1 seed still is not clinched. The way the bench responded matters for a different reason. Playoff benches are not supposed to win four-minute stretches by accident. They have to survive foul trouble, injuries and the ugly minutes when a starter needs air. Minnesota ranks last among the eight playoff teams in regular-season bench scoring. Tuesday did not magically make the Lynx the deepest team in the field. It did show that their reserves can defend, run and drag a game back into range when the stars are sitting. Golden State has the bench everybody else has to answer Golden State is in its own category. The Valkyries are around 36 bench points per game, roughly 13 more than the next playoff team. Janelle Salaun has 492 points off the bench, the most in the league, while shooting 39.7 percent from three. That depth already mattered after Berlin. With several World Cup players resting, Golden State still beat Portland 82-66 behind Laeticia Amihere and Kaitlyn Chen. That is not emergency depth. That is part of the system. The Sixth Woman board Salaun is the standard here. ESPN's four-person awards panel unanimously picked her for Sixth Player of the Year, and the production backs up the attention. Marine Johannes gives New York a different kind of weapon, Sophie Cunningham keeps Indiana's second unit connected to its spacing, and Jewell Loyd gives Las Vegas a scorer with starter-level experience. The playoffs will shrink rotations, but that makes these players more important, not less. The question is not who has ten playable bodies. It is who has a sixth and seventh player a coach actually trusts when the game gets tight. Shak's read Indiana earned the lead. Minnesota chose not to chase it with its starters. Both things can be true. The Fever got exactly what they needed: a win without having to beat Minnesota's best lineup for four quarters. The Lynx got something too: a long look at the players who may have to save a playoff possession, a quarter or a game when the plan goes sideways. Thursday's rematch is the one that tells us more. If Minnesota brings the full group and treats it like a playoff tune-up, then we finally get the matchup Tuesday was supposed to be. Did Minnesota make the right call pulling the starters? Which playoff bench do you trust most for a seven-minute stretch? Would you rather have one elite sixth woman or three dependable reserves? Paige Bueckers Arike Ogunbowale Jessica Shepard The final table is set. The trio rankings are here to argue. Minnesota finished first at 33-11, followed by Golden State, Las Vegas, Atlanta, Washington, Indiana, Dallas, and New York. Washington won the tiebreak over Indiana at 28-16. Every team played 44 games, so there is no projection left hiding under the table. Atlanta is the only team whose trio production rank matches its seed exactly: fourth and fourth. Golden State's No. 1 defense explains a second seed that its eighth-ranked trio scoring does not. Indiana owns the opposite problem. The Fever rank first in trio production, eighth in limiting scoring, and sixth in the standings. That is not a gap. That is a whole hallway. Minnesota earned the top seed with balance, not one runaway category. Olivia Miles, Napheesa Collier, and Kayla McBride rank third in combined scoring and fourth in defensive context. That top-four balance on both sides helps explain 33 wins. Miles creates the first bend, McBride punishes the help, and Collier connects the possession at either end. The return window was far less convincing. Minnesota went 2-2 and outscored opponents by one point total. Miles played only twice, and a 20-point win over Indiana on the final night pulled the margin back above water. The Lynx still own the best seed. They do not own the best post-break pulse. Golden State's second seed begins with the league's best playoff defense. Gabby Williams, Veronica Burton, and Kiah Stokes rank eighth in scoring because this trio is built to take something away. Golden State's 99.1 defensive rating is the best in the playoff field and the only one below 100. That is the number that looks like a second seed. The Valkyries went 3-1 after the break and allowed 72.0 points per game. Williams returned for the last two, Burton averaged 2.3 steals across the window, and Stokes blocked two shots per game. Golden State does not need this trio to win a scoring contest. It needs them to keep changing the questions. Las Vegas has the trio nobody wants to see in the last five minutes. A'ja Wilson, Jackie Young, and Chelsea Gray combine for 57.1 points and 16.7 assists per game. Wilson can finish the possession, Young can win the advantage, and Gray can keep touching the matchup that bends first. Their No. 2 production rank sits one place above the Aces' seed. The return was loud and complete: 4-0, a plus 21.5 margin, and seven straight wins to finish the season. The trio supplied 59.3 points and 18.0 assists per game in that stretch. That is not a tune-up. That is a warning label. Atlanta owns the most complete trio on the board. Allisha Gray, Rhyne Howard, and Angel Reese rank fourth in scoring and Atlanta ranks third in defense. They also lead every trio here with 7.5 combined steals and blocks per game. Gray and Howard make the floor wide. Reese makes the possession longer. The fourth seed fits them almost perfectly. Atlanta went 4-0 after the break and posted the best margin in the field at plus 24.5 per game. Reese averaged 19.3 points, and the trio produced 8.0 steals plus blocks per game. Fourth seed, first in the post-FIBA pulse, and no obvious weak side. Washington's fifth seed is carrying a second-ranked defense. Shakira Austin, Sonia Citron, and Kiki Iriafen rank seventh in trio scoring, but Washington finished second among playoff teams in defensive rating. The three also combine for 22.9 rebounds per game. The Mystics do not need every trip to be pretty if the opponent keeps getting one shot. Washington went 4-0 after the break with a plus 16.0 margin and climbed from seventh to fifth. Austin averaged 18.0 points and 10.3 rebounds in the window. Iriafen added 14.8 and 11.3. Their seed says middle of the field; their defense says make room. Indiana can win a shootout. The playoffs will ask for another answer. Kelsey Mitchell, Caitlin Clark, and Aliyah Boston are the production champions at 63.1 combined points per game. Indiana also owns the WNBA's best official team offensive rating. Mitchell's efficiency, Clark's passing range, and Boston's interior touch can make a defense choose its least comfortable way to lose. The other side is the issue. Indiana ranks eighth among playoff teams in defensive rating and eighth in the post-break pulse after a 2-2 finish. Boston averaged 9.0 points in the window, and Minnesota won the finale by 20. The Fever's No. 1 offense can erase a lot. It cannot be asked to erase everything. Dallas finished seventh, but its trio grades closer to the middle. Paige Bueckers, Arike Ogunbowale, and Jessica Shepard rank fifth in production, while Dallas ranks sixth in limiting scoring. Both sit above the Wings' seventh seed. Bueckers and Ogunbowale pull the defense outward; Shepard gives the possession somewhere smart to go next. Dallas went 3-1 after the break with a plus 9.0 margin. The trio supplied 55.8 points and 18.8 assists per team game, with Shepard averaging 8.8 assists. Seventh seed, yes. Seventh-best trio, no. New York's numbers sit above eighth. Its finish did not. Breanna Stewart, Sabrina Ionescu, and Jonquel Jones rank sixth in production, while New York ranks seventh in defense. Both are one or two places better than the Liberty's final seed. The names still carry championship muscle memory, but the final line is the final line. New York started the return with wins over Minnesota and Toronto, then lost twice to Atlanta and fell to eighth. The Liberty still posted a plus 5.0 margin across the four games because those first two wins were loud. The last two were louder in the wrong direction. Shak's call: the best trio depends on the question. Need the most points? Indiana. Need one closing possession? Las Vegas. Need to drag a game into the mud? Golden State. Need the best two-way blend with the hottest return? Atlanta. Need a lower seed that is better than its number? Washington and Dallas have receipts. The final standings reward 44 games, and they should. A playoff series asks a different question: can your three most important players keep solving the same opponent after the easy answers are gone? Atlanta enters with the fewest obvious weak spots. Las Vegas brings the most trustworthy closer. Minnesota owns the top seed. Indiana owns the biggest ceiling and the widest crack beneath it. The field is settled. The argument is not. Can Indiana's first-ranked trio offense survive a series with the playoff field's eighth-ranked defense? Is Atlanta's two-way balance more valuable than Las Vegas having the best closer in A'ja Wilson? Which lower seed is built to break the bracket first: Washington, Dallas, or New York? Does Minnesota's balance still make the Lynx the favorite after a 2-2 return from the break? A Big Three Is a Job Description Three famous names do not automatically make a playoff trio. Somebody has to create the advantage. Somebody has to finish it. Somebody has to stop the other team from doing the same thing. Indiana brings the biggest plate of points. Golden State takes the plate away. Atlanta finished the season looking like it could do both before anybody found a seat. items.title: One Free Throw, Sixteen Years, and Gold: USA Is Back on Top
items.type: Story · SNACK SHAK BYTE · USA WHEELCHAIR BASKETBALL
items.keywords: One Free Throw, Sixteen Years, and Gold: USA Is Back on Top Canada tied it with 39.1 seconds left. Courtney Ryan hit the free throw that made it 77–76. Twenty seconds later, Team USA had its first women’s wheelchair basketball world title since 2010 and a new runway toward LA 2028. IWBF World Championship · USA 77, Canada 76 SNACK SHAK BYTE · USA WHEELCHAIR BASKETBALL 50% 38% cover U.S. women’s wheelchair basketball. Photo via NBC Sports championship coverage. U.S. women’s wheelchair basketball game action byte SNACK SHAK BYTE · USA WHEELCHAIR BASKETBALL One Free Throw, Sixteen Years, and Gold: USA Is Back on Top IWBF World Championship · USA 77, Canada 76 United States Canada Lindsey Zurbrugg Courtney Ryan Rose Hollermann Ixhelt Gonzalez Arelle Middleton Canada tied it with 39.1 seconds left. Courtney Ryan hit the free throw that made it 77–76. Twenty seconds later, Team USA had its first women’s wheelchair basketball world title since 2010 and a new runway toward LA 2028. The last point became the whole story A championship game can hold an entire sixteen-year wait inside one free throw. Host Canada pulled even at 76 with 39.1 seconds left in Ottawa. Courtney Ryan went to the line with 20.8 seconds remaining, missed the first and made the second. That was the final point of the 2026 women’s world championship. Lindsey Zurbrugg led the United States with 26 points. Rose Hollermann and Ryan scored 17 each, and Ryan finished one rebound and one assist shy of a triple-double with nine assists and eight boards. Canada still had chances after the go-ahead free throw, but the U.S. defense survived the final possessions and the horn made 77–76 official. Sixteen years between world titles The United States won the first women’s wheelchair basketball World Championship in 1990 and its second in 2010. Ottawa makes three. The gap matters because this was not a program strolling back into a familiar seat. The Netherlands had won the previous two world titles, and the U.S. had not even reached a world final since 2010. That history made the last minute feel heavier. Team USA did not need a comfortable ending. It needed one more point, one more stop and one more possession that did not belong to Canada. Now LA 2028 looks different The U.S. women won Paralympic silver in Paris in 2024 after bronze in Tokyo. Now the same broader program enters the next Paralympic cycle as the reigning world champion. Eleven of the twelve players on the Ottawa roster had previous Paralympic wheelchair basketball experience, while 18-year-old Arelle Middleton brought Paralympic experience from track and field. A home Paralympics is still two years away, which is forever in roster time. But world gold changes the starting point. Team USA is no longer chasing proof that it can get back to the top. Ottawa just supplied the receipt. Does the 2026 world title change how you view Team USA heading toward LA 2028? Who was the championship-game difference maker: Zurbrugg’s 26 points, Ryan’s all-around line or the final defensive stand? What part of the veteran core should Team USA protect most as the roster evolves? Shak’s bite: one point, sixteen years Canada erased the lead. The building was ready for one more swing. Courtney Ryan made one free throw, the U.S. got the stop, and sixteen years disappeared at the horn. World champions again. Sometimes the whole meal is one point. items.title: Seven Passports, One Playbook: Are the Liberty the Post FIBA Finals Sleeper?
items.type: Story · SNACK SHAK BYTE · NEW YORK LIBERTY
items.keywords: Seven Passports, One Playbook: Are the Liberty the Post FIBA Finals Sleeper? New York sent a league-high seven players to the World Cup, then came out of the break and beat No. 1 Minnesota 93–81 on the road. The Liberty are 25–16 and sixth in the current playoff order. The sleeper question just got its first receipt. Post World Cup reset · Updated after NYL 93, MIN 81 SNACK SHAK BYTE · NEW YORK LIBERTY byte wnba-return SNACK SHAK BYTE · NEW YORK LIBERTY Seven Passports, One Playbook: Are the Liberty the Post FIBA Finals Sleeper? Post World Cup reset · Updated after NYL 93, MIN 81 contain Liberty players Pauline Astier, Marine Johannes, Breanna Stewart, Leonie Fiebich and Raquel Carrera in a national team composite Five Liberty players reached the World Cup semifinals: Pauline Astier and Marine Johannes with France, Breanna Stewart with USA, Leonie Fiebich with Germany and Raquel Carrera with Spain. Graphic via ClutchPoints. New York Liberty United States France Germany Spain China Nigeria Breanna Stewart Marine Johannes Pauline Astier Leonie Fiebich Raquel Carrera Han Xu Elizabeth Balogun Sabrina Ionescu Jonquel Jones New York sent a league-high seven players to the World Cup, then came out of the break and beat No. 1 Minnesota 93–81 on the road. The Liberty are 25–16 and sixth in the current playoff order. The sleeper question just got its first receipt. Player Country World Cup receipt Playoff translation Breanna Stewart United States 12.8 PPG, 7.3 RPG, MVP and gold The closer is already in championship rhythm. Marine Johannes France 14.0 PPG, a tournament-high 20 threes and silver New York needs her range and imagination, not just spot-up minutes. Pauline Astier France 5.7 PPG, 2.7 APG, 58.3% FG and silver A second organizer can keep the offense alive when pressure rises. Leonie Fiebich Germany 9.9 PPG, 8.6 RPG, 3.6 APG and All-Star Five Size, rebounding and connective passing travel in any lineup. Raquel Carrera Spain 8.0 PPG, 5.7 RPG and bronze A physical frontcourt option when playoff matchups get heavy. Han Xu China 18.8 PPG, 10.8 RPG and All-Second Team A matchup breaker, if New York makes room for meaningful minutes. Elizabeth Balogun Nigeria 9.0 PPG, 2.7 RPG and 2.0 steals plus blocks per game Length and activity deepen a defense that may need new answers. This is what a sleeper looks like A team with Breanna Stewart, Sabrina Ionescu and Jonquel Jones should not be able to sneak up on anybody. Yet New York reached the World Cup break at 24 wins and 16 losses, sitting sixth in a crowded playoff race. That seed has become camouflage for a roster with much more championship equity than its place in the standings suggests. No WNBA team sent more players to Berlin. Seven Liberty players represented six countries, and New York had at least one player on each of the four semifinal teams. They did not simply collect passport stamps. They carried offenses, cleaned the glass, created shots and made medal-winning decisions. The World Cup changed the question Stewart returned with gold, a second World Cup MVP award and a 22-point, 10-rebound performance in the final. Marine Johannes returned with silver after leading the tournament with 20 made threes. Leonie Fiebich became the first German player named to a Women's World Cup All-Star Five. Han Xu averaged 18.8 points and 10.8 rebounds. Raquel Carrera helped Spain win bronze, while Pauline Astier and Elizabeth Balogun showed they can make winning plays beyond the roles New York usually gives them. So the question is no longer whether the Liberty have enough talent. Berlin settled that rather loudly. The question is whether New York can bring those fuller versions of its players back into one system without asking everybody to shrink again. The first post-break receipt came in Minnesota The theory got a real test immediately. New York went to Minnesota and beat the top-seeded Lynx 93–81 despite having seven players return from the World Cup. Breanna Stewart led the way with 24 points and 10 rebounds, Sabrina Ionescu added 17 points and six assists, Pauline Astier scored 14, and Marine Johannès added 13 off the bench. That matters because the concern was never whether New York had enough individual talent. It was whether the international versions of these players could come back without shrinking into narrower club roles. Against Minnesota, the Liberty got creation, shooting and closing contributions from several places. They moved to 25–16 and sixth in the current playoff order while handing Minnesota a third straight loss. Can seven international weapons fit one playoff rotation? They can, but being dynamic together does not mean everybody needs more shots. It means more ways to start and finish a possession. Let Johannes bend the floor instead of parking her in the corner. Use Fiebich as a rebounder and connector. Let Han punish smaller lineups. Trust Astier to organize a second unit. Keep Stewart moving through actions instead of making every important possession a rescue mission. There is another advantage hiding in plain sight. While seven teammates competed in Berlin, Ionescu, Jones, Rebekah Gardner and the rest of New York's stay-home group had time to recover. The Liberty are not returning as one tired team. They are combining a rested core with an internationally sharpened one. That can be powerful, if the handoff is clean. The case against the sleeper pick A sixth seed still has to win difficult games away from home. The World Cup players also return with travel in their legs, different terminology in their heads and very little time to rebuild WNBA timing. International confidence can travel overnight. Chemistry usually prefers a connecting flight. Role compression is the larger danger. If New York returns to predictable possessions, watches Stewart and Ionescu create everything, and treats the international breakout performances as souvenirs, the roster will look deep without playing deep. The postseason will punish that gap quickly. Shak's call: 8.2 out of 10 sleeper heat Yes, the Liberty are a real Finals sleeper. They are not the favorite, and the sixth seed is not an accident, but few lower-seeded teams can change style this many ways. New York can play through elite stars, size, shooting, switching, secondary creation or a giant at center. Most opponents can solve one version. A connected Liberty team can keep changing the exam. The world just watched seven Liberty players become more of themselves. If New York lets them stay that way together, sixth place may become the most misleading number in the bracket. Should New York expand Han Xu's playoff role after her 18.8-point, 10.8-rebound World Cup? Can the Liberty preserve Marine Johannes' freedom when the offense returns to its usual hierarchy? Does international success make New York the most dangerous lower seed in the field?
