United States Breanna Stewart Paige Bueckers Jackie Young Angel Reese Kiki Iriafen Rhyne Howard Aliyah Boston Chelsea Gray Napheesa Collier Caitlin Clark Kahleah Copper Sonia Citron Three wins do not mean twelve identical performances. Breanna Stewart sets the standard, Chelsea Gray and Aliyah Boston receive credit the box score misses, and Caitlin Clark’s passing cannot completely erase 30.4 percent shooting. Rank Player W Impact Grade Team impact read 1 Breanna Stewart 94 A USA’s two way anchor leads the team at 18.0 efficiency and 8.3 rebounds per game. 2 Paige Bueckers 92 A Efficient connecting play, 10.3 points, 3.7 assists and 2.6 steals plus blocks per game. 3 Jackie Young 90 A A team high 11.3 points on 53.8 percent shooting, plus the calmest closing possessions. 4 Angel Reese 86 B+ Interior activity produced 8.7 points, 6.0 rebounds and 2.3 steals plus blocks per game. 5 Kiki Iriafen 83 B Seven rebounds and 2.0 steals plus blocks per game created major value in a two game sample. 6 Rhyne Howard 81 B A team high 1.7 steals and a plus 16.0 average margin reflect point of attack pressure. 7 Aliyah Boston 79 B− Interior gravity, screening and a plus 14.7 average margin create value beyond her scoring line. 8 Chelsea Gray 78 B− Pace control and lineup organization matter more than her modest scoring total suggests. 9 Napheesa Collier 76 C+ Switching value and rebounding helped, but her offensive influence was quieter than expected. 10 Caitlin Clark 74 C+ Her team high 6.3 assists lift the offense, but 30.4 percent shooting caps the grade. 11 Kahleah Copper 70 C Rebounding helped, but 21.4 percent shooting left too much offensive value on the table. 12 Sonia Citron 68 C− The 54.5 percent shooting was clean, but a 10.5 minute role cannot outrank larger two way responsibilities. The grade measures impact, not just the box score Team USA finished group play 3 and 0, but a report card should explain how the wins were built, not hand everyone the same gold star. The W Impact Score gives 60 percent of the grade to official FIBA production and 40 percent to role execution, lineup control, defensive responsibility and game context. That distinction matters. A reserve can shoot efficiently in a narrow assignment without carrying the same burden as a starter who organizes possessions, anchors coverages or absorbs the opponent’s best matchup. This is a three game Team USA snapshot, not a career ranking. Stewart sets the curve, Young owns the closer minutes Breanna Stewart earns the top grade because she has been USA’s most complete player. Her 18.0 efficiency rating leads the team, her 8.3 rebounds stabilize the interior and her decisions connect both ends of the floor. Paige Bueckers follows with efficient offense, 3.7 assists and 2.6 combined steals and blocks per game. Jackie Young completes the A tier. She leads USA at 11.3 points per game, is shooting 53.8 percent and delivered the late control that kept Italy from finishing its upset bid. When a game tightened, Young did not blink. Reese, Iriafen and Howard built the pressure layer Angel Reese has supplied the most consistent interior disruption outside Stewart. Her rebounding, hands and physicality translate whether she scores or not. Kiki Iriafen made a similar impact in only two appearances, while Rhyne Howard gave USA the point of attack defense and deflections needed to speed opponents up. Their grades reward repeatable tournament skills. Rebounding travels. Ball pressure travels. Defensive possessions that end without a second chance travel. Why Boston and Gray grade above Citron Aliyah Boston and Chelsea Gray are the clearest examples of why this cannot be a raw efficiency ranking. Boston’s screens, interior positioning and plus 14.7 average margin shape possessions before the box score records anything. Gray organizes spacing, controls tempo and places teammates where their strengths matter. Sonia Citron has been efficient in her 10.5 minutes per game, but the role is smaller and the responsibility is lighter. Clean execution deserves credit. It does not automatically outweigh the burden carried by Boston and Gray. Clark’s passing keeps her afloat, her shooting pulls her down Caitlin Clark leads USA with 6.3 assists per game and owns the team’s best average plus minus. Those are real impact markers. So is 30.4 percent shooting, including 25 percent from three. A 74 is not a dismissal of her playmaking. It reflects the full job. Clark has created quality offense for others, but the missed shots have kept her individual impact below the players delivering on both efficiency and role. What carries into the knockout rounds USA’s 88.7 team composite score reflects a strong unbeaten start with room to sharpen. The safest formula is Stewart as the two way hub, Young as the pressure release, Bueckers as the connector and the Reese, Iriafen, Howard group keeping the defense active. The ceiling rises if Clark’s shot normalizes and Gray’s command begins producing cleaner half court offense. Team USA already has enough talent to win. The report card asks which players are making that talent function. Should lineup control count as heavily as scoring efficiency when grading a tournament team? How high can Clark’s grade climb if her shooting catches up to her passing in the knockout rounds? Shak’s bite: winning earns respect, not automatic A’s A 3 and 0 record tells us Team USA handled the assignment. It does not tell us every player handled the same assignment. Stewart has been the standard, Young has been the closer, and the next jump depends on turning Clark’s creation and Gray’s control into cleaner half court possessions. items.keywords: One Possession From Overtime: How Two Near Upsets Almost Rewrote the World Cup Puerto Rico and Italy lost by five combined points. One more make might have changed the bracket, while Trinity San Antonio left behind the tournament's loudest defensive case. FIBA World Cup · Qualification round FOOD FOR THOUGHT · FIBA WORLD CUP feature FOOD FOR THOUGHT · FIBA WORLD CUP One Possession From Overtime: How Two Near Upsets Almost Rewrote the World Cup FIBA World Cup · Qualification round Trinity San Antonio walking toward the court in her Puerto Rico uniform at the 2026 FIBA Women's World Cup Puerto Rico China Italy Australia France United States Trinity San Antonio Xu Han Isobel Borlase Costanza Verona Gabby Williams Angel Reese Rhyne Howard Puerto Rico and Italy lost by five combined points. One more make might have changed the bracket, while Trinity San Antonio left behind the tournament's loudest defensive case. Five points from a different bracket Puerto Rico came within three points of China, while Italy came within two of Australia. Overtime was one clean possession away in both games, but the losses were built before the final shot. China made 57.1 percent of its twos and closed a 66 to 66 game with the decisive run. Italy erased most of a 26 point deficit, yet spent too much energy repairing three quarters of damage. That makes the what if worth considering. Puerto Rico had the best individual force on the floor in Trinity San Antonio. Italy had all the momentum after a 31 to 13 fourth quarter. Extra time guarantees neither upset, but it could have changed the emotional and tactical terms of both games. San Antonio's case survives Puerto Rico's exit San Antonio finished against China with 24 points, 9 rebounds, 7 assists and 5 steals. Her 5.0 steals per game remain the tournament standard. If Puerto Rico had reached overtime and advanced, one more high leverage defensive moment might have made her the clear favorite for Best Defensive Player. With Puerto Rico out, Gabby Williams carries the strongest active case in the We Know the W Defensive Impact Rating at 96. Angel Reese follows at 92, with Rhyne Howard at 90. San Antonio's elimination changes the runway, not the quality of the résumé. Should team survival matter more than four games of elite defensive disruption? Would Puerto Rico or Italy have controlled overtime after owning the late momentum? items.title: If We Knew Then What We Know Now: The 2024 WNBA Redraft
items.keywords: If We Knew Then What We Know Now: The 2024 WNBA Redraft Two seasons of WNBA evidence changed the board. Caitlin Clark still goes first, Angel Reese jumps to No. 2, Sydney Taylor rockets from undrafted to No. 6, and the international guards force their way up the first round. 2024 Draft class recheck · September 9, 2026 SNACK SHAK BYTE · REDRAFT 50% 38% cover 2024 WNBA Draft night. Photo via WNBA.com. byte SNACK SHAK BYTE · REDRAFT If We Knew Then What We Know Now: The 2024 WNBA Redraft 2024 Draft class recheck · September 9, 2026 Caitlin Clark holds her Indiana Fever jersey on 2024 WNBA Draft night Indiana Fever Los Angeles Sparks Chicago Sky Dallas Wings Washington Mystics Minnesota Lynx Connecticut Sun New York Liberty Atlanta Dream Caitlin Clark Angel Reese Kamilla Cardoso Rickea Jackson Carla Leite Sydney Taylor Leila Lacan Cameron Brink Aaliyah Edwards Jacy Sheldon Isobel Borlase Nyadiew Puoch Two seasons of WNBA evidence changed the board. Caitlin Clark still goes first, Angel Reese jumps to No. 2, Sydney Taylor rockets from undrafted to No. 6, and the international guards force their way up the first round. Redraft pick Player Original 2024 slot The read now 1 Caitlin Clark 1 → 1 Still the first call. Elite creation, range and playmaking keep the Fever right where they started. 2 Angel Reese 7 → 2 The rebounding, production and night to night impact make her the clearest riser into the top tier. 3 Kamilla Cardoso 3 → 3 Size, efficiency and two way value keep the 6 foot 7 center in the exact spot Chicago originally chose her. 4 Rickea Jackson 4 → 4 A polished scoring forward with three level tools. The talent still looks worthy of the fourth pick. 5 Carla Leite 9 → 5 Her growth as a creator pushes her four spots higher and gives Dallas a different answer at guard. 6 Sydney Taylor Undrafted → 6 The class's biggest draft night reversal. An undrafted guard has played her way into the middle of Round 1. 7 Leila Lacan 10 → 7 Defensive pressure, pace and playmaking move the French guard into the top seven. 8 Cameron Brink 2 → 8 The ceiling is still enormous, but a redraft has to weigh availability and the WNBA sample we have actually seen. 9 Aaliyah Edwards 6 → 9 Reliable frontcourt production keeps her safely in Round 1, even as several guards jump past her. 10 Jacy Sheldon 5 → 10 Still a first round guard, but the class has produced more high impact risers than draft night projected. 11 Isobel Borlase 20 → 11 The second round pick earns a first round seat in the redo after proving she belongs in a WNBA rotation. 12 Nyadiew Puoch 12 → 12 The upside and development case keep Atlanta's original final first round slot intact. The top stays Caitlin, but No. 2 changed everything Caitlin Clark is the easy part of this exercise. Indiana had the first pick in 2024 and still makes the same call. The harder question starts immediately after her, because Angel Reese has erased the idea that seventh was the right place for her to wait. Reese moves all the way to No. 2 in this redraft. Her rebounding has become a nightly game plan problem, her offensive responsibility has grown, and her impact is too large to leave outside the first two picks. That move alone reshapes the entire board. Cardoso and Jackson are the rare draft night holds Kamilla Cardoso stays third and Rickea Jackson stays fourth. That is not a lack of movement, it is a compliment to how well those original selections have aged. Cardoso gives Chicago a massive interior presence with two way value. Jackson has shown the scoring package and positional versatility that made her one of the safest offensive prospects in the class. In a redraft full of risers and slides, holding your original top four position is its own receipt. The middle of the round belongs to the risers Carla Leite climbs from ninth to fifth, Sydney Taylor goes from undrafted to sixth, and Leila Lacan moves from tenth to seventh. That is the section of the board that looks most different with hindsight. Leite and Lacan give this class two international guards whose WNBA translation looks stronger now than it did on draft night. Taylor is the loudest story of all. She was not one of the 36 names called in 2024. In this version, Washington takes her sixth. Draft night said undrafted. The floor said first round. Brink at eight is not a talent verdict Cameron Brink dropping from second to eighth will be the pick people argue about most. The defensive ceiling is still obvious, and healthy Brink can change a game without needing touches. But a redraft based on what players have shown in the WNBA has to count availability and sample size alongside upside. That makes eighth a statement about the evidence available today, not a claim that seven players have a higher long term ceiling. Round 1 has two new names Aaliyah Edwards and Jacy Sheldon remain in the first round, but both slide as the risers pass them. Isobel Borlase makes one of the quieter jumps, moving from pick 20 into the No. 11 slot. Nyadiew Puoch stays at 12, preserving Atlanta's original selection. The two original first rounders who fall out are Alissa Pili, originally eighth, and Marquesha Davis, originally eleventh. That does not erase what got them drafted. It shows how quickly a class can reorder itself once projection turns into professional evidence. Shak's takeaway: draft night is the opening sentence The fun of a redraft is not pretending front offices should have known the future. It is seeing which skills translated, which opportunities changed careers, and which players forced the league to reconsider the label attached to them. The 2024 class now has a No. 1 who still looks like No. 1, a No. 7 who looks like No. 2, and an undrafted player who looks like a lottery level selection. That is why the draft matters, but development, health, fit and opportunity get the last word. One important note about the team logos The teams on this redraft board follow the original 2024 first round draft order. They are not the players' current teams. The question is simple: if each franchise could make its 2024 selection again with what we know now, who would it take? Does Angel Reese have the strongest case for the biggest rise in the 2024 class? How high would a fully healthy Cameron Brink go if the redraft were based on ceiling instead of WNBA evidence to date? Is Sydney Taylor the best undrafted success story from this class? Which international guard would you take first today, Carla Leite or Leila Lacan? Draft Night Is a Receipt, Not a Life Sentence Caitlin still goes one. Angel refuses to wait until seven. Carla and Leila move up the line, and Sydney Taylor walks into the first round without ever hearing her name called on draft night. That is the whole point of the redo. Scouts draft projections. The league grades translation. Two years later, this class has handed us a very different receipt. WNBA 2024 Draft Board WNBA 2024 Draft official results WNBA Stats

items.title: Four Months, Four Receipts: Is the Rookie of the Year Race Already Olivia Miles’ ?
items.keywords: Four Months, Four Receipts: Is the Rookie of the Year Race Already Olivia Miles’ ? Olivia Miles has won every Kia Rookie of the Month award available this season. That makes her the clear leader, but Flau'jae Johnson, Sydney Taylor, Azzi Fudd and Kiki Rice still tell us something important about how deep this rookie class really is. Rookie race check · Sept. 2, 2026 FOOD FOR THOUGHT 50% 38% cover Olivia Miles. Official game photography via the Minnesota Lynx. Olivia Miles in a Minnesota Lynx uniform during a game feature FOOD FOR THOUGHT Four Months, Four Receipts: Is the Rookie of the Year Race Already Olivia Miles’ ? Rookie race check · Sept. 2, 2026 Minnesota Lynx Seattle Storm Chicago Sky Dallas Wings Toronto Tempo Olivia Miles Flau'jae Johnson Sydney Taylor Azzi Fudd Kiki Rice Olivia Miles has won every Kia Rookie of the Month award available this season. That makes her the clear leader, but Flau'jae Johnson, Sydney Taylor, Azzi Fudd and Kiki Rice still tell us something important about how deep this rookie class really is. Candidate Current case What keeps the conversation alive 1 Olivia Miles 19.7 PPG, 4.6 RPG, 6.0 APG through 38 games, plus all four Kia Rookie of the Month awards. 2 Flau'jae Johnson 14.1 PPG, 4.8 RPG, 2.9 APG with two way impact, plus the No. 1 W Score on the latest We Know the W Rookie of the Week board. 3 Sydney Taylor 14.7 PPG as an undrafted rookie, one of the best pure scoring stories in the class. 4 Azzi Fudd 13.1 PPG and 1.7 steals per game before a right knee procedure ended her rookie season. 5 Kiki Rice 11.2 PPG, 4.0 RPG and 2.8 APG while carrying real creation responsibility for an expansion team. Four months is a pattern, not a hot streak There is a point in every award race when we have to stop asking who is ahead and start asking what someone else would have to do to catch them. Olivia Miles has reached that point. May belonged to Miles. June belonged to Miles. July belonged to Miles. August belonged to Miles. Four months in the league, four Kia Rookie of the Month awards. The August receipt might be the loudest one yet. Miles averaged 20.6 points, 4.3 rebounds and 6.5 assists for the month. That is not rookie production being graded on a curve. That is lead guard production on a team trying to win the whole thing. The strongest challenger is making the weekly argument Flau'jae Johnson has not matched Miles month for month, but she keeps building the kind of case that survives beyond one statistic. She scores, rebounds, defends and has taken on important possessions for Seattle without looking like the moment is too big. The latest We Know the W Rookie of the Week board is a perfect example. Johnson finished Week 14 at No. 1 with a 29.1 W Score after averaging 19.5 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.0 assists across two games. A weekly board does not decide Rookie of the Year, but it shows who is applying pressure right now. Sydney Taylor is the reminder that draft night is not destiny Sydney Taylor was not drafted. She also entered September averaging 14.7 points per game. Those two sentences belong next to each other because they explain why this rookie class deserves more attention than one trophy race can hold. Taylor's Rookie of the Year path is harder because Miles has the stronger all around case and a full season of monthly hardware, but Taylor has already turned an undrafted label into a footnote. That is a different kind of rookie victory. Azzi Fudd's season ended, her impact did not The No. 1 pick was still firmly in the rookie conversation before right knee soreness led to a season ending arthroscopic procedure. Fudd finished her year at 13.1 points, 1.7 rebounds, 1.8 assists and 1.7 steals per game, while shooting 39.7 percent from three. Availability matters in an award race, especially against a player producing at Miles' level across a longer season. Still, Fudd's rookie year gave Dallas shooting, point of attack defense and a historic All Star weekend moment when she became the first rookie to win the WNBA three point contest. Kiki Rice has the expansion tax Kiki Rice's numbers do not jump off the page the way Miles' do, but context matters. Toronto is building a team and an identity at the same time, and Rice has been asked to create inside that uncertainty. An 11 point scoring average with rebounding and playmaking responsibility is a strong foundation for a first year guard. The Rookie of the Year ballot is not a projection award, so upside alone cannot move Rice ahead of Miles today. But if we are asking which rookies look like long term franchise pieces, Rice belongs in the conversation. So, is there still a race? Technically, yes. Basketball still has games left, and awards should not be handed out before the schedule is finished. Practically, Olivia Miles has built a gap that now requires an extraordinary closing argument from everyone behind her and a real decline from Miles herself. The better question might be what kind of Rookie of the Year season we are watching. Miles is not simply leading rookies in a weak class. She is putting up nearly 20 points and six assists a night for Minnesota while sweeping the league's monthly rookie awards. That makes this less about whether she belongs at the top and more about how high her rookie season will eventually sit in WNBA history. What I am watching next The weekly archive matters now because it can show us whether the gap is tightening before a season average catches up. If Johnson keeps stacking No. 1 weekly W Scores, if Taylor keeps scoring at this level and if Rice closes with a bigger creation load, the race gets more interesting even if the favorite does not change. For now, the ballot starts with Olivia Miles. The rest of the rookie class is not disappearing behind her. It is giving us several different versions of what a successful first season can look like. items.title: Golden State Takes the Apron, Minnesota Gets Served
items.keywords: Golden State Takes the Apron, Minnesota Gets Served Golden State swept a four-game week, Atlanta answered one ugly loss by serving Minnesota another, and Angel Reese grabbed enough rebounds to stock the pantry. Games from Aug. 24 through 30, 2026 50% 38% cover Golden State game action from August 24. Photo via the Golden State Valkyries. Cecilia Zandalasini shoots against Minnesota byte Golden State Takes the Apron, Minnesota Gets Served Games from Aug. 24 through 30, 2026 Golden State swept a four-game week, Atlanta answered one ugly loss by serving Minnesota another, and Angel Reese grabbed enough rebounds to stock the pantry. Golden State Valkyries Up 4 29 wins, 11 losses. Golden State went 4 wins and 0 losses, beat Minnesota by 14, held New York to 60 points, and closed the week on a four-game streak. The Valkyries own this week’s apron. Atlanta Dream Same 26 wins, 14 losses. Atlanta went 2 wins and 1 loss, with Angel Reese setting rebounding records before the Dream handed Minnesota its second straight defeat. The Portland loss keeps them out of the top spot. Las Vegas Aces Same 27 wins, 13 losses. Las Vegas beat Toronto, 93 to 73, for a third straight win, but losing NaLyssa Smith for the season changes the championship recipe. Minnesota Lynx Down 3 31 wins, 9 losses. The league leaders lost to Golden State and Atlanta, their second pair of consecutive losses this season. Still the best full-season record, but not the best plate this week. Indiana Fever Down 1 26 wins, 14 losses. Indiana scored 111 against Connecticut as Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell delivered 34 points apiece. One scorching win was not enough to hold off bigger weeks above them. Dallas Wings Up 2 24 wins, 16 losses. Dallas extended its winning streak to four and finished the week by routing Connecticut, 97 to 71. The Wings are heating up at exactly the right time. Washington Mystics Same 24 wins, 16 losses. Washington reached sixth in the standings after Georgia Amoore’s career-high 25 points against Phoenix, then let an 11-point halftime lead escape against Los Angeles. New York Liberty Down 2 24 wins, 16 losses. New York split two games, scoring a season-low 60 against Golden State before beating Chicago. The bounce-back helped, but the Valkyries matchup is now a real concern. Los Angeles Sparks Up 2 15 wins, 25 losses. Los Angeles lost to Atlanta, then beat Washington and Seattle. Two straight wins and three victories in four games finally put some spark back in the pan. Portland Fire Same 16 wins, 24 losses. Portland stopped Atlanta’s four-game streak behind Carla Leite and Emily Engstler, then lost by 17 to Golden State. Dangerous, inconsistent, and never bland. Phoenix Mercury Up 1 14 wins, 26 losses. Phoenix lost to Washington before blowing out Toronto, 101 to 69. One family-sized win cannot erase a 3 win, 7 loss stretch. Chicago Sky Down 3 15 wins, 25 losses. Chicago lost both games and has dropped three straight. The contender-upset flavor from the prior edition cooled fast. Seattle Storm Up 2 8 wins, 32 losses. Seattle beat short-handed Toronto before losing to Los Angeles. The record is rough, but Flau’jae Johnson and Dominique Malonga keep giving the rebuild something worth tasting. Connecticut Sun Same 10 wins, 30 losses. Connecticut went 1 win and 3 losses and surrendered 208 points across its final two games. Aaliyah Edwards’ 26 against Dallas was one bright bite in a difficult week. Toronto Tempo Down 2 11 wins, 29 losses. Toronto lost all three games by a combined 64 points and enters the break on a four-game skid. The injury-shortened roster has reached the expansion wall. Facts on the bottom Golden State produced the week’s only 4 win, 0 loss record and moved to 29 wins and 11 losses, two games behind Minnesota. The Valkyries beat the Lynx, Sun, Liberty, and Fire, holding Minnesota to a season-low 66 points and New York to a season-low 60. Minnesota remains first in the official standings at 31 wins and 9 losses, but the Lynx lost consecutive games to Golden State and Atlanta. Las Vegas, Atlanta, and Indiana are next at 27 wins, 26 wins, and 26 wins. New York, Washington, and Dallas are tied at 24 wins and 16 losses. The main course, Golden State stole the apron Facts first: Golden State beat Minnesota, 80 to 66, Connecticut, 89 to 64, New York, 79 to 60, and Portland, 86 to 69. The Valkyries defeated the league leader, swept the Liberty season series, and won the second night of back-to-back games in New York. Snack Shak opinion: that is the best week any contender served. Golden State’s defense is not garnish. It is the whole cast-iron skillet. Until somebody proves they can score comfortably against it in a playoff series, the Valkyries belong in the championship conversation with Minnesota, Atlanta, Las Vegas, and Indiana. Players who brought the flavor Angel Reese grabbed a WNBA single-game record 26 rebounds with 11 points against Los Angeles, passing Chamique Holdsclaw’s record of 24. The performance also pushed Reese past A’ja Wilson’s single-season rebounding record. Six days later, Reese recorded her 29th double-double of the season, another WNBA record, as Atlanta beat Minnesota. Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell scored 34 points apiece in Indiana’s 111 to 91 win over Connecticut. Clark added 12 assists, and both guards shot 12 of 19. Two cooks, one kitchen, 68 points, no leftovers. Cecilia Zandalasini scored 18 against Minnesota and 20 against New York during Golden State’s sweep. Veronica Burton added 13 assists without a turnover against the Liberty, while the Valkyries held New York to 30.2 percent shooting. Carla Leite scored 26 points and Emily Engstler added a career-high 25 as Portland upset Atlanta, 101 to 83. Nneka Ogwumike closed Los Angeles’ two-win finish with 23 points and 12 rebounds against Seattle. Olivia Miles scored 21 against Atlanta and passed Seimone Augustus for the most points by a Lynx rookie. She finished the game with 749 rookie-season points. Injury and roster radar Las Vegas announced that NaLyssa Smith will miss the remainder of the season after a non-contact left leg injury. Smith was averaging 11.7 points and 6.4 rebounds while leading the league at 63.8 percent from the field. The Aces signed 6 foot 7 center Kalani Brown to a rest-of-season hardship contract. Atlanta signed six-time All-Star and two-time champion DeWanna Bonner after her contract with Phoenix ended. Bonner debuted against Minnesota. The Dream released Jaylyn Sherrod and waived Aaliyah Nye while making room for the veteran addition. Los Angeles waived Kate Martin on Aug. 29. Toronto cycled through seven-day help while playing without Brittney Sykes and Aneesah Morrow, both already ruled out for the season. Olivia Miles took a hard fall on a late driving layup against Atlanta and was slow to rise, but she walked off under her own power. No diagnosis or confirmed absence had been announced as of Aug. 31, so this is a watch item, not a declared injury. Did Golden State’s 4 win, 0 loss week make the Valkyries the league’s most trustworthy playoff team right now? Should back-to-back losses knock Minnesota from the top power-ranking spot even while the Lynx own the best overall record? Is Angel Reese’s record-breaking rebounding season enough to put her into the MVP top three? Can Las Vegas replace NaLyssa Smith’s efficiency well enough to win another championship? Which 24 win team would you trust most in a playoff series: New York, Washington, or red-hot Dallas? The Valkyries’ Four-Burner Takeover Welcome back to Snack Shak, where the food gets seasoned, the rankings get debated, and everybody gets served. Golden State just turned on all four burners. Burner one, the Valkyries held Minnesota to a season-low 66 points. Burner two, Connecticut got served by 25. Burner three, New York scored only 60 while Cecilia Zandalasini dropped 20. Burner four, Portland lost by 17. That is four games, four wins, and one defense locking the pantry after every possession. Facts on the bottom, spice on top: Minnesota still owns the league’s best record, but Golden State cooked the best plate this week. So here is the debate: are the Valkyries the team nobody wants in a playoff series, or are we over-seasoning one perfect week? I say the apron is theirs until somebody takes it. Keep your takes spicy and your turnovers low. items.title: Atlanta Sets the Table, Minnesota Owns the Kitchen
items.keywords: Atlanta Sets the Table, Minnesota Owns the Kitchen Atlanta swept a statement week, Minnesota kept its grip on the league, Chicago crashed the contender party, and the playoff table became considerably less polite. Games from Aug. 17 through 23, 2026 50% 38% cover Dallas–Seattle game action. Photo via the Dallas Wings. Dallas Wings guard Paige Bueckers dribbles against Seattle byte Atlanta Sets the Table, Minnesota Owns the Kitchen Games from Aug. 17 through 23, 2026 Atlanta swept a statement week, Minnesota kept its grip on the league, Chicago crashed the contender party, and the playoff table became considerably less polite. Minnesota Lynx Same 31 wins, 7 losses. Minnesota won both games and extended its streak to six. The Lynx remain the league’s deepest, steadiest, and best seasoned plate. Atlanta Dream Up 4 24 wins, 13 losses. Atlanta went 3 wins and 0 losses, beat Las Vegas, demolished Los Angeles, defeated Phoenix, and clinched a playoff berth. Nobody brought more heat this week. Las Vegas Aces Up 1 26 wins, 13 losses. The Aces recovered from a 97 to 82 loss to Atlanta with two straight victories. A’ja Wilson remains the ingredient that can rescue almost any recipe. Indiana Fever Down 1 25 wins, 14 losses. Indiana split four games, lost to Dallas and New York, then poured in 113 points against Chicago. The offense is elite, but the week exposed defensive questions. Golden State Valkyries Down 3 25 wins, 11 losses. Golden State finished the week with consecutive losses, including a 73 to 70 defeat against Chicago. The full season remains excellent, but the pan cooled quickly. New York Liberty Down 1 23 wins, 15 losses. New York lost to Chicago before defeating Indiana, 109 to 102. Leonie Fiebich’s return immediately made the Liberty look more balanced. Washington Mystics Same 22 wins, 15 losses. Washington went 2 wins and 1 loss, then clinched its first playoff berth since 2023 behind Shakira Austin’s career night in Portland. Dallas Wings Same 22 wins, 16 losses. Dallas defeated Indiana and Seattle, with Paige Bueckers delivering a historic shooting performance. The Wings finally found some crunch around the edges. Chicago Sky Up 2 15 wins, 23 losses. Chicago beat New York and Golden State before Indiana ended the run. Two wins over contenders make this the week’s best gate crasher story. Portland Fire Down 1 15 wins, 22 losses. Portland dropped both games, including a painful late collapse against Washington. Carla Leite keeps producing, but the playoff door is nearly closed. Los Angeles Sparks Up 1 13 wins, 24 losses. Los Angeles finished the week with a win over Connecticut, but the victory was overshadowed by Dearica Hamby’s ejection and Raegan Beers leaving with a jaw injury. Phoenix Mercury Down 2 13 wins, 24 losses. Phoenix lost its only game of the week to Atlanta and has dropped two straight. Adding scoring has not solved the defensive recipe. Toronto Tempo Up 2 11 wins, 26 losses. Toronto finally ended a 12 game losing streak, but season ending injuries to Brittney Sykes and Aneesah Morrow turned celebration into concern. Connecticut Sun Same 9 wins, 27 losses. Connecticut managed one victory in three games, then lost to Los Angeles. The offense still makes every possession feel like cooking without a stove. Seattle Storm Down 2 7 wins, 31 losses. Seattle lost its only game of the week by 22 in Dallas and has dropped three straight. The season is now entirely about development and evaluation. Facts on the plate Minnesota leads the official standings at 31 wins and 7 losses, with six consecutive victories and a 9 win, 1 loss record over its last ten games. Golden State remains second in the standings, while Las Vegas, Atlanta, Indiana, New York, and Washington have also clinched playoff berths. Atlanta produced the week’s cleanest team performance. The Dream beat Las Vegas, Los Angeles, and Phoenix to finish 3 wins and 0 losses. Chicago supplied the surprise, defeating both New York and Golden State before losing to Indiana. The main course, Atlanta is done asking for attention The Dream did not sneak through this week. They kicked in the kitchen door. Atlanta beat Las Vegas by 15, overwhelmed Los Angeles, and finished the sweep with a 99 to 89 victory over Phoenix. That run moved Atlanta to 24 wins and 13 losses and secured a playoff berth. The factual case is strong, three victories, quality opponents, and sustained scoring. The Snack Shak opinion is spicier, Atlanta belongs in the championship conversation right now, not in the waiting room outside it. Players who brought the flavor Paige Bueckers scored 32 points on 12 of 16 shooting against Seattle and made all six of her three point attempts. That tied the WNBA record for the most threes made in a game without a miss. Natasha Cloud erupted for a career high 35 points, nine rebounds, and six assists as Chicago defeated New York, 93 to 86. She became the first Sky player to record at least 35 points, five rebounds, and five assists in one game. Shakira Austin produced a career high 31 points with 10 rebounds as Washington defeated Portland, 105 to 100, and clinched a playoff berth. Kiki Iriafen added 18 points and 10 rebounds. Kelsey Mitchell scored 37 points against Dallas and extended her WNBA record to 21 consecutive games with at least 20 points. Caitlin Clark answered Chicago with 37 points and 10 assists in Indiana’s 113 to 90 victory. A’ja Wilson finished the week with 27 points, seven rebounds, and seven assists against Toronto, helping Las Vegas secure an 88 to 78 victory. Injury and roster radar Toronto announced that Brittney Sykes and Aneesah Morrow will miss the remainder of the season. Sykes sustained a left foot injury and Morrow injured her left knee during Toronto’s victory over Portland. Neither injury is expected to require surgery. Leonie Fiebich returned from a foot injury and supplied 20 points, five rebounds, and five assists in New York’s win over Indiana. Satou Sabally remained away from the Liberty while dealing with lingering effects from a head injury. Dearica Hamby was ejected after receiving a flagrant foul for striking Connecticut rookie Raegan Beers in the face. Beers left with a jaw injury, and the league may review the incident further. Is Atlanta now the second most trustworthy championship contender behind Minnesota? Should Golden State’s full season excellence outweigh consecutive losses to end the week? Can Indiana win a title while allowing opponents to keep pace with its explosive offense? Did Chicago reveal a real late season identity, or was this simply one beautifully seasoned week? How much pressure should fall on Paige Bueckers after Dallas lost Azzi Fudd and entered the stretch run needing consistency? The Dream’s Three Alarm Peach Cobbler Welcome back to Snack Shak, where Atlanta just pulled a three alarm peach cobbler out of the oven! First scoop, the Dream walked into Las Vegas and won by 15. Second scoop, Los Angeles got served the family sized portion. Third scoop, Atlanta beat Phoenix, finished the week undefeated, and clinched a playoff seat. That is not a cute little hot streak. That is contender crust, MVP level filling, and championship seasoning around the edges. Minnesota still owns the kitchen, but Atlanta is standing at the counter with a spoon and absolutely no interest in waiting its turn. So here is the spicy question, are the Dream really the league’s second best team right now, or did they simply catch everybody before the oven timer went off? Either way, this cobbler is hot, and the playoff table just got crowded. items.title: Indiana Turns Up the Heat
items.keywords: Indiana Turns Up the Heat Indiana brought the full three course feast, Minnesota remained the head chef, and Washington discovered that Las Vegas keeps a fire extinguisher specifically for hot streaks. Games from Aug. 10 through 16, 2026 50% 38% cover Indiana–Atlanta game action from August 16. Photo via the Indiana Fever. Indiana Fever guard Kelsey Mitchell drives against Atlanta byte Indiana Turns Up the Heat Games from Aug. 10 through 16, 2026 Indiana brought the full three course feast, Minnesota remained the head chef, and Washington discovered that Las Vegas keeps a fire extinguisher specifically for hot streaks. Minnesota Lynx Same 29 wins, 7 losses. Minnesota beat Portland and Las Vegas while improving to 15 wins and 2 losses on the road. Still the league’s most complete meal. Golden State Valkyries Same 24 wins, 9 losses. Golden State extended its winning streak to five by routing Chicago, 91 to 71, despite missing key rotation players. Quietly terrifying. Indiana Fever Up 3 23 wins, 12 losses. Indiana swept New York, Dallas, and Atlanta. Four straight victories have moved the Fever from exciting contender to legitimate championship threat. Las Vegas Aces Up 1 24 wins, 12 losses. Las Vegas ended Washington’s seven game streak twice before falling to Minnesota. The veteran machinery remains dangerous. New York Liberty Down 1 22 wins, 14 losses. New York recovered from a 106 to 92 loss to Indiana with victories over Los Angeles and Connecticut. Its depth is carrying the team through significant absences. Atlanta Dream Up 1 21 wins, 13 losses. Atlanta crushed Connecticut by 35 before losing an overtime thriller to Indiana. Strong, but still searching for consistency against the league’s top teams. Washington Mystics Down 4 20 wins, 14 losses. Las Vegas swept the two game series and cooled Washington’s seven game streak. A win over Los Angeles stopped the slide. Dallas Wings Same 20 wins, 15 losses. Dallas completed a season sweep of Toronto, then surrendered 98 points to Indiana. Injuries matter, but a stretch of 3 wins and 7 losses raises real concerns. Portland Fire Same 15 wins, 20 losses. Portland pushed Minnesota before beating Seattle and Phoenix. The Fire may be outside the playoff field, but nobody should want them on the schedule. Phoenix Mercury Up 3 13 wins, 23 losses. Phoenix beat Los Angeles but surrendered an eight point fourth quarter lead to Portland during Diana Taurasi’s jersey retirement night. Chicago Sky Down 1 13 wins, 22 losses. Chicago lost badly to Golden State and split two close games with Seattle. Still alive mathematically, but the burner is barely on. Los Angeles Sparks Down 1 12 wins, 22 losses. Los Angeles competed with New York before falling to Washington. Four straight losses have left the Sparks serving cold leftovers. Seattle Storm Up 2 7 wins, 30 losses. Seattle snapped an 11 game losing streak with 97 points against Chicago, then lost two games by a combined four points. Small progress still counts. Connecticut Sun Down 2 8 wins, 25 losses. Connecticut lost by 35 to Atlanta and by seven to New York. Its offense remains the plain oatmeal of this week’s rankings. Toronto Tempo Down 1 10 wins, 23 losses. Toronto has lost ten consecutive games. The expansion wall is now reinforced concrete. This week’s plate The Fever delivered the week’s strongest statement by defeating New York, Dallas, and Atlanta while scoring at least 95 points in every game. Minnesota continued to set the league’s standard, Golden State quietly collected its fifth consecutive victory, and Portland strengthened its case as the most dangerous team currently outside the playoff picture. Minnesota continued to lead the league with 29 wins and 7 losses, followed by Golden State with 24 wins and 9 losses. Indiana climbed within half a game of third place Las Vegas, while eighth place Dallas maintained a six game cushion over Portland. The main course, Indiana is no longer just promising The Fever entered the week surrounded by questions about whether their explosive offense could consistently defeat playoff caliber opponents. Three victories later, Indiana supplied a rather loud answer. Caitlin Clark recorded 29 points and 10 assists against Dallas before producing 26 points and nine assists in Indiana’s 95 to 91 overtime win over Atlanta. Kelsey Mitchell extended her WNBA record single season streak to 19 consecutive games with at least 20 points. Mitchell provides the reliable scoring pressure. Clark controls the pace and creates opportunities. Aliyah Boston gives Indiana a steady interior option. Together, they have transformed the Fever into something more dangerous than a fun offensive team. Indiana now looks capable of surviving different types of games, and that matters much more in the playoffs than simply piling up regular season points. Players who brought the flavor Olivia Miles continued to make her rookie season look suspiciously veteran. She finished with 23 points and eight assists in Minnesota’s 92 to 87 victory over Las Vegas. Napheesa Collier added 19 points, while Natasha Howard contributed 13 points and 11 rebounds. Minnesota did not merely beat another contender, it demonstrated how many different players can carry the plate. A’ja Wilson still delivered 32 points and seven rebounds in the loss. Las Vegas may have fallen short, but Wilson reminded everyone that a close playoff game can change quickly when she starts demanding the ball. Golden State received an unexpected burst from Tiffany Hayes, who scored a season high 22 points in only 17 minutes during the Valkyries’ 91 to 71 win over Chicago. Golden State was missing Kiah Stokes and Janelle Salaün, yet still won by 20. That is the kind of depth that travels well in the postseason. Allisha Gray poured in 32 points against Indiana, while Angel Reese produced 15 points, 14 rebounds, and six assists. Atlanta had two opportunities to win at the end of regulation but could not convert, allowing the Fever to take control in overtime. Portland rookie Carla Leite added another chapter to her impressive season by playing through discomfort and finishing with 21 points and five assists against Phoenix. The Fire erased an eight point fourth quarter deficit and escaped with an 88 to 85 victory. Injury and roster radar Indiana added veteran center Mercedes Russell through a season ending injury exception after Damiris Dantas underwent surgery for a torn meniscus. Russell brings size, frontcourt flexibility, and experience from two WNBA championship teams. Clark briefly left the Dallas game after appearing to turn her ankle, but she returned after halftime, finished with 29 points and 10 assists, and played in the following game against Atlanta. It remains something to watch, but it was not a confirmed absence. New York continued to navigate more serious concerns. Satou Sabally stepped away from the team while experiencing lingering effects from a head injury. Sabrina Ionescu missed the Connecticut game with a foot issue, while Leonie Fiebich remained unavailable. Dallas faced Indiana without Azzi Fudd, Jessica Shepard, and Aziaha James. Shepard appeared to be approaching a return, but Fudd remained sidelined with a right knee injury. Portland added Nigerian international Amy Okonkwo on a rest of season hardship contract, while Toronto signed guard Zaay Green to a player development contract. Does Indiana have two legitimate MVP candidates in Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell? Is Golden State being overlooked because Minnesota has been so dominant? Did Las Vegas expose Washington as a hot team that is still one tier below the true championship contenders? Can Dallas be trusted in the playoffs while injuries and recent defensive struggles continue to pile up? Is Portland building the strongest long term foundation among the league’s newest teams? The Three Course Fever Feast Welcome back to Snack Shak, where the rankings are hot and Indiana just ordered the full three course meal! First course, the Liberty. The Fever dropped 106 points and sent New York home with a doggie bag. Second course, Dallas. Caitlin Clark served 29 points and 10 assists, while Kelsey Mitchell kept her historic scoring streak cooking. Then came dessert in Atlanta, an overtime win that pushed Indiana’s streak to four. Minnesota still owns the kitchen, and Golden State has reservations at the championship table. But Indiana is no longer serving promising young team. This is contender cuisine. Can Clark, Mitchell, and Aliyah Boston keep feeding everybody during the playoffs, or will an experienced defense finally send the check? Either way, the Fever are cooking, and somebody forgot to turn off the stove. Official WNBA standings Fever and Dream recap Fever and Wings coverage Lynx and Aces recap WNBA transactions

Two Finals coaches, two paths Karl Smesko brings 26 college seasons and an unbeaten 5–0 2026 playoff run to Atlanta’s first Finals appearance. Natalie Nakase was the 2025 Coach of the Year after guiding an expansion team to a 23–21 record and an inaugural playoff berth; Golden State is back in the Finals after a 32–12 regular season. Was Smesko robbed? For 2025 Coach of the Year, no: Nakase received 53 of 72 votes and Smesko placed second with 15. For 2026, Smesko was shut out despite Atlanta’s 30–14 regular season. That is a credible snub argument, while Cheryl Reeve’s league-best 33–11 and Nakase’s 32–12 remain strong award cases. items.title: The Title Is the Lynx’s to Lose
items.keywords: The Title Is the Lynx’s to Lose Minnesota owns the league’s best record and the deepest résumé, but eight losses have left a scouting report. The real question is which lessons still apply now that Napheesa Collier is back. Playoff picture through Aug. 25, 2026 FOOD FOR THOUGHT feature FOOD FOR THOUGHT The Title Is the Lynx’s to Lose Playoff picture through Aug. 25, 2026 Minnesota owns the league’s best record and the deepest résumé, but eight losses have left a scouting report. The real question is which lessons still apply now that Napheesa Collier is back. Date Who beat Minnesota Score What worked May 9 Atlanta Dream 91–90 A 19-point comeback, five double-digit scorers and clutch rim defense May 17 Chicago Sky 86–79 Physical interior play and a 28–10 bench scoring edge June 13 Las Vegas Aces 100–97 A 32-point first quarter, star shot-making and a 22–7 bench edge June 21 Washington Mystics 84–79 A 12–0 closing run and second-unit pressure July 3 New York Liberty 99–86 Breanna Stewart’s shot creation plus paint and transition pressure July 6 Connecticut Sun 90–89 Brittney Griner’s interior gravity and Kennedy Burke’s late threes Aug. 6 Los Angeles Sparks 89–82 Ball movement, a 46–28 paint advantage and an 8–0 finish Aug. 24 Golden State Valkyries 80–66 Turnover pressure, five scorers in double figures and half-court strangulation Eight losses are a scouting report, not a verdict Minnesota enters the final stretch at 31 wins and 8 losses with the league’s best record and the best overall statistical profile. The Lynx are second in scoring, top three defensively, and sit first in net rating. That is why this title is theirs to lose. It is not a prediction that nobody can beat them. It is a statement about burden of proof. Everybody else has to show it can solve Minnesota repeatedly in a playoff series before Minnesota has to explain anything. The eight teams that have done it once are Atlanta, Chicago, Las Vegas, Washington, New York, Connecticut, Los Angeles and Golden State. The variety matters. There is no single magic trick. Minnesota has been beaten by comeback basketball, bench production, paint pressure, elite individual shot-making, transition scoring, late-game execution and, most recently, suffocating half-court defense. The first six losses need an asterisk The loudest caveat is Napheesa Collier. Minnesota’s first six losses all came before her July 22 season debut. The Lynx were already the league’s best team without their best player, which makes those early defeats useful as film but imperfect as a playoff blueprint. Collier changes the geometry. She gives Minnesota another scorer who can punish switches, another rebounder who ends defensive possessions and another defender who can erase a mistake without the scheme collapsing. The version of Minnesota that Atlanta, Chicago, Las Vegas, Washington, New York and Connecticut beat is not the version a playoff opponent will see if the Lynx are healthy. The two losses that matter most now Los Angeles supplied the first post-Collier warning. The Sparks shot 50 percent, moved the ball for 27 assists, won the paint 46 to 28 and closed the game on an 8 to 0 run. Minnesota’s defense could not simply load up on one creator because the ball kept finding the next advantage. That is a playoff lesson: make the Lynx guard movement, not just a star. Golden State supplied the sharper defensive blueprint. The Valkyries held Minnesota to a season-low 66 points, forced 18 turnovers and used a 14 to 1 fourth-quarter run to break the game open. Veronica Burton had five steals, five Valkyries scored in double figures and no Lynx player scored more than 13. Courtney Williams was out with a right ankle injury, so this was not a full-strength Minnesota backcourt, but the pressure points were unmistakable. Make Minnesota start offense late. Crowd the first action. Turn every loose pass into a possession you do not have to defend. What has actually beaten Minnesota First, somebody has to win the possession battle. Chicago and Washington flipped games with bench production. Golden State created 18 Minnesota turnovers. Los Angeles turned paint touches into assists and second-side attacks. A challenger cannot give the Lynx extra possessions and expect talent to cover the bill. Second, the rim has to matter. Connecticut used Brittney Griner. Los Angeles won the paint by 18. New York repeatedly created advantages inside before spraying the ball back out. Minnesota is too connected defensively to beat with jumpers alone for a full series. The defense has to be made to collapse. Third, closing possessions have to belong to the challenger. Atlanta came back from 19 down. Washington ended on a 12 to 0 run. Connecticut hit late threes. Los Angeles finished 8 to 0. Golden State broke open the fourth quarter. Minnesota’s consistency means a good first 35 minutes is only an invitation to lose respectably. Which playoff teams can reproduce the recipe? Golden State has already shown the most repeatable defensive formula: length at the point of attack, multiple switchable defenders and enough balanced scoring that Minnesota cannot hide a weaker matchup. Las Vegas has the most obvious late-game answer in A’ja Wilson and Chelsea Gray. Atlanta has the size, athleticism and multiple creators to turn a series physical. New York has Breanna Stewart and Jonquel Jones, which means it can manufacture elite possessions even when the first action dies. Indiana can make any opponent survive an offensive track meet, Washington has already shown it can win with young legs and bench pressure, and Dallas has enough shot creation to make a favorite uncomfortable now that its playoff ticket is punched. None of that changes the hierarchy. It only explains why the bracket is not a coronation route. The verdict Minnesota should be the championship favorite. The record says it. The net rating says it. The roster says it. Collier’s late arrival makes the full-strength version more dangerous than the season-long record can even show. But the eight losses have left ingredients on the counter for everybody else. Pressure the guards. Win the paint. Bring more than one creator. Get real production from the bench. Close the game instead of merely surviving it. A contender probably needs three or four of those things in the same night, and then needs to repeat the recipe in a series. That is why the title is the Lynx’s to lose, not the Lynx’s to be handed. Is Golden State’s defensive pressure the most repeatable playoff blueprint against Minnesota? How much should the six pre-Collier losses matter when judging the current Lynx? Which playoff opponent can combine paint pressure, perimeter shot-making and bench production for an entire series? Would Minnesota’s biggest vulnerability be a team with one unstoppable star, or a team with five interchangeable threats? The Lynx Plate Is Still the One to Beat Minnesota still owns the kitchen, but eight teams have left recipe cards on the counter. Atlanta brought the comeback. Chicago brought the bench. Vegas brought star power. Washington brought the late squeeze. New York and Connecticut attacked the paint. Los Angeles kept the ball moving. Golden State turned the whole thing into a pressure cooker. The problem for everybody else is that most of those recipes were cooked before Napheesa Collier even walked into the restaurant. So yes, the title is the Lynx’s to lose. But if somebody can mix Golden State pressure, Los Angeles ball movement and Vegas-level shot creation in the same pan, Minnesota might finally have to share the stove. items.title: A’ja and Taurasi Stand Alone in the WNBA’s 25-Point Century Club
items.keywords: A’ja and Taurasi Stand Alone in the WNBA’s 25-Point Century Club The headline is true when career means regular season plus playoffs, but the stat deserves a clean label: Wilson has 99 regular-season 25+ point games and 16 more in the postseason, putting her comfortably beyond 100 combined WNBA games. Scoring milestone audit through Aug. 23, 2026 MILESTONE MOMENTS 50% 38% cover Photo: Jordan Jones / NBAE, via the Las Vegas Aces August 23 game gallery. A’ja Wilson attacks the basket against Toronto on August 23, 2026 feature MILESTONE MOMENTS A’ja and Taurasi Stand Alone in the WNBA’s 25-Point Century Club Scoring milestone audit through Aug. 23, 2026 The headline is true when career means regular season plus playoffs, but the stat deserves a clean label: Wilson has 99 regular-season 25+ point games and 16 more in the postseason, putting her comfortably beyond 100 combined WNBA games. A’ja Wilson 25+ point games Total What the number means Regular season 99 Current total through Aug. 23, 2026 Playoffs 16 Career postseason games with at least 25 points Combined WNBA career 115 Regular season plus playoffs Diana Taurasi regular-season benchmark 140 The long-standing regular-season standard First, clean up the stat The viral graphic says A’ja Wilson has joined Diana Taurasi as the only players in WNBA history with 100 career 25-point games. The spirit of the claim is right, but the definition matters. Current regular-season game logs put Wilson at 99 games with at least 25 points through her 27-point performance in Toronto. She also owns 16 postseason games with at least 25, giving her 115 when regular-season and playoff games are combined. So Aug. 23 was not Wilson’s 100th regular-season 25-point game. It was another high-level scoring night that pushed the conversation back into view. The clean version is even more interesting: Wilson is one regular-season 25-point performance away from a separate 100-game threshold, while her full WNBA résumé has already cleared the century mark. One hundred is not a hot streak Wilson scored 27 points, grabbed seven rebounds and handed out seven assists in Las Vegas’ 88 to 78 win over Toronto on Aug. 23. It looked like a normal A’ja line because she has made abnormal production routine. Twenty-five points once is a heater. Doing it across triple-digit career games is a body of work. The threshold sits in a useful middle ground: career scoring totals reward longevity, while single-game records reward explosions. Repeated 25-point games measure how often a player can carry premium scoring volume without needing a once-in-a-lifetime night. The regular-season chase is now one game away Official Aces historical notes listed Wilson at 80 career regular-season games with at least 25 points at the end of the 2025 regular season, behind Diana Taurasi’s 140. Wilson has stacked 19 more in 2026 through the Toronto game, bringing the regular-season total to 99. That means the next 25-point night has its own clean milestone attached to it: 100 in the regular season. Taurasi remains the historical benchmark, but Wilson is now the only active player sitting on the doorstep of triple digits. The postseason strengthens the case Wilson has already produced 16 playoff games with at least 25 points, including eight during Las Vegas’ 2025 championship run. Add those to her 99 regular-season games and the combined career count is 115. That distinction is worth preserving rather than flattening. Regular-season and playoff records answer different questions. One measures sustained production across the calendar. The other measures whether that scoring travels when opponents have time to scheme for you. Wilson has volume in both columns. Different routes to the same rare air Taurasi built her scoring résumé through unmatched perimeter confidence, longevity and a career spent treating difficult shots like suggestions. Wilson’s route is more interior-out. She can overpower a smaller matchup, face up a slower big, live at the foul line and now stretch defenses farther from the rim than she did early in her career. The comparison does not require pretending they are the same scorer. The milestone is compelling precisely because they are not. Two completely different offensive ecosystems have produced sustained scoring volume that almost nobody else has matched. History keeps arriving during a title chase Las Vegas left Toronto at 26 wins and 13 losses with its playoff berth secured. Wilson’s 27-point, seven-rebound, seven-assist night was not ceremonial scoring after the race was decided. The Aces still need every bit of her production while fighting for seeding and trying to make another postseason run. That is the strange thing about Wilson’s résumé now. History keeps arriving in the middle of normal business. A milestone flashes on the screen, everybody applauds, and then the next possession still asks her to switch onto a guard, clean the glass and go get another bucket. Should regular-season and playoff scoring milestones always be displayed separately? Which is more impressive: Taurasi’s longevity at 140 regular-season 25-point games or the pace at which Wilson is approaching 100? How should Wilson’s two-way workload change the way her scoring milestones are evaluated? At what point does Wilson’s combination of peak dominance and accumulating volume reshape all-time WNBA conversations? Count the Plates Before You Serve Them A’ja Wilson is absolutely in the century club, but Snack Shak checks the receipt before the plate hits the table. Regular season? Ninety-nine 25-point games. Playoffs? Sixteen more. Combined? One hundred fifteen. So the viral graphic has the right destination, but it skipped a turn on the way there. The fun part is that A’ja is now one regular-season 25-point night away from another clean milestone anyway. No need to season the number when the actual résumé already tastes this good. items.title: DeWanna Bonner Chooses Atlanta. The Dream Were Already Dangerous.
items.keywords: DeWanna Bonner Chooses Atlanta. The Dream Were Already Dangerous. Phoenix gave DeWanna Bonner the freedom to chase one more title. Atlanta gave her a team that did not need rescuing, only another veteran who knows exactly what playoff basketball asks for. Atlanta playoff push · Aug. 26, 2026 ROSTER SHAKEUP 50% 38% cover DeWanna Bonner signing announcement. Courtesy of the Atlanta Dream. Atlanta Dream signing announcement featuring DeWanna Bonner feature ROSTER SHAKEUP DeWanna Bonner Chooses Atlanta. The Dream Were Already Dangerous. Atlanta playoff push · Aug. 26, 2026 Atlanta Dream Phoenix Mercury DeWanna Bonner Angel Reese Allisha Gray Rhyne Howard Phoenix gave DeWanna Bonner the freedom to chase one more title. Atlanta gave her a team that did not need rescuing, only another veteran who knows exactly what playoff basketball asks for. What Atlanta adds Bonner brings Why it matters in a series Playoff experience 15 postseason appearances and two WNBA championships Atlanta adds a player who has already lived through every version of a long playoff run Frontcourt flexibility 6-foot-4 size with guard-forward mobility Bonner can play next to Angel Reese or slide across bigger wing and forward matchups Rebounding 6.1 rebounds per game with Phoenix in 2026 Extra possessions matter more when every postseason possession gets expensive Bench scoring 10.6 points per game in 2026 Atlanta does not have to ask its stars to carry every second-unit minute Late-season urgency A veteran explicitly freed to chase a title The move arrives with Atlanta already in the playoff field rather than trying to sneak into it Phoenix opened the door. Atlanta walked through it. DeWanna Bonner's 2026 season changed direction in less than forty-eight hours. Phoenix and Bonner agreed to a contract buyout on Monday, with the Mercury framing the move as an opportunity for the six-time All-Star to pursue a title in what could be her final postseason. By Wednesday, ESPN's Alexa Philippou reported that Atlanta had signed Bonner to a $116,000 contract. The destination matters because Atlanta is not a desperation landing spot. The Dream entered Wednesday at 25 wins and 13 losses, already holding a playoff berth and sitting fourth in the league standings. Bonner is joining a team with something to protect, not something to invent. The Dream did not need a savior. They added playoff insurance. Atlanta already has a clear identity. Allisha Gray gives the Dream perimeter scoring and two-way steadiness. Rhyne Howard supplies shot creation, length and defensive disruption. Angel Reese controls the glass so violently that she just set a WNBA single-game record with 26 rebounds and pushed the single-season rebounding record even higher. This is already a team that can win with pace, size, second chances and multiple creators. That is exactly why Bonner fits. Atlanta does not need her to be the first option. It needs her to survive playoff possessions that turn ugly. It needs another 6-foot-4 body that can rebound, switch, attack a mismatch and score without needing the entire offense built around her. It needs somebody who can play twenty minutes one night and thirty-two the next without the role becoming the story. Her 2026 numbers are not the headline. Her postseason résumé is. Bonner averaged 10.6 points and 6.1 rebounds in 37 games for Phoenix this season. Her 39.4 percent shooting and 26.2 percent mark from three are real caveats; Atlanta is not adding a perfect floor spacer. The value is broader than that one column. Bonner is a two-time WNBA champion, a six-time All-Star and the only three-time Sixth Player of the Year in league history. She is the WNBA's all-time postseason rebounding leader and has appeared in 15 postseasons. Last year alone, she came off the bench during Phoenix's run to the Finals and became the only player in league postseason history to record at least 90 points, 60 rebounds and 10 steals as a reserve in one postseason. That kind of utility is hard to manufacture in September. The most interesting fit is next to Angel Reese. Reese is the gravitational force on the glass. Bonner gives Atlanta another long rebounder who can operate outside the paint and defend multiple frontcourt shapes. Together, they can make the Dream enormous without making them stationary. One can crash while the other leaks into transition. One can switch onto a wing while the other protects the possession by ending it with the rebound. There is also a quieter benefit. Reese does not need to carry every physical matchup for forty minutes. Bonner has spent seventeen WNBA seasons learning where playoff contact arrives and how officials let games change in September. For a team with championship ambition, that knowledge is not sentimental. It is rotational depth. Atlanta's problem is now finding minutes, which is a contender problem. The Dream already have established scorers, rebounders and role players. Adding Bonner means somebody's minutes will tighten. That can create friction on an ordinary team. On a contender, it can also create matchup options. Atlanta can choose size against Minnesota, extra switching against Golden State, another veteran creator against Las Vegas, or a more physical frontcourt against New York. Bonner's arrival does not guarantee anything. Minnesota still owns the league's best record, Golden State has built the league's most disruptive defensive identity, and Las Vegas has A'ja Wilson. But Atlanta just added one of the most postseason-tested players in league history without needing her to become the center of the team. That is the kind of move contenders get to make when the foundation is already strong. The verdict: the Dream just became harder to solve. Phoenix gave Bonner a clean exit from an eliminated team. Atlanta gave her a playoff seat with a real chance to matter. The transaction works because the motivations line up: Bonner gets another shot at a title, and Atlanta gets a veteran who can help without asking the Dream to become something different. The Dream were already dangerous. Now the bench has another scorer, the frontcourt has another rebounder, the locker room has another champion, and the coaching staff has another piece to move around the board. Atlanta did not make a rescue move. It made a luxury move. Those are usually the ones that become very annoying in May, June and July. In September, they can become the difference between a good season and a parade. Should Bonner close games for Atlanta, or is her best value as a matchup-dependent sixth player? Does Bonner's rebounding and playoff experience matter more than her declining three-point percentage? Which contender matchup benefits Atlanta most from adding another 6-foot-4 veteran forward? Did Atlanta just become the most complete challenger to Minnesota? Atlanta Added a Veteran to an Already Full Plate Phoenix cleared the table and DeWanna Bonner went straight to a kitchen that was already serving. Atlanta did not need a new head chef. It already has Allisha Gray cooking, Rhyne Howard bringing the heat, and Angel Reese grabbing every plate before it hits the floor. Bonner is the veteran sous-chef who has worked fifteen postseason dinner rushes and already owns two championship recipes. The three-point seasoning has been light this year, but the rebounding, size and playoff memory still travel. Atlanta was already dangerous. Now the Dream have one more ingredient nobody wants to deal with in a seven-game series. A’ja Wilson sweeps the top two awards, Olivia Miles owns the rookie race, Natalie Nakase stays in the Coach of the Year seat, and one crowded 94 point tie decides the First Team. 2026 WNBA awards · W Composite edition FOOD FOR THOUGHT · 2026 MOCK AWARDS feature FOOD FOR THOUGHT · 2026 MOCK AWARDS The Grades Made Their Case: Shak’s 2026 WNBA Mock Awards 2026 WNBA awards · W Composite edition contain We Know the W 2026 mock WNBA awards card with A'ja Wilson as MVP and Defensive Player of the Year, Olivia Miles as Rookie of the Year, Megan DiLeo as Most Improved Player, Janelle Salaün as Sixth Player of the Year and Natalie Nakase as Coach of the Year We Know the W mock ballot using W Composite grades through September 16, 2026. A’ja Wilson sweeps the top two awards, Olivia Miles owns the rookie race, Natalie Nakase stays in the Coach of the Year seat, and one crowded 94 point tie decides the First Team. Award Pick Composite receipt The case MVP A'ja Wilson 96 · A+ The highest grade on the board, with 26.0 points, 9.4 rebounds and a 32.0 PER. Defensive Player A'ja Wilson 96 · A+ · 2.0 BPG The same player who drives the offense also protects the rim at an award level. Rookie of the Year Olivia Miles 95 · A+ The top rookie grade and second best grade in the entire league. Most Improved Megan DiLeo 60 to 87 · plus 27 The largest meaningful year over year W Score jump among established rotation players. Sixth Player Janelle Salaün 85 · B+ · 0 starts Starter quality production and efficiency delivered entirely from a reserve role. Coach of the Year Natalie Nakase Golden State · 29 and 11 The Valkyries sit second overall, two games off the league lead, with a four game winning streak. All WNBA First Team A'ja Wilson · Olivia Miles · Aliyah Boston · Jackie Young · Natasha Howard 96 · 95 · 94 · 94 · 94 The top two scores plus three selections from the five player 94 point tie. All Rookie Team Olivia Miles · Kiki Rice · Pauline Astier · Lauren Betts · Azzi Fudd 95 · 87 · 85 · 83 · 81 The five highest rookie grades on this editorial board. Start with the score, then make the ballot The W Composite is the base layer. It blends league relative percentiles for PER, true shooting, scoring, assists, rebounding, steals and blocks, win shares per 40 and assist to turnover ratio. The scale runs from 55 to 99, and players with small samples are marked provisional. A formula can organize the conversation, but it should not pretend to finish it. Award categories have their own rules. Role matters for Sixth Player. Year over year growth matters for Most Improved. Team performance and problem solving matter for Coach of the Year. The score gives us the receipts, then Shak makes the basketball call. A’ja Wilson owns both ends of the headline Wilson is the only player at 96, and the gap is not created by one loud category. She is averaging 26.0 points and 9.4 rebounds with a 32.0 PER and 62.0 percent true shooting. That is an MVP résumé before the defense enters the room. Then the defense enters anyway. Wilson is averaging 2.0 blocks while carrying the largest offensive burden on this board. Giving her both MVP and Defensive Player of the Year is not double counting. It is recognizing that the league’s best composite season is elite on both sides of the floor. Olivia Miles turns the rookie race into a leaguewide statement Miles does not merely lead rookies. Her 95 is the second highest W Score in the league. Through 38 games she is producing 19.7 points, 6.0 assists and 4.6 rebounds with 60.8 percent true shooting. That makes Rookie of the Year the simplest choice on the board. Kiki Rice, Pauline Astier, Lauren Betts and Azzi Fudd complete the All Rookie group, but Miles is playing on a different shelf. The role awards reward real change Megan DiLeo moves from a 60 in 2025 to an 87 in 2026. The leap is backed by 13.2 points per game, a 19.7 PER and 64.7 percent true shooting in a much larger role. Most Improved should reward the player whose game became meaningfully more valuable, not simply the player who received more minutes. DiLeo did both. Janelle Salaün earns Sixth Player with an 85 grade, 12.9 points per game and no starts. Her case is exactly what the category is supposed to capture: a reserve whose production changes the level of a good team without needing a starter label. Natalie Nakase stays in the Coach of the Year seat Golden State is 29 and 11, second overall, two games behind Minnesota, riding a four game winning streak and carrying an 8 and 2 record over its last ten. That is the profile of a team that has built answers across a long season. Nakase remains the pick because the Valkyries keep translating depth, role clarity and defensive commitment into wins. Coach of the Year should ask which team most consistently looks prepared for the problem in front of it. Golden State keeps answering yes. The 94 point tie needs an editorial tiebreaker Aliyah Boston, Caitlin Clark, Jackie Young, Natasha Howard and Paige Bueckers all carry a 94. There are only three First Team places left after Wilson and Miles, so the composite cannot separate the entire group by itself. This ballot takes Boston, Young and Howard. Boston supplies interior efficiency and two way value. Young gives the lineup another creator, elite shooting efficiency and size at guard. Howard supplies frontcourt mobility, 7.7 rebounds, 1.7 steals and a 23.0 PER across 40 games. Clark and Bueckers are not outside because their seasons were weak. They are outside because a five player tie has to be broken somewhere, and this version favors lineup balance and two way coverage. Would your 94 point tiebreaker favor Caitlin Clark’s creation, Paige Bueckers’ scoring balance or the two way combination of Jackie Young and Natasha Howard? Can any defensive candidate overcome A’ja Wilson’s value at both the rim and the center of Las Vegas’ offense? Does Golden State’s closing stretch strengthen Natalie Nakase’s Coach of the Year case enough to make her the clear choice? The score starts the argument. It does not get the last word. A ballot without numbers is just a feeling. A ballot made only by numbers is just a spreadsheet. The W Composite tells us where the cases begin. Jackie Young runs Shak’s All FIBA Starting Five, Gabby Williams brings the havoc, Stewie brings the MVP, Emma Meesseman brings the tournament’s loudest efficiency, and the Bench Mob is loaded enough to start an argument by itself. United States France Germany Belgium Puerto Rico Türkiye China Mali Japan Spain Australia Hungary Jackie Young Gabby Williams Leonie Fiebich Breanna Stewart Emma Meesseman Trinity San Antonio Sevgi Uzun Angel Reese Xu Han Sika Kone Ramu Tokashiki Iyana Martin Steph Talbot Nyara Sabally Janelle Salaun Dorka Juhasz One World Cup, sixteen names, three tiers. Jackie Young runs Shak’s All FIBA Starting Five, Gabby Williams brings the havoc, Stewie brings the MVP, Emma Meesseman brings the tournament’s loudest efficiency, and the Bench Mob is loaded enough to start an argument by itself. Group Player Country Tournament case Starting Five Jackie Young USA 12.3 PPG, 3.7 RPG, 3.2 APG, plus 18 points, 6 rebounds and 5 assists in the final Starting Five Gabby Williams France 18.7 PPG, 4.0 APG, 2.8 SPG, All-Star Five and Best Defensive Player Starting Five Leonie Fiebich Germany 9.9 PPG, 8.6 RPG, 3.6 APG and an All-Star Five place Starting Five Breanna Stewart USA 12.8 PPG, 7.3 RPG, first two time Women's World Cup MVP Starting Five Emma Meesseman Belgium 21.0 PPG and 25.0 EFF, tournament leader in scoring and efficiency Bench Mob Trinity San Antonio Puerto Rico 15.5 PPG, 4.8 APG and a tournament best 5.0 SPG Bench Mob Sevgi Uzun Türkiye 17.7 PPG and a tournament best 8.3 APG Bench Mob Angel Reese USA 7.2 PPG, 5.0 RPG and 2.5 offensive rebounds per game in a compact role Bench Mob Xu Han China 18.8 PPG, 10.8 RPG and 21.8 EFF Bench Mob Sika Kone Mali 16.0 PPG, 10.3 RPG and 60.6 percent shooting Bench Mob Ramu Tokashiki Japan Tournament leader at 2.3 blocks per game Honorable Mention Iyana Martin Spain Rising Star, All-Star Five, 17.5 PPG, 4.2 APG and 2.2 SPG Honorable Mention Steph Talbot Australia 13.8 PPG, 8.6 RPG, 4.4 APG and 21.0 EFF Honorable Mention Nyara Sabally Germany 12.1 PPG, 6.0 RPG and All-Second Team recognition Honorable Mention Janelle Salaun France 11.2 PPG, 5.8 RPG and All-Second Team recognition Honorable Mention Dorka Juhasz Hungary 12.6 PPG, 10.4 RPG and a tournament double double The five I would actually start Jackie Young gets the ball first. Her championship game made the case even louder, but the fit is what seals it. Young can organize, defend and score without needing every possession. Gabby Williams gives the backcourt a second creator and the tournament's most disruptive perimeter defender. Leonie Fiebich adds size, rebounding and connective passing on the wing. Breanna Stewart is the automatic frontcourt choice after another gold medal and a second World Cup MVP. Emma Meesseman gets the final spot because lineup balance matters more to me than copying the official awards sheet. She led the tournament in scoring and efficiency while still creating for teammates. That is too much offense, size and intelligence to leave outside the first five. The Bench Mob would change the game Trinity San Antonio and Sevgi Uzun give the second unit pressure at both ends. San Antonio led the tournament in steals, while Uzun led it in assists. Angel Reese is there to turn one missed shot into another possession. Xu Han supplies a true interior scorer. Sika Kone brings efficient power, and Ramu Tokashiki gives the group a tournament leading rim protector. That is the point of a Bench Mob. The second unit should not imitate the starters. It should introduce a new problem. This one can speed the game up, dominate the glass, pound the paint or lock down the rim depending on what the matchup needs. Honorable mention is not a consolation prize Iyana Martin was brilliant enough to make the official All-Star Five and win Rising Star while carrying Spain to bronze. Steph Talbot did everything for Australia. Nyara Sabally helped Germany make history. Janelle Salaun was central to France's first finals run, and Dorka Juhasz left Berlin averaging a double double. There was no clean top ten in Berlin. There were too many players with real cases, which is exactly why the honorable mention group belongs on the board instead of disappearing beneath the cut line. Would you start Emma Meesseman over Iyana Martin if the goal is lineup balance rather than matching FIBA's official five? Which Bench Mob player would force her way into your closing five first? Did Iyana Martin do enough to make your first group despite Jackie Young's championship finish? Shak’s bite: this roster would be rude Jackie organizes it, Gabby wrecks it, Fiebich connects it, Stewie closes it and Emma makes every matchup uncomfortable. Then Trinity, Sevgi, Angel, Xu Han, Sika Kone and Ramu Tokashiki walk in off the bench. That is not a rotation. That is an international problem. items.keywords: One Streak. One Drought. One Trophy: USA vs France for the World USA brings 35 straight World Cup wins and a 71 game run across World Cup and Olympic play. France brings the tournament's biggest average scoring margin and its first World Cup final. Paris 2024 was one point. Berlin gets the rematch. France brings the tournament's biggest average scoring margin and its first World Cup final. Paris 2024 was one point. Berlin gets the rematch. Dynasty meets the team with the loudest margin USA enters the title game with 35 consecutive World Cup wins, four straight World Cup championships and a 71 game winning streak across World Cup and Olympic play. France enters 5 and 0, averaging 96.2 points and winning by 35.6 points per game through the semifinals. Both teams are unbeaten. Only one arrives with eleven world titles. Only one arrives in its first World Cup final. Paris was one point. Berlin gets the rematch. The 2024 Olympic gold medal game ended USA 67, France 66. Now Gabby Williams and France get another championship shot at the Americans, while Breanna Stewart and USA try to make a fifth consecutive World Cup title feel inevitable one more time. Can France's tournament best scoring margin survive USA's depth and late game defense? Does the pressure sit heavier on the program protecting a 35 game streak or the program playing its first World Cup final? Which matters more in one game, USA's history or France's current form? One Streak, One Drought, One Trophy USA walks in with 35 straight World Cup wins and four straight titles. France walks in with zero world titles, but also with the bigger scoring margin in Berlin and a first ever trip to the final. Paris 2024 came down to one point. So no, this is not a coronation. It is a rematch with receipts.
